1.  DOCUMENT PURPOSE & AUTHORITY

1.1 Purpose

master.txt is the single source of truth for the StackSense project.

This document defines the approved product vision, architecture, technology choices, engineering boundaries, implementation contracts, development roadmap, testing requirements, security requirements, operational expectations, and collaboration rules for StackSense.

The purpose of this document is to ensure that:

all developers work against the same architectural contract;
all AI coding collaborators operate from the same specification;
implementation decisions remain consistent across modules;
architectural decisions are not accidentally changed during implementation;
frontend and backend implementations remain compatible;
new contributors can understand the system without reconstructing decisions from previous conversations;
future implementation does not depend on undocumented assumptions;
the project remains consistent with the approved system-design objectives.

This document intentionally contains substantially more detail than a conventional README because it is an implementation specification and architectural contract, not merely project documentation.

1.2 Authority

This document has the highest project-level authority for StackSense implementation decisions.

When implementing StackSense, the following priority order applies:

Explicitly approved decisions recorded in this document.
Explicit contracts and invariants defined in this document.
Existing implementation that demonstrably conforms to this document.
Implementation-level engineering judgment.
Personal preference of an individual developer or AI coding agent.

A lower-priority consideration must never silently override a higher-priority decision.

For example, an implementation agent must not replace:

RabbitMQ with Kafka;
Celery with another task framework;
React Flow with Mermaid;
ELK with another layout engine;
PostgreSQL with another primary persistence system;
the canonical Architecture Model with Neo4j as the source of truth;
deterministic architecture extraction with LLM-generated architecture;
SSE with polling;

merely because the alternative appears simpler, faster, more popular, or more convenient.

Such a change requires explicit architectural approval and an update to this document.

1.3 Single Source of Truth

There must be exactly one active StackSense master specification.

The project must not maintain multiple competing architecture documents that independently claim to define the current system.

If an older project specification, README, design document, conversation, implementation comment, AI-generated plan, or historical ADR conflicts with this document, this document takes precedence unless an explicit approved change has subsequently updated it.

Older documents may be retained for historical or reference purposes, but they must not be treated as authoritative implementation specifications.

The purpose of consolidating the project into one master specification is specifically to prevent developers and AI coding agents from following different versions of the architecture.

1.4 Frozen Decisions

A decision marked as FROZEN is an approved architectural decision.

Frozen decisions are not implementation suggestions.

They are constraints.

Implementation must conform to them unless the decision is explicitly reopened and changed.

Examples of frozen decisions include:

approved technologies;
supported languages and frameworks;
analysis pipeline boundaries;
asynchronous analysis behavior;
RabbitMQ and Celery job architecture;
SSE-based analysis progress;
IR boundaries;
Architecture Model as the canonical architecture source of truth;
Neo4j as an architecture and knowledge projection rather than the canonical source;
Elasticsearch as a search and retrieval infrastructure component;
React Flow plus ELK as the diagram rendering and layout stack;
deterministic architecture extraction;
AI provider abstraction;
graceful degradation requirements;
security boundaries;
repository analysis restrictions.

A developer must not reinterpret a frozen decision simply because an alternative implementation appears easier.

1.5 Contract vs Implementation Detail

Not every statement in this document has the same level of rigidity.

StackSense distinguishes between architectural contracts and implementation details.

Frozen Contract:

A required behavior or architectural boundary.

Example:

"The Architecture Model is the canonical source of architectural truth."

Implementation must preserve this regardless of internal implementation details.

Frozen Technology:

A technology explicitly selected for a particular responsibility.

Example:

"RabbitMQ is the asynchronous message transport."

Replacing it requires explicit approval.

Implementation Detail:

A technical choice left to the implementation phase as long as the architectural contract remains intact.

Examples may include:

internal class naming;
private helper methods;
exact algorithm implementation;
internal caching strategy where not otherwise specified;
exact database indexing strategy;
exact worker class structure.

Implementation details may evolve without requiring an architectural change if they do not violate a frozen contract.

Future Capability:

A capability intentionally planned for later but not required for the current implementation.

Future capabilities must not be implemented prematurely unless explicitly requested.

For example:

Local Storage
↓
Future
↓
S3/Object Storage

does not mean S3 must be implemented in the current MVP.

1.6 AI Coding Agent Authority

AI coding agents are implementation assistants.

They are not architectural decision-makers.

An AI coding agent must:

Read STACKSENSE_MASTER.txt before beginning substantial implementation work.
Identify the relevant section, phase, and module before modifying code.
Follow all applicable frozen contracts.
Reuse existing approved abstractions where they exist.
Avoid introducing technologies that are not approved.
Avoid silently changing architectural boundaries.
Avoid inventing requirements that are not present in this document.
Avoid removing existing behavior merely because it is inconvenient.
Add or update tests for implemented behavior.
Report uncertainty rather than making an architectural assumption silently.
Stop and request clarification when two frozen requirements genuinely conflict.
Explicitly identify any required deviation from this specification.
Never treat generated code as evidence that an architectural decision has been approved.
Never infer approval from the absence of an explicit objection.
Never replace an approved architecture with a personal preference or commonly used alternative.

An AI coding agent must not say, implicitly or explicitly:

"I changed this because it is a better architecture."

unless the change has first been explicitly approved.

AI coding agents are expected to optimize implementation quality within the approved architecture, not optimize the architecture itself.

1.7 No Silent Architecture Changes

The following are considered architectural changes:

replacing a frozen technology;
changing a major data flow;
changing the source of truth;
changing domain boundaries;
changing asynchronous execution strategy;
changing persistence ownership;
changing frontend/backend boundaries;
changing analysis pipeline stages;
changing supported language or framework boundaries;
changing the canonical Architecture Model;
changing AI responsibility boundaries;
changing diagram-generation architecture;
changing tenant or security boundaries;
introducing a major new infrastructure dependency;
removing a frozen subsystem;
moving responsibility from one architectural layer to another;
changing the ownership of persistent state;
changing how derived projections are generated;
changing how analysis results are versioned;
changing how real-time progress is delivered.

Such changes must not be introduced silently through implementation commits.

A change is still architectural even if it is introduced through:

a refactor;
a "cleanup";
a dependency replacement;
a performance optimization;
a temporary workaround;
a migration;
generated code;
an AI-generated pull request.

The mechanism used to introduce the change does not determine whether approval is required.

1.8 Architecture Change Process

When an implementation problem requires a change to a frozen decision, the process is:

Identify Problem
↓
Document Why Existing Contract Is Insufficient
↓
Propose Alternative
↓
Evaluate Architectural Impact
↓
Obtain Explicit Approval
↓
Update STACKSENSE_MASTER.txt
↓
Implement Approved Change
↓
Update Tests and Documentation

The implementation must not precede approval when the change affects a frozen architectural decision.

A developer or AI coding agent may still create a proof of concept or isolated experiment to evaluate an alternative, provided that:

it is clearly marked as experimental;
it does not replace the approved implementation;
it does not become an undeclared project dependency;
it does not modify the canonical architecture;
the experiment is not represented as an approved design.

1.9 Change Requests Must Explain Why

A proposed architectural change must include:

current decision;
problem with the current decision;
why the problem cannot reasonably be solved within the current architecture;
proposed change;
alternatives considered;
effect on existing modules;
effect on data flow;
effect on persistence;
effect on testing;
effect on deployment;
effect on security;
effect on performance;
operational implications;
migration implications;
effect on existing data;
effect on existing APIs;
effect on frontend behavior;
effect on AI behavior;
whether existing implementations must be changed;
whether the change affects other frozen contracts.

A change must not be approved solely because:

"This technology is more popular."

or:

"This implementation is easier."

or:

"This is how most projects do it."

Architectural changes must be evaluated against StackSense's actual requirements and constraints.

1.10 Backward Compatibility of Approved Changes

When a frozen contract is changed, the change must explicitly identify whether it is:

backward compatible;
additive;
migration-required;
breaking.

If the change is breaking, the affected modules and migration steps must be documented before implementation.

Breaking changes must identify at minimum:

affected APIs;
affected database structures;
affected worker jobs;
affected events;
affected frontend consumers;
affected stored artifacts;
affected tests;
affected deployment configuration;
rollback considerations.

A migration must not assume that all existing data can simply be discarded unless data deletion has explicitly been approved.

1.11 No Architectural Drift

Architectural drift occurs when the implementation gradually diverges from the approved architecture without an explicit decision.

Examples include:

Architecture Model
↓
Neo4j
↓
Frontend

being gradually changed into:

Neo4j
↓
Frontend

because querying Neo4j became convenient.

Another example:

API
↓
RabbitMQ
↓
Worker

gradually becoming:

API
↓
Long-running synchronous operation

because the first implementation was easier.

Another example:

Architecture Model
↓
Diagram Specification
↓
ELK
↓
React Flow

gradually becoming:

Architecture Model
↓
LLM
↓
React Flow code

because generating diagrams directly through an LLM appeared faster.

Such drift is prohibited.

When implementation becomes difficult, the correct response is to improve the implementation while preserving the architectural contract, or explicitly reopen the architecture decision.

1.12 Implementation Order

The existence of a frozen architecture does not require every component to be implemented simultaneously.

Components may be implemented incrementally.

However, temporary implementation shortcuts must not become accidental permanent architecture.

If a temporary stub, mock, local implementation, simplified adapter, or placeholder is introduced, it must:

be clearly identified;
preserve the intended interface where practical;
avoid creating a conflicting architecture;
be replaceable without rewriting unrelated domains;
have a clear reason for existing;
not be mistaken for the production implementation.

Example:

Current MVP:
LocalStorageProvider

Future:
S3StorageProvider

The current implementation may use local storage while preserving the storage abstraction required for future migration.

1.13 Documentation Synchronization

Whenever an approved architectural change occurs, this document must be updated as part of the same change process.

The project must not have:

Architecture changed
↓
Implementation changed
↓
Documentation updated "later"

Instead:

Approved Change
↓
Master Specification Updated
↓
Implementation Updated
↓
Tests Updated

This prevents future AI collaborators and developers from implementing obsolete decisions.

If implementation reveals that the specification is inaccurate or incomplete, the discrepancy must be reported rather than silently ignored.

1.14 Conversation History Is Not the Specification

Previous ChatGPT conversations may contain:

discussions;
rejected alternatives;
temporary designs;
outdated implementations;
exploratory ideas;
superseded architecture;
implementation experiments;
abandoned technologies.

They must not be treated as authoritative merely because they occurred earlier.

Only decisions incorporated into the current STACKSENSE_MASTER.txt are authoritative.

If an earlier conversation conflicts with this document, the current document wins.

If a useful decision exists in an earlier conversation but is absent from this document, it must be treated as unconfirmed until explicitly incorporated into the Master Specification.

1.15 Comments and Code Are Not Architectural Approval

Code comments, TODOs, commit messages, branch names, issue descriptions, pull request descriptions, or AI-generated plans do not independently override this specification.

They may describe:

implementation details;
temporary decisions;
technical debt;
proposals;
experiments;
future work.

They do not constitute architectural approval unless the approved change has been incorporated into this document.

Similarly, the existence of a working implementation does not retroactively mean that the architecture was approved.

1.16 Handling Ambiguity

When a requirement is ambiguous but does not conflict with a frozen contract, the implementation agent should:

prefer the simplest implementation consistent with the architecture;
reuse existing project conventions;
avoid introducing new dependencies;
preserve extensibility where the architecture explicitly requires it;
preserve testability;
preserve observability;
document the assumption when it materially affects behavior;
avoid creating a new architectural abstraction unless justified.

When ambiguity could change a frozen architectural decision, the agent must stop and request clarification.

For example:

If the specification says:

"Store repository snapshots locally initially."

the implementation agent may choose a reasonable local directory structure.

It may not interpret this as permission to introduce S3 immediately.

1.17 Handling Conflicting Requirements

If two requirements appear to conflict:

Requirement A
+
Requirement B
↓
Potential Conflict

the implementation agent must not arbitrarily choose one if the conflict affects architecture.

Instead:

Identify Conflict
↓
Explain Both Constraints
↓
Identify Affected Architecture
↓
Identify Possible Resolutions
↓
Request Decision

The conflict should then be resolved by updating this specification if necessary.

When the conflict is purely implementation-level and does not affect a frozen contract, the implementation agent may resolve it using standard engineering judgment and document the chosen interpretation.

1.18 Scope of This Document

This document governs:

product vision;
product boundaries;
architectural principles;
technology stack;
supported languages and frameworks;
repository processing;
artifact classification;
resource limits;
analysis lifecycle;
asynchronous processing;
workers and queues;
analysis engine;
IR;
symbol resolution;
Architecture Model;
graph projection;
knowledge projection;
search;
retrieval;
RAG;
AI integration;
diagrams;
reports;
REST APIs;
SSE;
frontend/backend boundaries;
authentication;
authorization;
multi-tenancy;
storage;
security;
observability;
reliability;
testing;
CI/CD;
deployment;
roadmap;
implementation collaboration rules.

It does not prescribe every private implementation detail.

The objective is:

"Enough specification to prevent architectural hallucination and divergence, without unnecessarily constraining ordinary engineering implementation decisions."

1.19 Core Rule

The fundamental rule for every StackSense implementation is:

"Implement the approved architecture; do not redesign it silently."

If an implementation can satisfy the requirement while preserving the frozen architecture, it should do so.

If it cannot, the architectural decision must be explicitly revisited before changing the implementation.

A technically superior implementation that violates a frozen architectural contract is still an incorrect StackSense implementation until the contract is changed.

1.20 Document Status

Current status:

ACTIVE — MASTER SPECIFICATION

All architectural decisions incorporated into this document are considered authoritative unless explicitly superseded by a later approved revision.

This document is a living specification, but changes require explicit approval and must never occur accidentally through implementation.

The latest approved version of this document represents the current StackSense architecture.

When this document is updated:

obsolete decisions must be replaced rather than left ambiguously active;
superseded decisions should be identified when historical context is useful;
contradictory rules must not remain unresolved;
implementation-impacting changes must identify affected modules;
tests and implementation must eventually converge on the updated contract.

End of Section 1.


2.  PROJECT VISION & PRODUCT DEFINITION

2.1 Project Identity

Project Name:

StackSense

StackSense is an enterprise-oriented software architecture intelligence platform designed to analyze software repositories, reconstruct their architecture, represent that architecture as structured knowledge, and present the resulting understanding through interactive diagrams, searchable evidence, reports, and AI-assisted explanations.

StackSense is fundamentally an architecture intelligence and developer understanding platform.

It is not primarily an AI chatbot.

It is not primarily a code-generation tool.

It is not primarily a static code visualization tool.

It is not merely a documentation generator.

Its primary purpose is to build a reliable, evidence-backed understanding of an existing software system and make that understanding accessible to developers, architects, reviewers, educators, and technical decision-makers.

2.2 Core Product Problem

Modern software repositories contain large amounts of information distributed across:

source code;
directory structures;
classes;
functions;
modules;
API routes;
configuration;
dependencies;
databases;
tests;
documentation;
infrastructure;
message queues;
external integrations;
frontend applications;
backend services.

Understanding how these pieces work together is difficult, especially when:

the repository is unfamiliar;
documentation is incomplete;
the architecture has evolved over time;
multiple frameworks are used;
frontend and backend are separated;
dependencies are indirect;
infrastructure is configured outside application code;
architectural decisions are not explicitly documented.

StackSense addresses this problem by transforming repository evidence into a structured architecture representation and then exposing that representation through multiple interfaces.

2.3 Product Vision

The long-term vision of StackSense is:

Give a developer the ability to provide a software repository and quickly obtain a reliable, navigable, evidence-backed understanding of how that system is structured, how its components interact, why those relationships exist, and where important architectural concerns may exist.

The desired experience is:

Repository
↓
Analysis
↓
Architecture Reconstruction
↓
Interactive Architecture
↓
Knowledge & Search
↓
Evidence
↓
Explanation

The system should make a complex repository understandable without requiring a developer to manually trace the entire codebase.

2.4 Core Product Philosophy

StackSense follows five foundational product principles.

Evidence First

Architecture must be derived from repository evidence.

Deterministic Truth

Important architectural facts must be established through deterministic analysis wherever possible.

AI as an Intelligence Layer

AI assists with explanation, interpretation, summarization, and presentation, but does not become the source of architectural truth.

Interactive Understanding

Architecture should not be presented as a static generated image alone. Users should be able to explore, filter, drill down, search, and inspect evidence.

Graceful Degradation

Failure of an optional subsystem must not destroy capabilities that do not depend on that subsystem.

2.5 StackSense Is Not an LLM-First Product

AI is an important component of StackSense, but StackSense must not be architected around the assumption that an LLM understands the entire repository.

The system must not follow this architecture:

Repository
↓
LLM
↓
"Explain the architecture"

This approach would make the system:

difficult to validate;
difficult to reproduce;
vulnerable to hallucination;
difficult to test;
dependent on a specific model;
expensive for large repositories;
difficult to reason about architecturally.

Instead, StackSense follows:

Repository
↓
Deterministic Analysis
↓
IR
↓
Architecture Model
↓
Knowledge / Graph / Diagram Projections
↓
Evidence Retrieval
↓
AI Explanation

The LLM operates on structured and retrieved evidence rather than being responsible for discovering the entire architecture by itself.

2.6 Primary Product Output

The most important output of StackSense is the Architecture Model.

The Architecture Model represents the system in a structured, versioned, validated, and evidence-backed form.

It becomes the common foundation for:

diagrams;
graph exploration;
search;
knowledge retrieval;
reports;
AI explanations;
architecture comparison;
future analysis capabilities.

The Architecture Model is therefore more important than any individual UI visualization.

2.7 Primary User Experience

The intended high-level user experience is:

User creates or selects a project.
User provides a repository or supported source artifact.
User starts an analysis.
The analysis immediately becomes asynchronous.
The user receives real-time analysis progress.
Background workers continue processing.
Important intermediate results become available progressively.
Initial high-value architecture diagrams become available.
Additional analysis continues in the background where applicable.
The completed Architecture Model becomes available.
Knowledge and search projections become available.
The user can explore architecture interactively.
The user can inspect evidence behind architectural facts.
The user can ask questions using the retrieved knowledge.
AI provides grounded explanations based on evidence.

2.8 Analysis Must Be Asynchronous

Repository analysis is considered a potentially long-running operation.

The frontend must not remain blocked waiting for the complete analysis.

The expected lifecycle is:

User Action
↓
Create Analysis
↓
Return Immediately
↓
Queue Background Work
↓
Workers Process Analysis
↓
SSE Progress Events
↓
Intermediate Results
↓
Final Architecture
↓
Knowledge / Search Completion

The system must be designed to support multiple analyses and concurrent users.

2.9 Real-Time Analysis Experience

The user should be able to observe meaningful analysis progress.

Examples of progress stages may include:

repository acquisition;
artifact discovery;
file classification;
source parsing;
symbol extraction;
dependency analysis;
framework detection;
architecture construction;
architecture validation;
graph projection;
knowledge indexing;
diagram generation;
analysis completion.

The exact internal worker/task structure does not need to be exposed directly to the user.

The public progress experience should use stable semantic events rather than exposing fragile internal implementation details.

2.10 Progressive Results

StackSense should not require every subsystem to finish before presenting anything useful.

Where safe and architecturally consistent, the system may progressively expose completed results.

For example:

Analysis Started
↓
Repository Parsed
↓
Architecture Available
↓
Initial Diagrams Available
↓
Knowledge Search Available
↓
AI Explanation Available
↓
Analysis Fully Completed

Progressive availability must never compromise correctness.

An incomplete or partially indexed result must be explicitly represented as incomplete rather than silently presented as complete.

2.11 Primary MVP Experience

The MVP should focus on demonstrating the following complete flow:

Repository
↓
Analyze
↓
Understand Architecture
↓
Explore Diagrams
↓
Inspect Components
↓
Search Knowledge
↓
Ask Architecture Questions
↓
Receive Evidence-Grounded Explanation

The MVP should prioritize the quality and reliability of this flow over adding a large number of unrelated features.

2.12 Diagram Experience

Interactive diagrams are a major MVP showcase of StackSense.

The system must not limit itself to a single diagram.

The diagram system should maintain a broader catalog of applicable diagram types while initially showing only a small curated set of high-value views.

Potential diagram categories include:

System Overview;
Application Architecture;
Component Dependency;
API Architecture;
Data Flow;
Service Communication;
Module Dependency;
Database Interaction;
Event / Message Flow;
Frontend Architecture;
Backend-Frontend Architecture;
External Integration Map;
Dependency Impact View;
Custom Architecture Exploration;
future deployment architecture;
future security boundary views;
future sequence or interaction views.

Not every repository will support every diagram type.

Diagram eligibility must be determined from the analyzed architecture.

The system must not show empty or meaningless diagram categories when the required architecture evidence does not exist.

2.13 Initial Diagram Strategy

The initial analysis experience should display only a small number of high-value diagrams.

The objective is to avoid overwhelming the user with dozens of diagrams immediately after analysis.

The system should prioritize diagrams that provide the strongest immediate understanding of the analyzed repository.

Additional applicable diagram types should be available through exploration or generated on demand.

Therefore:

Small initial set
+
Broader diagram catalog
+
Lazy generation
=
Rich architecture exploration without excessive initial processing

2.14 Professional Visualization Requirement

The diagram system is an important part of the StackSense product identity.

Generated diagrams must aim for a modern, professional, high-quality visual experience.

The product must not rely on basic text-based Mermaid diagrams as its primary visualization mechanism.

The approved visualization architecture uses:

React Flow for interactive rendering;
ELK for graph layout;
deterministic diagram specifications;
optional AI-assisted presentation intelligence.

The goal is to produce diagrams that feel like a modern architecture intelligence product rather than a basic automatically generated flowchart.

2.15 Diagram Stability

Previously generated diagrams must remain logically stable when unrelated background knowledge processing occurs.

For example:

Initial Architecture
↓
Diagram A

Later:
Documentation indexed
↓
Knowledge enriched

Diagram A must not unexpectedly change simply because additional knowledge was discovered.

If the underlying Architecture Model changes and a new architecture version is created, a new diagram version may be generated.

Diagram generation must therefore be tied to an explicit architecture version and diagram specification.

2.16 Knowledge Experience

The knowledge system exists to make the analyzed repository searchable and explainable.

It may incorporate:

architecture entities;
architecture relationships;
documentation;
source semantic units;
configuration;
API specifications;
tests;
diagnostics;
other approved evidence sources.

Knowledge is derived from the repository and architecture.

It is not an independent source of truth.

2.17 Search Experience

StackSense should support searching across the analyzed system using both textual and semantic understanding.

Search should be capable of answering questions such as:

Where is authentication implemented?
Which service handles user creation?
What depends on UserService?
Where is Redis configured?
Which APIs interact with PostgreSQL?
Which components consume this queue?
Where is this external service used?
Which files implement this architecture component?

The search system should combine lexical and semantic retrieval where appropriate.

2.18 Evidence-Backed Understanding

A central StackSense principle is that users should be able to move from an architectural conclusion back to its supporting evidence.

For example:

UserService
↓
DEPENDS_ON
↓
UserRepository

should be traceable to evidence such as:

source references;
dependency declarations;
configuration;
framework metadata;
relevant tests;
other deterministic analysis results.

The product should avoid presenting unexplained architectural claims whenever supporting evidence can be provided.

2.19 AI Explanation Experience

AI should help users understand the architecture rather than replace the architecture analysis.

Example user question:

"Why does the payment service depend on Redis?"

Expected flow:

User Question
↓
Retrieval
↓
Graph Evidence
↓
Source Evidence
↓
Documentation Evidence
↓
Evidence Planner
↓
Context Builder
↓
LLM
↓
Grounded Explanation

The AI response should be based on retrieved evidence.

If sufficient evidence does not exist, the system should communicate uncertainty instead of inventing an explanation.

2.20 Product Personas

The primary intended personas are:

Backend Engineer

Needs to quickly understand an unfamiliar backend repository, dependencies, services, APIs, databases, and implementation structure.

Software Architect

Needs a high-level architecture representation, dependency relationships, integration boundaries, and evidence for architectural decisions.

Developer / Maintainer

Needs to locate relevant code and understand the impact of modifying a component.

SRE / Infrastructure Engineer

Needs to understand service dependencies, databases, queues, external services, and operational relationships.

DBA / Database-Focused Engineer

Needs to understand how application components interact with databases and data infrastructure.

Technical Lead

Needs a high-level understanding of system structure, technical risks, and architectural dependencies.

Student / Educator

Can use StackSense as a practical system-design and software-architecture exploration tool.

2.21 Core Product Capabilities

The product is expected to eventually provide:

repository ingestion;
repository analysis;
supported language/framework detection;
artifact classification;
source parsing;
IR generation;
symbol and dependency analysis;
Architecture Model generation;
architecture validation;
graph projection;
knowledge projection;
hybrid search;
evidence retrieval;
AI explanations;
interactive diagrams;
architecture reports;
architecture exploration;
analysis history;
architecture versioning;
comparison between architecture versions;
user/project/environment organization;
database connection management;
authentication;
authorization;
scheduling;
notifications;
audit logging;
observability;
operational diagnostics.

Not every capability is required in the first implementation milestone.

The roadmap determines implementation order.

2.22 Product Boundaries

StackSense is focused on understanding software systems.

The following are outside the primary MVP purpose:

general-purpose code generation;
replacing an IDE;
acting as a full software development environment;
automatic modification of repositories without explicit user workflows;
autonomous architectural decision-making;
executing arbitrary repository code as part of normal static analysis;
replacing production monitoring platforms;
replacing enterprise source-control platforms;
functioning primarily as a generic chatbot.

Future integrations may exist, but they must not distort the core product identity.

2.23 Supported Repository Philosophy

StackSense should support multiple common software ecosystems rather than being limited to one programming language.

The initial framework boundary includes major supported ecosystems that have been explicitly approved.

The architecture must therefore be extensible enough to support:

Python;
JavaScript;
JSX;
TypeScript;
TSX;

and their approved frameworks and runtimes.

The supported framework matrix is defined separately in the technology and framework sections of this document.

2.24 Source-to-Understanding Principle

The complete StackSense product can be summarized as:

Source
↓
Evidence
↓
Structure
↓
Architecture
↓
Knowledge
↓
Visualization
↓
Explanation

Each stage has a specific responsibility.

Source provides the raw material.

Evidence establishes what can be supported.

Structure organizes source information.

Architecture represents system-level relationships.

Knowledge makes the information searchable.

Visualization makes the architecture understandable.

Explanation communicates the meaning to the user.

No stage should silently assume the responsibility of another stage.

2.25 Product Quality Definition

A successful StackSense implementation is not defined only by whether it produces a diagram.

Quality is measured by:

architectural correctness;
evidence traceability;
consistency between diagrams and architecture;
reproducibility of deterministic analysis;
useful retrieval;
grounded AI explanations;
professional visualization;
predictable failure behavior;
performance;
security;
testability;
maintainability;
extensibility;
clear system boundaries.

A visually impressive diagram that contains incorrect architecture is considered a failure.

A technically correct architecture model that cannot be understood by the user is also insufficient.

The product must balance correctness, usability, and explainability.

2.26 Core Product Principle

The central product principle of StackSense is:

"Turn software repositories into a reliable, explorable, evidence-backed understanding of their architecture."

Everything implemented in StackSense should ultimately support this objective.

2.27 Section Summary

StackSense is an enterprise-oriented architecture intelligence platform.

Its core flow is:

Repository
↓
Deterministic Analysis
↓
IR
↓
Architecture Model
↓
Graph / Knowledge / Diagram / Report Projections
↓
Evidence Retrieval
↓
AI-Assisted Explanation

The Architecture Model is the central representation.

AI is an enhancement layer, not the source of truth.

Interactive diagrams are a major MVP capability.

The diagram system supports a broad catalog of applicable visualizations while initially presenting only a curated subset.

Analysis is asynchronous and progressively observable.

Knowledge and search are evidence-oriented.

Reports and explanations must remain grounded in the same architectural facts used by the diagrams.

The final product must prioritize correctness, evidence, usability, professional visualization, and architectural integrity over superficial AI functionality.

End of Section 2.


3.  NON-NEGOTIABLE ARCHITECTURAL PRINCIPLES

3.1 Purpose

This section defines the principles that govern every major StackSense architectural decision.

These principles are not optional design preferences.

They exist to ensure that implementation remains consistent as the project grows, multiple developers contribute code, AI coding agents participate in implementation, and additional infrastructure is introduced.

When a lower-level implementation decision conflicts with one of these principles, the implementation must be changed or the principle must be explicitly reopened and approved.

3.2 Deterministic Truth Before AI

StackSense must establish important system facts through deterministic analysis wherever technically possible.

The preferred flow is:

Repository
↓
Deterministic Analysis
↓
Evidence
↓
IR
↓
Architecture Model
↓
AI

AI must not be responsible for discovering fundamental architectural facts that deterministic analysis can establish reliably.

Examples of facts that should primarily be deterministic include:

files;
modules;
classes;
functions;
imports;
dependencies;
API routes;
framework structures;
database connections;
queue/topic relationships when detectable;
architecture entities;
architecture relationships;
source references;
version identifiers.

AI may interpret these facts, summarize them, explain them, or assist with presentation.

It must not silently replace deterministic analysis.

3.3 Architecture Model Is the Canonical Source of Truth

The Architecture Model is the canonical representation of the analyzed software architecture.

It is the authoritative source for architectural facts within StackSense.

The following are projections or consumers of the Architecture Model:

Neo4j;
diagrams;
reports;
knowledge indexes;
retrieval;
API responses;
AI context.

None of these systems may independently become the authoritative architecture source.

The conceptual relationship is:

Architecture Model
├── Graph Projection
├── Knowledge Projection
├── Diagram Projection
├── Report Projection
└── API Projection

3.4 Projections Must Not Become Sources of Truth

Derived systems must remain rebuildable from authoritative inputs whenever practical.

Examples:

Neo4j is a graph projection.
Elasticsearch is a search/retrieval projection.
embeddings are derived data.
React Flow diagrams are visual projections.
generated reports are derived outputs.
AI explanations are generated outputs.

If a derived projection is lost, StackSense should be able to rebuild it from the appropriate authoritative artifacts.

The loss of a projection must not imply the loss of the canonical Architecture Model.

3.5 Evidence Must Be Traceable

Important architectural facts should have provenance.

Where possible, StackSense must be able to answer:

"Why does StackSense believe this relationship exists?"

Evidence may include:

source file;
source location;
import;
function or class reference;
configuration;
framework metadata;
API specification;
test;
documentation;
dependency declaration;
analysis result.

Evidence should be associated with the fact or relationship it supports.

The product must prefer traceable evidence over unsupported assertions.

3.6 Architecture and Presentation Must Be Separate

Architecture semantics must remain independent from visualization.

The Architecture Model should describe:

entities;
relationships;
hierarchy;
metadata;
evidence;
version;
status.

It should not contain presentation-specific information such as:

screen coordinates;
colors;
font sizes;
React Flow-specific state;
zoom level;
UI collapse state;
ELK spacing configuration;
visual layout decisions.

The diagram system transforms architecture semantics into presentation.

Architecture Model
↓
Diagram Specification
↓
ELK
↓
React Flow

This separation ensures that the same architecture can be represented through different visualizations without modifying the underlying architecture.

3.7 Diagram Generation Must Be Hybrid

StackSense uses a hybrid diagram generation architecture.

Deterministic logic is responsible for:

selecting valid architecture entities;
selecting valid relationships;
enforcing identity;
validating graph structure;
ensuring consistency;
controlling architecture-derived semantics.

AI may assist with:

presentation prioritization;
semantic grouping suggestions;
labels;
titles;
visual emphasis;
determining which available information is most useful for a particular user request.

AI must not:

invent architecture entities;
invent architecture relationships;
generate arbitrary architecture facts;
bypass validation;
directly become the source of React Flow nodes;
directly become the source of architecture coordinates.

ELK remains responsible for graph layout.

React Flow remains responsible for rendering and interaction.

3.8 Analysis Is Asynchronous

Repository analysis must be treated as a potentially long-running operation.

The user-facing API must not synchronously wait for the complete analysis pipeline.

The intended model is:

Client
↓
Create Analysis
↓
Immediate Response
↓
Queue
↓
Workers
↓
Analysis Pipeline

This allows:

concurrent analyses;
scalable worker processing;
retries;
progress reporting;
cancellation;
background processing;
fault isolation.

3.9 REST Represents State, SSE Represents Progress

REST APIs provide authoritative resource state.

SSE provides real-time notifications and progress information.

The frontend must not treat SSE as the permanent source of truth.

The conceptual relationship is:

REST
=
Current State

SSE
=
Progress / Notification

If an SSE connection is interrupted, the frontend must be able to reconnect and retrieve authoritative state through REST.

3.10 Background Work Must Be Decoupled From HTTP

Long-running analysis must not depend on the lifetime of the HTTP request that initiated it.

The API creates the analysis/job state and submits background work.

Workers execute the work independently.

This provides:

retryability;
resilience;
scalability;
failure isolation;
better API responsiveness.

3.11 Persistent State Must Have an Authoritative Owner

Every important piece of persistent state must have a clearly defined owner.

RabbitMQ transports messages.

Celery executes tasks.

PostgreSQL stores authoritative application/job state.

Neo4j stores graph projections.

Elasticsearch stores search projections.

Object/local storage stores artifacts.

No transient infrastructure component should silently become the authoritative owner of business state.

11.12 Idempotency

Background operations that can be retried must be designed to tolerate duplicate execution wherever practical.

Examples include:

indexing;
graph projection;
knowledge projection;
diagram generation;
notification generation;
analysis stages.

A retry must not blindly create duplicate architecture entities, graph nodes, search documents, or other derived artifacts.

Operations should use deterministic identifiers, version boundaries, and idempotent writes where appropriate.

3.13 Versioned Architecture

Architecture results are versioned.

An Architecture Version represents a specific analyzed architectural state.

Historical versions must not be silently mutated.

If a new analysis changes the architecture:

Architecture V1
↓
Architecture V2

rather than:

Architecture V1
↓
mutated into V2

This enables:

historical inspection;
architecture comparison;
reproducibility;
stable diagrams;
auditability;
regression detection.

3.14 Versioned Projections

Derived projections must be associated with the architecture or analysis version they represent.

Examples:

Graph Projection V12;
Diagram V12;
Knowledge Projection V12.

A projection must not silently mix information from unrelated architecture versions.

Historical information may be intentionally queried, but it must be explicitly version-aware.

3.15 No Silent Mixing of Versions

StackSense must avoid situations where:

Architecture V1
+
Knowledge V2
+
Diagram V3

are presented as though they represent one current architecture.

Version relationships must be explicit.

Current-state queries should retrieve mutually compatible artifacts.

Historical queries may intentionally combine historical information only when the requested operation explicitly requires it.

3.16 Graceful Degradation

StackSense must fail at the smallest possible layer.

Optional subsystem failure must not unnecessarily bring down the entire platform.

Examples:

LLM unavailable
↓
AI explanation unavailable
↓
Architecture still works

Elasticsearch unavailable
↓
Search unavailable/degraded
↓
Architecture still works

Neo4j unavailable
↓
Graph exploration degraded
↓
Canonical Architecture Model remains intact

Diagram generation fails
↓
Diagram unavailable
↓
Architecture/report/search may continue

One source file fails to parse
↓
That artifact is marked failed
↓
Other analyzable artifacts continue where safe

Critical foundation failures are different.

For example:

Repository acquisition failure
↓
Analysis cannot begin

Architecture validation failure
↓
Invalid architecture must not be published as valid

3.17 Partial Results Must Be Explicit

StackSense may expose partial results when safe.

However, partial results must never be represented as complete.

The system must distinguish states such as:

queued;
running;
partially completed;
completed;
completed with warnings;
failed;
cancelled.

A user must be able to understand whether an architecture or knowledge result is complete.

3.18 Failures Must Be Observable

Failures must not disappear silently.

Where a stage fails, StackSense should preserve enough diagnostic information to determine:

what failed;
when it failed;
which analysis was affected;
which stage was running;
whether retry is possible;
whether partial results remain valid;
whether user intervention is required.

User-facing errors should remain safe and understandable.

Internal diagnostics may contain additional technical information subject to security and secret-redaction requirements.

3.19 Security by Default

Security must be treated as a foundational architectural concern.

The system follows:

least privilege;
zero trust;
defense in depth;
secure defaults;
server-side authorization;
tenant isolation;
secret protection.

Security cannot depend solely on frontend behavior.

The backend must independently enforce authorization and resource ownership.

3.20 Untrusted Repository Principle

Repositories submitted to StackSense must be considered untrusted input.

Static analysis must not execute arbitrary repository code as part of normal analysis.

StackSense must not blindly execute:

package installation scripts;
post-install scripts;
setup scripts;
Makefiles;
arbitrary shell scripts;
repository-provided executables;
build hooks.

unless an explicitly isolated and separately approved execution subsystem exists.

Repository acquisition and extraction must also defend against malicious archives and unsafe paths.

3.21 Least Privilege

Each subsystem should receive only the permissions required for its responsibility.

Examples:

analysis workers should not automatically have unrestricted infrastructure access;
frontend clients should not access databases directly;
AI providers should not receive unnecessary credentials;
repository analysis should not automatically receive host-level permissions;
workers should not receive credentials unrelated to their tasks.

Permissions should be scoped according to responsibility.

3.22 Secrets Must Remain Outside Normal Data Flows

Secrets must not become ordinary application data.

Sensitive values include:

database passwords;
API keys;
JWT signing secrets;
OAuth secrets;
cloud credentials;
LLM provider keys;
internal service credentials.

Secrets must not be intentionally included in:

logs;
frontend responses;
embeddings;
knowledge documents;
AI prompts;
reports;
diagrams;
error messages.

Sensitive information must be redacted where it can accidentally appear in diagnostics.

3.23 AI Must Be Provider-Agnostic

StackSense must not be tightly coupled to one AI provider.

The architecture uses provider abstractions.

Conceptually:

AI Service
↓
Provider Interface
├── Gemini
├── Ollama
└── Future Providers

The application should depend on the provider interface rather than provider-specific SDK behavior throughout the codebase.

This allows:

provider replacement;
local development;
fallback providers;
cost optimization;
experimentation;
future model upgrades.

3.24 AI Is Optional Infrastructure

Core StackSense functionality must not require an LLM to remain operational.

The system should continue providing deterministic capabilities such as:

repository analysis;
Architecture Model;
architecture validation;
graph projection;
diagram generation;
reports;
search where available;

even if an AI provider is unavailable.

AI enhances understanding.

It does not determine whether the underlying architecture exists.

3.25 AI Must Be Evidence-Grounded

AI explanations must be based on retrieved evidence.

The preferred flow is:

User Question
↓
Retrieval
↓
Evidence Planner
↓
Context Builder
↓
LLM
↓
Explanation

The LLM should not be given an expectation to reconstruct the entire repository from memory or from an unstructured dump.

When evidence is insufficient, the system should communicate uncertainty rather than fabricate a confident answer.

3.26 Retrieval and Reasoning Are Separate

The following responsibilities must remain distinct:

Retriever:

Find potentially relevant evidence.

Evidence Planner:

Select the evidence required to answer the question.

Context Builder:

Organize selected evidence into structured AI context.

LLM:

Generate the natural-language explanation.

Renderer:

Present the explanation to the user.

This separation improves:

testing;
observability;
provider independence;
explainability;
debugging;
retrieval quality.

3.27 Hybrid Retrieval

Search should not rely exclusively on semantic embeddings.

StackSense should support a combination of:

lexical relevance;
semantic relevance;
architecture relevance;
evidence strength;
source authority;
version relevance;
metadata filters.

This allows both exact technical searches and conceptual questions to work effectively.

3.28 Derived Data Must Be Rebuildable

Derived systems should be considered rebuildable wherever practical.

Examples include:

embeddings;
Elasticsearch indexes;
Neo4j projections;
diagram caches;
generated reports.

The canonical source should remain recoverable independently.

This allows operational actions such as:

Delete Index
↓
Rebuild Index
↓
Continue Using Canonical Data

without requiring complete repository re-analysis.

3.29 Frontend and Backend Separation

The frontend must interact with StackSense through approved backend interfaces.

The frontend must not directly access:

PostgreSQL;
Neo4j;
Elasticsearch;
RabbitMQ;
worker internals;
secret stores;
internal filesystem paths.

The frontend communicates through:

REST APIs;
SSE;
approved future frontend-specific interfaces.

Business rules that affect authorization, resource ownership, architecture correctness, or security belong on the backend.

3.30 Backend Layering

The backend should preserve clear responsibility boundaries between:

API/presentation;
application services;
domain logic;
interfaces/ports;
infrastructure.

Infrastructure-specific concerns must not unnecessarily leak into domain logic.

For example:

Domain
↓
LLMProvider Interface
↓
GeminiProvider

rather than:

Domain
↓
Gemini SDK

The same principle applies to:

storage;
search;
graph databases;
queues;
external APIs;
AI providers.

3.31 Explicit Ownership of Responsibilities

Every major capability must have a clear owner.

Examples:

Repository ingestion:
Ingestion subsystem

Parsing:
Analysis subsystem

IR:
Analysis/IR subsystem

Architecture construction:
Architecture subsystem

Canonical architecture:
Architecture Model

Graph projection:
Graph subsystem

Knowledge projection:
Knowledge subsystem

Search:
Retrieval subsystem

Diagram generation:
Diagram subsystem

AI explanation:
AI/Explanation subsystem

HTTP exposure:
API subsystem

Background execution:
Worker subsystem

No major responsibility should exist as an unowned collection of helper functions distributed throughout the codebase.

3.32 Separation of Concerns

A component should not simultaneously own unrelated responsibilities merely because combining them is convenient.

For example, an API endpoint should not:

parse an entire repository;
construct architecture;
write directly to Neo4j;
generate embeddings;
call an LLM;
render a diagram.

Instead, it should orchestrate the appropriate application services.

This keeps the system testable and maintainable.

3.33 Explicit Interfaces for External Infrastructure

Infrastructure integrations should be accessed through explicit boundaries where appropriate.

Examples:

StorageProvider

LLMProvider

EmbeddingProvider

GraphRepository

SearchRepository

MessagePublisher

This makes the application easier to:

test;
replace infrastructure;
run locally;
evolve deployments;
isolate vendor-specific code.

3.34 Technology Must Have a Responsibility

Every major technology included in StackSense must have a clearly defined responsibility.

The project must avoid adding infrastructure merely because it is popular or technically interesting.

For example:

RabbitMQ:
Asynchronous message transport.

Celery:
Background task execution.

PostgreSQL:
Primary application and authoritative job state.

Neo4j:
Graph projection and graph-oriented retrieval.

Elasticsearch:
Search and retrieval projection.

React Flow:
Interactive diagram rendering.

ELK:
Graph layout.

Each technology should have a clear boundary.

3.35 Avoid Premature Infrastructure

A future requirement does not automatically justify implementing the infrastructure now.

Examples:

S3 can remain a future storage provider while local storage is used initially.
OAuth can remain future authentication functionality while JWT is implemented initially.
Kubernetes can remain a future deployment target while Docker Compose is used for MVP development.
additional AI providers can remain future implementations behind the provider abstraction.

The current implementation should satisfy current requirements while preserving the explicitly required extension boundaries.

3.36 Testability Is an Architectural Requirement

Important architecture components must be testable independently.

The architecture should make it possible to test:

parsers;
IR generation;
symbol resolution;
architecture construction;
architecture validation;
graph projection;
retrieval;
ranking;
diagram specification;
report generation;
AI context construction;
API behavior;
worker behavior.

A design that makes core behavior impossible or unnecessarily difficult to test should be reconsidered.

3.37 Deterministic Components Should Be Preferentially Tested Deterministically

Where a component produces deterministic output, tests should assert deterministic behavior.

Examples:

IR generation;
architecture entities;
architecture relationships;
validation;
graph projection;
diagram specification;
ranking algorithms.

AI-generated prose should not normally be tested through exact string matching.

AI behavior should instead be evaluated using appropriate semantic and structural criteria.

3.38 Golden Repository Testing

StackSense should maintain representative fixture repositories for supported ecosystems.

These fixtures should be used to verify:

parsing;
framework detection;
IR;
architecture entities;
relationships;
endpoints;
diagrams;
reports;
regression behavior.

Changes to the analysis engine should be evaluated against known expected outputs.

3.39 Reproducibility

Given the same:

repository snapshot;
analyzer version;
IR schema version;
architecture schema version;
relevant configuration;

deterministic analysis should produce equivalent architecture results.

AI-generated explanations may vary because LLMs are probabilistic.

Therefore:

Deterministic Architecture
=
Reproducible

AI Explanation
=
Evidence-Grounded but Potentially Variable

3.40 Observability Is Part of the Architecture

Observability must not be added only after the system becomes difficult to debug.

Major operations should have correlation information such as:

request ID;
analysis ID;
job ID;
stage ID;
architecture version;
relevant project/environment identifiers.

Logs should be structured.

Metrics should measure important operational behavior.

Distributed operations should be traceable where practical.

3.41 Fail the Smallest Possible Boundary

A failure should be contained to the smallest reasonable subsystem.

For example:

One parser fails
↓
Mark affected artifact
↓
Continue independent analysis

One worker retries
↓
Other jobs continue

AI provider fails
↓
AI explanation unavailable

Search index fails
↓
Search degraded

The entire application should not fail merely because an optional downstream component failed.

3.42 Correctness Before Completeness

An incomplete architecture with explicit warnings is preferable to a complete-looking architecture containing invented or unsupported facts.

StackSense should prefer:

"Architecture partially reconstructed. Three files could not be analyzed."

over:

"Architecture successfully reconstructed."

when the latter would imply unsupported completeness.

3.43 User Trust Over Visual Impressiveness

The system should never sacrifice architectural correctness merely to produce a visually impressive diagram.

A beautiful diagram containing incorrect relationships is worse than a simpler diagram containing accurate information.

Visual quality is important.

Correctness is foundational.

3.44 User Experience Must Reflect System State

The frontend should accurately communicate states such as:

queued;
running;
partially available;
indexing;
generating diagrams;
completed;
completed with warnings;
failed;
cancelled.

The UI must not show a completed state while critical background processing is still incomplete unless the product explicitly defines that subsystem as independently complete.

3.45 Progressive Disclosure

StackSense should reveal complexity progressively.

The user should not be forced to understand every architectural detail immediately.

The product should support:

High-Level Overview
↓
Module
↓
Component
↓
Dependency
↓
Source Evidence

This principle applies to:

diagrams;
reports;
search;
architecture exploration;
AI explanations.

3.46 Initial Results Must Be Curated

StackSense should not automatically overwhelm the user with every available graph and diagram.

Initial results should prioritize high-value information.

Additional detail should remain available through:

drill-down;
filters;
search;
on-demand diagram generation;
component inspection;
dependency exploration.

3.47 Background Work Must Not Invalidate Previous Results

When workers continue processing after initial results are available, newly discovered knowledge must not arbitrarily modify previously published results.

For example:

Initial Architecture Version V1
↓
Initial Diagram V1

Later:
Knowledge indexing completes

The diagram must remain logically consistent with Architecture V1.

If architecture itself changes:

Architecture V2
↓
New Diagram V2

This distinction is required for stable user experience and reproducibility.

3.48 Explicit Dependency Direction

Dependencies between architectural layers should follow defined direction.

Higher-level orchestration may depend on lower-level abstractions.

Domain logic should not depend directly on infrastructure implementations when an abstraction boundary is required.

Infrastructure implements interfaces defined by appropriate higher-level layers.

This principle supports dependency inversion and keeps vendor-specific details isolated.

3.49 Minimize Coupling

Modules should communicate through explicit contracts rather than reaching into each other's internal implementation.

A module should not:

directly modify another module's database tables without ownership;
depend on another module's private classes;
bypass application services;
access another subsystem's internal infrastructure implementation.

Cross-module communication should use approved interfaces.

3.50 Prefer Explicit State Machines for Long-Running Work

Analysis lifecycle and other important asynchronous workflows should use explicit states rather than relying on implicit assumptions.

For example:

CREATED
↓
QUEUED
↓
RUNNING
↓
PARTIAL
↓
COMPLETED

with explicit failure/cancellation paths.

State transitions must be validated.

Invalid state transitions must not be silently accepted.

3.51 API and Domain State Must Remain Consistent

The API layer must not invent a state that does not exist in the underlying domain/application model.

For example, if an analysis is actually QUEUED, the API should not represent it as RUNNING merely because a request was accepted.

User-visible state must reflect authoritative application state.

3.52 Auditability

Important system actions should be traceable.

Examples include:

authentication changes;
organization membership changes;
role changes;
database connection changes;
analysis creation;
analysis deletion;
API key creation;
configuration changes;
security-sensitive actions.

Auditability supports debugging, security investigation, and enterprise readiness.

3.53 Security and Observability Must Not Conflict

Observability must not become a mechanism for leaking secrets or sensitive repository content.

Logs and telemetry should contain enough information to diagnose problems without unnecessarily storing:

passwords;
API keys;
private credentials;
full repository contents;
sensitive user data;
unnecessary AI prompt contents.

Sensitive values must be redacted where applicable.

3.54 Performance Must Be Designed Into Boundaries

Performance should be considered at architectural boundaries rather than patched only after implementation.

Important targets include:

fast API responses for non-long-running operations;
asynchronous processing for expensive analysis;
bounded resource consumption;
background worker scalability;
efficient retrieval;
lazy diagram generation;
caching of rebuildable derived results;
avoidance of unnecessary repeated parsing.

Expensive work should not execute synchronously inside user-facing HTTP requests.

3.55 Resource Limits Are Safety Boundaries

Repository analysis must operate under explicit resource limits.

Limits exist to protect:

system stability;
worker availability;
memory;
CPU;
disk;
queue capacity;
indexing infrastructure;
AI costs.

A larger repository must not be allowed to consume unlimited resources merely because it was submitted by a valid user.

Exact resource limits are defined in the dedicated resource-limit section.

3.56 Cost Awareness

External AI services and other expensive infrastructure must be treated as controlled resources.

StackSense should avoid:

unnecessary repeated LLM calls;
embedding the same content repeatedly;
generating every possible diagram immediately;
reprocessing unchanged artifacts unnecessarily;
sending excessive context to AI models.

Derived data and caching should be used where appropriate without compromising correctness.

3.57 Extensibility Without Premature Abstraction

StackSense must be extensible in areas explicitly identified as future extension points.

Examples:

AI providers;
embedding providers;
storage providers;
supported languages;
supported frameworks;
deployment targets.

However, extensibility must not become an excuse for creating unnecessary abstractions everywhere.

An abstraction should exist when it protects an actual architectural boundary or future replacement point.

3.58 Explicit Source Ownership

Every source artifact must have a clear origin and relationship to the analyzed snapshot.

StackSense should preserve enough metadata to understand:

where the artifact came from;
which snapshot it belongs to;
which analysis processed it;
which architecture version was generated from it;
whether it was successfully analyzed.

This is important for evidence and reproducibility.

3.59 No Hidden Business Logic in Presentation

Frontend components must not become the authoritative implementation of domain rules.

For example:

authorization;
ownership;
architecture validity;
analysis state transitions;
resource limits;
security decisions.

must be enforced server-side.

The frontend may provide UX validation, but it must not be trusted as the final enforcement layer.

3.60 No Hidden Architecture in Infrastructure

Infrastructure configuration must not silently redefine application architecture.

Docker, Kubernetes, deployment files, queue configuration, or cloud configuration may implement the approved architecture.

They must not introduce undeclared architectural relationships merely because they are convenient to configure.

Architecture must remain understandable from the canonical system model and its approved infrastructure definitions.

3.61 Principle of Explicitness

Important system behavior should be explicit rather than dependent on hidden conventions.

Examples:

explicit job states;
explicit architecture versions;
explicit provider selection;
explicit storage provider;
explicit tenant ownership;
explicit evidence provenance;
explicit failure state;
explicit diagram type;
explicit source references.

This makes StackSense easier for both humans and AI collaborators to understand.

3.62 Principle of Bounded Complexity

StackSense should prefer a system that is understandable and maintainable over unnecessary technical sophistication.

New infrastructure should be introduced only when it solves a real requirement.

The goal is not to maximize the number of technologies.

The goal is to build a coherent system in which every technology and subsystem has a clear purpose.

3.63 Principle of Replaceable Infrastructure

Infrastructure should be replaceable where the architecture explicitly requires it.

For example:

Local Storage
↓
StorageProvider
↓
S3 in the future

AI Provider
↓
LLMProvider
↓
Gemini / Ollama / Future Provider

The business/domain layer should not become tightly coupled to a specific vendor implementation.

3.64 Principle of Stable Contracts

Internal implementation may evolve, but externally meaningful contracts should remain stable.

Important contracts include:

API contracts;
analysis states;
event semantics;
Architecture Model semantics;
entity identities;
version semantics;
diagram specification semantics;
evidence references.

When a contract must change, it must be treated as an intentional change rather than an incidental refactor.

3.65 Principle of Evidence Over Assumption

Whenever StackSense has a choice between:

presenting a fact supported by evidence;
presenting an inference;
presenting an unsupported assumption;

the system should prefer the strongest supported representation.

Inferred information should be distinguishable from confirmed information when relevant.

Unsupported information must not be presented as confirmed architecture.

3.66 Principle of Human-Understandable Architecture

The architecture must remain understandable to a human engineer.

This means:

responsibilities should be clear;
data flows should be traceable;
major boundaries should be explicit;
terminology should be consistent;
diagrams should correspond to real system behavior;
AI explanations should be grounded in inspectable evidence.

The architecture should not become so abstract that only the implementation author understands it.

3.67 Principle of AI-Compatible Engineering

Because StackSense will be implemented with assistance from multiple AI coding collaborators, architecture must be written and structured so that another agent can understand:

what a subsystem owns;
what it must not own;
what it consumes;
what it produces;
what contracts it must preserve;
which technologies it may use;
which technologies it must not introduce;
where authoritative state lives;
which failures are expected;
what tests are required.

Ambiguity that would be manageable for a human developer can become dangerous when interpreted independently by multiple AI agents.

Therefore explicit boundaries are a first-class engineering requirement.

3.68 Principle of Consistency Across Projections

The same Architecture Model must produce logically consistent:

diagrams;
reports;
graph data;
API responses;
knowledge;
AI explanations.

If two projections disagree, the problem must be resolved at the projection or source-model level.

The system must not maintain separate independently generated interpretations of the same architecture.

3.69 Principle of Minimal Duplication of Truth

The same architectural fact should not be independently authored in multiple systems.

For example:

UserService
DEPENDS_ON
UserRepository

should originate from the Architecture Model.

The diagram should project it.

Neo4j should project it.

The report should reference it.

The AI context should retrieve it.

Duplicating the fact manually across these systems creates synchronization risk and is prohibited where avoidable.

3.70 Principle of Explicit Failure Over Silent Success

If StackSense cannot establish a required fact or complete a required stage, it must represent that limitation explicitly.

Examples:

parser failure;
incomplete architecture;
indexing failure;
diagram failure;
AI provider failure;
dependency resolution failure.

A visible warning is preferable to a false impression of successful complete analysis.

3.71 Principle of Smallest Possible Failure Domain

A component should fail without unnecessarily taking down unrelated components.

This principle applies at:

API level;
worker level;
analysis stage level;
projection level;
AI provider level;
storage level;
search level;
frontend level.

Failure isolation is an architectural feature, not merely an operational optimization.

3.72 Principle of Progressive Capability

StackSense should become useful as soon as enough reliable information is available.

The system should not unnecessarily wait for unrelated background work.

For example:

Architecture ready
↓
Architecture can be explored

while:

Knowledge indexing
↓
continues independently

provided that the user is clearly informed about subsystem availability.

3.73 Principle of No Unbounded Background Work

Background workers must not create uncontrolled recursive or repeated work.

Examples:

Indexing
↓
must not continuously trigger itself

Diagram generation
↓
must not regenerate indefinitely

Knowledge enrichment
↓
must not create endless feedback loops

Events and task triggers must have clear ownership and termination conditions.

3.74 Principle of Explicit Asynchronous Boundaries

Any operation that may take significant time must have an explicit asynchronous boundary.

Examples include:

repository analysis;
indexing;
embedding generation;
large diagram generation;
report generation when expensive;
scheduled analysis.

The HTTP request should create or request the operation rather than performing the entire operation synchronously.

3.75 Principle of Safe Retries

Retries must be bounded and intentional.

A failure should not automatically result in infinite retries.

Retries should consider:

retryable vs non-retryable errors;
maximum attempts;
backoff;
idempotency;
dependency availability;
user-visible status.

Permanent failures should eventually transition into explicit failure states.

3.76 Principle of Operational Recovery

Derived systems should be recoverable.

If:

Elasticsearch data is lost;
Neo4j projection is lost;
embeddings are deleted;
diagram cache is deleted;

the system should have a defined rebuild path.

Operational recovery must not require manually reconstructing architecture from memory.

3.77 Principle of Clean Boundaries Before Optimization

Performance optimizations must not bypass architectural boundaries without explicit justification.

For example, directly accessing a database from a frontend or bypassing an application service because it is faster is not an acceptable optimization.

Correct boundaries come first.

Optimization must happen within the architecture or through an approved architectural change.

3.78 Principle of Explicit Trade-Offs

When StackSense deliberately chooses a trade-off, the reason should be documented.

Examples:

local storage instead of S3 initially;
JWT before OAuth;
curated initial diagrams instead of generating all diagrams immediately;
asynchronous processing instead of synchronous simplicity;
deterministic analysis before AI interpretation.

The purpose is to ensure future contributors understand that these choices are intentional rather than accidental omissions.

3.79 Fundamental StackSense Rule

All previous principles can be reduced to one system-wide rule:

StackSense must produce the most reliable and understandable representation of a software system that can reasonably be derived from available evidence, while keeping architectural truth deterministic, projections consistent, AI grounded, infrastructure replaceable, failures isolated, and implementation boundaries explicit.

3.80 Section Summary

The non-negotiable architectural principles of StackSense are:

Deterministic truth before AI.
Architecture Model as the canonical architecture source of truth.
Projections must not become sources of truth.
Evidence must be traceable.
Architecture and presentation must remain separate.
Diagram generation uses a deterministic plus AI-assisted hybrid model.
Analysis is asynchronous.
REST represents state and SSE represents progress.
Persistent state has explicit ownership.
Background operations should be idempotent and retry-safe.
Architecture and projections are version-aware.
Graceful degradation is mandatory.
Partial results must be explicit.
Security is foundational.
Repositories are untrusted input.
AI is provider-agnostic and optional.
AI explanations must be evidence-grounded.
Retrieval, evidence planning, context construction, and generation are separate responsibilities.
Frontend and backend boundaries are enforced.
Infrastructure responsibilities are explicit.
Derived data should be rebuildable.
Testing is an architectural requirement.
Deterministic outputs should be tested deterministically.
Reproducibility is required for deterministic analysis.
Observability is part of the architecture.
Failures must be isolated to the smallest reasonable boundary.
Correctness is more important than completeness or visual impressiveness.
Progressive disclosure and progressive capability should guide the user experience.
Resource limits and cost controls are mandatory.
Infrastructure should be replaceable where explicitly required.
Architectural contracts must remain stable.
Evidence is preferred over assumption.
Important responsibilities must remain human-understandable.
AI collaborators must follow explicit architectural boundaries.
Multiple projections must remain consistent with the same Architecture Model.
Architectural truth must not be unnecessarily duplicated.
Failure must be explicit rather than represented as false success.
Background work must remain bounded and recoverable.
Optimization must not silently bypass architectural boundaries.
Intentional architectural trade-offs should be documented.

End of Section 3.


4.  FROZEN TECHNOLOGY STACK

4.1 Purpose

This section defines the technologies that have been explicitly selected for StackSense and the architectural responsibility assigned to each technology.

These choices are frozen unless explicitly reopened through the architecture change process defined in Section 1.

The purpose of freezing the technology stack is to prevent implementation agents from independently replacing technologies or introducing unnecessary alternatives during development.

Technology selection must always be interpreted together with the responsibility assigned to that technology.

A technology being present in the stack does not mean every module may use it directly.

4.2 Technology Selection Principles

The StackSense technology stack follows these principles:

prefer mature and well-supported technologies;
use each technology for a clearly defined responsibility;
avoid unnecessary infrastructure;
preserve replaceability where explicitly required;
prefer technologies that support production-quality architecture;
keep the development environment practical for local development;
allow future migration to more scalable infrastructure without rewriting core domain logic;
avoid introducing technologies merely because they are popular;
avoid duplicate technologies that solve the same responsibility without a concrete requirement.

4.3 Backend Language

Primary backend language:

Python

Python is the primary language for the StackSense backend and analysis engine.

Python is responsible for:

backend application logic;
domain logic;
analysis pipeline;
source analysis;
IR generation;
architecture construction;
knowledge processing;
background task orchestration;
AI integration;
retrieval orchestration;
report generation;
other backend capabilities defined by the architecture.

Python is the primary implementation language for deterministic repository analysis.

4.4 Python Version

The project must use a single explicitly selected supported Python version for the active development environment.

The exact version must be defined in the project environment configuration and must not vary arbitrarily between modules.

Individual modules must not independently select incompatible Python versions.

If the supported Python version changes, the project environment, dependency configuration, CI environment, and compatibility tests must be updated together.

4.5 Python Framework Boundary

StackSense must support analysis of repositories using the approved Python framework ecosystem.

The initial Python framework boundary includes:

Django;
Flask;
FastAPI.

These frameworks are important targets for framework-aware repository analysis.

Framework support means StackSense should be capable of recognizing and extracting framework-specific architectural information where practical.

It does not mean StackSense itself must use every listed framework for its own backend implementation.

4.6 JavaScript / TypeScript Runtime

Node.js is an approved runtime for JavaScript and TypeScript ecosystems.

Node.js is a runtime, not a framework.

It is included in the supported repository ecosystem because StackSense must be able to analyze repositories whose applications execute on Node.js.

StackSense must distinguish:

Runtime:
Node.js

from:

Framework:
Express
NestJS
Next.js

The presence of Node.js must therefore not be treated as equivalent to the presence of a particular framework.

4.7 JavaScript and TypeScript Language Boundary

StackSense must support analysis of:

JavaScript;
JSX;
TypeScript;
TSX.

These are separate artifact/language concerns and must be recognized appropriately during repository analysis.

The analysis system must not assume that all JavaScript/TypeScript repositories have the same architecture.

For example:

JavaScript
+
Express

is different from:

TypeScript
+
NestJS

and:

TypeScript
+
Next.js

Framework-specific analysis must therefore be applied only when corresponding framework evidence exists.

4.8 Approved JavaScript / TypeScript Frameworks

The initial approved framework boundary includes:

Express;
NestJS;
Next.js.

These frameworks must be treated as separate framework targets during analysis.

Express is primarily relevant to server-side HTTP/application architecture.
