NestJS is primarily relevant to structured backend/module architecture.

Next.js is relevant to full-stack React-based application architecture, including frontend and server-side capabilities.

StackSense must preserve the distinction between framework detection and generic JavaScript/TypeScript analysis.

4.9 PostgreSQL

PostgreSQL is the primary relational database for StackSense.

PostgreSQL is responsible for authoritative application state and persistent relational data.

It may store:

users;
organizations;
projects;
environments;
analysis records;
job state;
architecture version metadata;
configuration metadata;
audit information;
application-level relationships;
other authoritative domain state.

PostgreSQL must not be replaced by Neo4j or Elasticsearch as the primary application state store.

4.10 Neo4j

Neo4j is approved for graph-oriented architecture and knowledge representation.

Neo4j is responsible for:

graph projection;
relationship traversal;
architecture graph queries;
dependency exploration;
graph-oriented knowledge relationships;
path and subgraph queries.

Neo4j is not the canonical source of architecture truth.

The canonical relationship is:

Architecture Model
↓
Graph Projection
↓
Neo4j

Neo4j data must therefore be rebuildable from the appropriate authoritative architecture/knowledge artifacts where practical.

4.11 Elasticsearch

Elasticsearch is approved as the primary search and retrieval infrastructure.

It is responsible for:

lexical search;
full-text search;
metadata filtering;
semantic retrieval where configured;
knowledge document indexing;
retrieval candidate generation;
search-oriented projection of repository knowledge.

Elasticsearch is not the source of truth for repository architecture.

The conceptual relationship is:

Knowledge Projection
↓
Elasticsearch
↓
Retrieval

If the Elasticsearch index is lost, it must be possible to rebuild it from authoritative knowledge/source artifacts.

4.12 RabbitMQ

RabbitMQ is the approved asynchronous message broker for StackSense.

RabbitMQ is responsible for:

asynchronous message transport;
background job/task delivery;
decoupling producers from workers;
buffering workload;
supporting worker scalability;
supporting retry-oriented processing where configured.

RabbitMQ is not the authoritative owner of application/job state.

RabbitMQ must not be used as a substitute for persistent domain state.

4.13 Celery

Celery is the approved background task execution framework.

Celery is responsible for:

executing asynchronous tasks;
distributing work to workers;
task retry behavior;
task execution lifecycle;
background processing.

The relationship is:

Application
↓
RabbitMQ
↓
Celery Workers

RabbitMQ provides message transport.

Celery provides task execution.

PostgreSQL provides authoritative persistent application/job state.

These responsibilities must remain distinct.

4.14 SSE

Server-Sent Events (SSE) is the approved mechanism for delivering real-time analysis progress to the frontend.

SSE is responsible for:

analysis progress;
stage transitions;
meaningful user-facing events;
background processing notifications;
completion/failure notifications.

SSE is not the authoritative source of application state.

The frontend must be able to recover from an interrupted SSE connection by querying the REST API.

The architectural distinction is:

REST
↓
Authoritative State

SSE
↓
Real-Time Progress / Notification

4.15 REST API

REST is the approved primary frontend/backend API style.

Public APIs must use the versioned API boundary:

/api/v1/

REST APIs are responsible for:

resource creation;
resource retrieval;
resource modification;
resource deletion where applicable;
querying current state;
analysis management;
architecture retrieval;
diagram retrieval;
knowledge/search requests;
authentication and authorization endpoints;
other approved application capabilities.

Long-running operations must not block the request until completion.

4.16 React Flow

React Flow is the approved frontend graph rendering technology for StackSense architecture diagrams.

React Flow is responsible for:

interactive nodes;
interactive edges;
pan;
zoom;
selection;
diagram interaction;
node inspection;
diagram navigation;
frontend graph rendering;
other interactive visualization behavior.

React Flow must not become the source of architecture semantics.

The frontend should receive a validated diagram representation derived from the Architecture Model.

4.17 ELK

ELK is the approved graph layout engine for StackSense diagrams.

ELK is responsible for:

graph layout;
node positioning;
hierarchical arrangement;
spacing;
edge routing;
layout direction;
collision avoidance;
other graph-layout responsibilities.

AI must not be responsible for calculating final graph coordinates.

The diagram pipeline is:

Architecture Model
↓
Diagram Specification
↓
Validated Graph
↓
ELK
↓
React Flow

4.18 React / Frontend Boundary

The StackSense frontend may use the approved React-based frontend ecosystem associated with the selected framework.

Frontend implementation must preserve the following responsibility boundary:

Frontend
↓
REST / SSE
↓
Backend
↓
Application / Domain
↓
Infrastructure

The frontend must not directly access:

PostgreSQL;
Neo4j;
Elasticsearch;
RabbitMQ;
Celery;
internal filesystem paths;
secret stores;
internal worker APIs.

4.19 Local Storage

Local storage is the approved initial artifact-storage implementation.

It is suitable for:

local development;
MVP deployment;
repository snapshots;
generated artifacts;
intermediate files where appropriate.

The application must access storage through an abstraction where storage replacement is required.

The intended architecture is:

Application
↓
StorageProvider
↓
Local Storage

The application must not hard-code its entire storage architecture around a specific local filesystem path if future provider replacement is required.

4.20 S3 / Object Storage

S3-compatible object storage is a planned future storage implementation.

The intended progression is:

MVP:
Local Storage

Future:
S3 / Object Storage

S3 is therefore not a mandatory initial infrastructure dependency.

The storage abstraction must make future migration possible without requiring major changes to domain logic.

Object storage may eventually support:

repository snapshots;
generated reports;
large artifacts;
analysis outputs;
exported diagrams;
other large files.

4.21 Encryption

Encryption is an approved architectural direction for sensitive stored information.

Sensitive data, particularly credentials and connection information, must not be stored casually as plaintext application data.

The exact encryption/key-management implementation may be finalized during the security/infrastructure implementation section, provided that it preserves the frozen security requirements.

The architecture must allow secure handling of:

database credentials;
API keys;
provider credentials;
authentication secrets;
other sensitive configuration.

4.22 AI Provider Abstraction

StackSense must use an abstraction around AI providers.

Conceptually:

AI Service
↓
LLM Provider Interface
├── Gemini Provider
├── Ollama Provider
└── Future Providers

Provider-specific SDKs and APIs must remain inside provider implementations.

Core application logic must depend on the provider abstraction rather than directly depending on one vendor.

4.23 Gemini

Gemini is an approved external LLM provider option for StackSense.

Gemini may be used for:

architecture explanation;
knowledge-grounded question answering;
report narrative generation;
diagram presentation assistance;
other approved AI rendering responsibilities.

Gemini must not become the canonical source of architectural facts.

4.24 Ollama

Ollama is an approved local AI provider option.

Ollama may be used for:

local development;
local experimentation;
privacy-sensitive development environments where appropriate;
reducing external API dependency during development;
testing provider abstraction behavior.

The application must not assume that Ollama is always available.

AI availability must be treated as a potentially optional capability.

4.25 Embedding Provider Abstraction

Embedding generation must be abstracted similarly to LLM generation.

Conceptually:

Embedding Service
↓
Embedding Provider Interface
├── Local Provider
├── Remote Provider
└── Future Provider

Embeddings are derived data.

They are not authoritative architectural information.

If embeddings are deleted, they should be regenerable from the appropriate knowledge artifacts.

4.26 Containerization

Docker is the approved containerization technology for local and deployment environments.

The MVP development environment should support Docker-based infrastructure.

Docker may be used for:

PostgreSQL;
RabbitMQ;
Elasticsearch;
Neo4j;
application services;
workers;
supporting infrastructure.

The exact container topology may evolve while preserving the approved architectural responsibilities.

4.27 Local Development Deployment

The initial local deployment target is Docker Compose.

The intended development environment may contain:

frontend;
backend/API;
worker processes;
scheduler;
PostgreSQL;
RabbitMQ;
Neo4j;
Elasticsearch;
supporting services.

Not every service must necessarily be started for every development task.

The architecture should allow individual components to be developed and tested independently where practical.

4.28 Future Deployment Targets

The architecture should remain compatible with future deployment environments including:

single-server deployment;
containerized production deployment;
Kubernetes;
cloud infrastructure.

These are future deployment targets and do not require immediate implementation.

The domain and application layers must not become tightly coupled to Docker Compose-specific behavior.

4.29 Technology Responsibility Matrix

The approved high-level responsibility mapping is:

4.30 Technologies That Are Not Automatically Approved

The existence of a technology in the wider software ecosystem does not make it an approved StackSense dependency.

Examples include:

Kafka;
RabbitMQ alternatives;
Celery alternatives;
Mermaid as the primary diagram engine;
arbitrary graph visualization libraries;
arbitrary vector databases;
arbitrary cloud storage providers;
arbitrary AI providers;
arbitrary ORM replacements;
arbitrary message brokers;
arbitrary search engines.

A technology may be evaluated and proposed in the future.

It must not be introduced into the core architecture without explicit approval when it changes a frozen responsibility or introduces a significant dependency.

4.31 Redis Boundary

Redis is not the primary asynchronous message broker.

RabbitMQ holds that responsibility.

If Redis is introduced for a specific supporting responsibility such as caching, rate limiting, ephemeral state, or another explicitly approved use case, that responsibility must remain separate from RabbitMQ's message-transport role.

Redis must not be introduced merely because it is commonly used in backend systems.

Any concrete Redis adoption must identify its responsibility and avoid creating overlapping ownership with PostgreSQL or RabbitMQ.

4.32 Kafka Boundary

Kafka is not part of the current frozen StackSense technology stack.

Kafka may be considered as a future architectural option only through the architecture change process.

It must not be introduced as a replacement for RabbitMQ during normal implementation without explicit approval.

The current decision is:

RabbitMQ:
Approved message broker.

Kafka:
Not currently approved.

4.33 Mermaid Boundary

Mermaid is not the primary StackSense architecture visualization engine.

The approved diagram architecture is:

Diagram Specification
↓
ELK
↓
React Flow

Mermaid may be used for internal documentation or simple explanatory material if useful, but it must not replace the production interactive diagram architecture.

The primary StackSense product diagrams must use the approved React Flow + ELK architecture.

4.34 Technology Version Policy

This section freezes technology choices and responsibilities, not arbitrary version numbers unless a specific version is explicitly defined elsewhere.

Version selection must be:

compatible with the project;
reproducible;
pinned or constrained appropriately;
tested in CI;
documented in dependency configuration.

A dependency version must not be upgraded blindly if the upgrade changes behavior, compatibility, security posture, or architectural assumptions.

Dependency upgrades must be treated as engineering changes and tested accordingly.

4.35 Dependency Management

Dependencies must be explicitly declared.

The project must not rely on undeclared packages being available because another package happens to install them.

Each module must declare the dependencies it actually requires according to the project's dependency-management strategy.

Unused dependencies should not be introduced.

Large dependencies should be justified when they materially affect:

build size;
startup time;
security;
deployment;
maintenance;
resource usage.

4.36 Technology Selection and AI Coding Agents

AI coding agents must not introduce a new technology because:

it is more familiar;
it is easier to implement;
training data commonly uses it;
it is popular;
a tutorial uses it;
another project uses it;
the agent considers it "best practice."

The agent must first determine whether an approved StackSense technology already satisfies the requirement.

If a new technology appears genuinely necessary, the agent must identify the architectural reason and request approval when the change affects the frozen stack.

4.37 Technology Replacement Rule

Replacing a frozen technology requires explicit architectural approval.

The replacement proposal must identify:

existing technology;
current responsibility;
reason for replacement;
proposed replacement;
migration strategy;
effect on existing code;
effect on data;
effect on operations;
effect on testing;
effect on performance;
effect on security;
effect on future architecture.

No replacement should be performed solely as a refactor without considering its architectural implications.

Node.js

4.39 Section Summary

The StackSense technology stack is intentionally designed around clear responsibilities.

The primary backend and analysis language is Python.

StackSense must understand Python repositories using Django, Flask, and FastAPI, as well as JavaScript/TypeScript repositories using Node.js, Express, NestJS, and Next.js.

PostgreSQL remains the authoritative relational application store.

RabbitMQ provides asynchronous message transport.

Celery executes background tasks.

Neo4j provides graph-oriented projections and traversal.

Elasticsearch provides search and retrieval infrastructure.

REST provides the primary application API.

SSE provides real-time progress and notification delivery.

React Flow provides interactive diagram rendering.

ELK provides diagram layout.

Docker provides containerization.

Local storage is used initially for artifacts, with S3/object storage planned as a future provider.

Gemini and Ollama are approved AI provider options behind an abstraction layer.

No technology is allowed to silently replace a frozen responsibility.

The fundamental rule is:

Every technology must have a clearly defined responsibility, and no implementation agent may introduce, replace, or repurpose a major technology without respecting the frozen architecture and change-control process.

End of Section 4.


5.  SUPPORTED LANGUAGES, FRAMEWORKS & RUNTIME BOUNDARY

5.1 Purpose

This section defines exactly which programming languages, file types, runtimes, and frameworks StackSense is expected to understand as part of its repository analysis boundary.

The purpose of this boundary is to prevent the analyzer from treating every repository as an undifferentiated collection of source files.

StackSense must first determine:

what languages are present;
what runtimes are present;
what frameworks are present;
what source artifacts belong to those ecosystems;
what framework-specific architectural patterns can be detected;
what analysis capabilities are available for the detected ecosystem.

This section defines the currently approved support boundary.

It does not require every supported language or framework to have identical analysis depth.

5.2 Supported Language Families

The current StackSense analysis boundary includes:

Python
JavaScript
TypeScript

The frontend-related syntax variants:

JSX
TSX

are also explicitly supported.

Therefore the initial source-analysis boundary is:

Python
JavaScript
JSX
TypeScript
TSX

These are the primary programming-language artifacts that the MVP analyzer is expected to understand.

5.3 Python

Python is a first-class supported analysis language.

StackSense should be capable of extracting architectural information from Python repositories including, where detectable:

modules;
packages;
classes;
functions;
methods;
imports;
inheritance;
function calls;
class relationships;
decorators;
API routes;
framework structures;
configuration;
dependency declarations;
tests;
database interaction;
service boundaries.

Python analysis should form one of the strongest initial analyzer capabilities because Python is the primary backend language of StackSense itself.

5.4 Python Framework Targets

The approved Python framework targets are:

Django;
Flask;
FastAPI.

Framework detection must be evidence-based.

StackSense must not classify a repository as using a framework merely because a similarly named file or directory exists.

Framework detection should consider appropriate evidence such as:

dependencies;
imports;
application initialization;
framework-specific decorators;
routing structures;
configuration;
conventional project structures;
framework-specific APIs.

5.5 Django

Django is a supported Python framework target.

The analyzer should recognize relevant Django architectural structures where practical, including:

Django applications;
URL routing;
views;
models;
serializers where applicable;
forms where applicable;
middleware;
management commands;
settings;
application configuration;
templates;
migrations;
tests;
common dependency relationships.

Django-specific extraction should enrich the generic Python architecture model rather than create a completely separate architecture representation.

5.6 Flask

Flask is a supported Python framework target.

The analyzer should recognize relevant Flask structures where practical, including:

application initialization;
routes;
blueprints;
views;
extensions;
configuration;
services;
database integrations;
templates;
tests;
dependency relationships.

Flask-specific structures should be represented using the same broader architecture model used for other supported frameworks.

5.7 FastAPI

FastAPI is a supported Python framework target.

The analyzer should recognize relevant structures where practical, including:

FastAPI application instances;
routers;
route handlers;
dependencies;
request/response models;
middleware;
configuration;
services;
database integrations;
background tasks;
tests.

FastAPI-specific information should enrich the generic Python analysis rather than bypass the common IR and Architecture Model.

5.8 JavaScript

JavaScript is a first-class supported analysis language.

The analyzer should be capable of identifying, where practical:

modules;
imports;
exports;
functions;
classes;
methods;
calls;
dependencies;
routes;
configuration;
package metadata;
framework structures;
frontend structures;
tests.

JavaScript repositories must not automatically be classified as Node.js backend applications.

The runtime and framework must be detected separately.

5.9 TypeScript

TypeScript is a first-class supported analysis language.

The analyzer should understand, where practical:

modules;
imports;
exports;
classes;
interfaces;
types;
functions;
methods;
decorators;
generics where relevant to structural analysis;
dependency relationships;
framework structures;
API definitions;
frontend structures;
tests;
configuration.

TypeScript-specific type information may enrich architecture extraction when it contributes useful architectural evidence.

5.10 JSX

JSX is explicitly supported as a source artifact.

JSX commonly represents React-oriented frontend code.

The analyzer should be able to recognize, where practical:

React components;
component relationships;
imports;
exports;
hooks;
props;
state-related structures;
routing;
API client usage;
component composition.

JSX must not automatically imply Next.js.

Framework detection must remain separate from syntax detection.

5.11 TSX

TSX is explicitly supported as a source artifact.

TSX combines TypeScript and JSX.

The analyzer should support both:

TypeScript structural information;
React/component-oriented JSX information.

TSX must not automatically imply Next.js.

The framework must be determined from repository evidence.

5.12 Node.js Runtime

Node.js is an approved runtime target.

Node.js is not a programming language and not a framework.

The analyzer should distinguish:

Language:
JavaScript / TypeScript

Runtime:
Node.js

Framework:
Express / NestJS / Next.js / other detected framework if later approved

This distinction is important for correctly reconstructing repository architecture.

5.13 Runtime Detection

Runtime detection should use repository evidence such as:

package metadata;
runtime-specific dependencies;
configuration;
source patterns;
package scripts;
framework conventions;
lockfiles;
runtime-specific configuration files.

The analyzer should avoid assuming a runtime solely from a file extension.

For example:

.ts

does not automatically mean:

Node.js backend.

It may represent:

frontend code;
Next.js code;
shared library code;
browser-side TypeScript;
another runtime.

5.14 Express

Express is a supported JavaScript/TypeScript framework target.

The analyzer should recognize relevant Express architecture where practical, including:

application initialization;
routers;
middleware;
route handlers;
controllers;
services;
request/response flow;
error middleware;
configuration;
database integrations;
external integrations;
tests.

Express analysis should work for both JavaScript and TypeScript repositories where the framework is used.

5.15 NestJS

NestJS is a supported JavaScript/TypeScript framework target.

The analyzer should recognize relevant NestJS structures where practical, including:

modules;
controllers;
providers;
services;
dependency injection;
guards;
interceptors;
pipes;
middleware;
decorators;
configuration;
database integrations;
external integrations;
tests.

NestJS's module/provider architecture should be represented in the common Architecture Model.

The analyzer must not create a framework-specific architecture model that is incompatible with other supported ecosystems.

5.16 Next.js

Next.js is a supported JavaScript/TypeScript framework target.

The analyzer should recognize relevant Next.js structures where practical, including:

application routes;
pages/routes;
layouts;
server components where detectable;
client components where detectable;
API routes or route handlers;
server-side logic;
middleware;
configuration;
data-fetching relationships;
external API interactions;
frontend component relationships.

Next.js may contain both frontend and backend/server-side behavior.

The analyzer must therefore avoid assuming that all Next.js code belongs to the frontend layer.

5.17 Framework Detection Hierarchy

Framework detection should follow an evidence-based hierarchy.

Conceptually:

Repository
↓
Language Detection
↓
Runtime Detection
↓
Framework Detection
↓
Framework-Specific Analysis
↓
Generic Analysis
↓
Architecture Model

Framework-specific analyzers should augment generic language analysis rather than replace it.

5.18 Multiple Frameworks in One Repository

A repository may contain multiple frameworks.

Examples:

Next.js frontend
+
Express backend

or:

React frontend
+
FastAPI backend

or:

Django application
+
Node.js service

StackSense must not force the repository into a single-framework classification when evidence shows multiple independent applications or services.

The architecture model should represent the detected applications and their relationships.

5.19 Monorepo Support

A repository may contain multiple applications or packages.

For example:

frontend/
backend/
shared/
worker/

or:

apps/
web/
api/
packages/
ui/
common/

The analyzer must not assume that the repository root represents a single application.

Where possible, it should identify:

applications;
packages;
services;
shared libraries;
infrastructure;
tests;
configuration boundaries.

The resulting Architecture Model should represent these boundaries.

5.20 Mixed-Language Repositories

Repositories may contain multiple supported languages.

Examples:

Python backend
+
TypeScript frontend

or:

FastAPI
+
Next.js
+
TypeScript shared package

The analyzer must preserve language identity while constructing a unified architecture representation.

Language-specific analysis should produce common IR concepts wherever possible.

5.21 Shared Code

Shared libraries and packages must be distinguished from applications where evidence supports that distinction.

For example:

frontend/
backend/
packages/shared/

should not automatically result in:

three independent applications.

The analyzer should use:

package metadata;
imports;
build configuration;
framework structures;
dependency direction;
repository structure;

to determine whether an artifact represents:

application;
service;
library;
shared package;
infrastructure component.

5.22 Generic Analysis vs Framework Analysis

StackSense uses two complementary analysis levels.

Generic analysis:

Extracts language-independent structural information.

Examples:

files;
modules;
classes;
functions;
imports;
calls;
dependencies.

Framework-aware analysis:

Adds framework-specific architectural meaning.

Examples:

Django views;
FastAPI routers;
Express middleware;
NestJS modules;
Next.js routes;
React components.

Framework-specific information should enrich the generic representation.

5.23 Framework Detection Must Not Create False Positives

The analyzer must use multiple signals when possible.

A single filename must not be sufficient evidence for framework classification.

For example:

manage.py

may strongly suggest Django, but framework classification should be validated using broader repository evidence where practical.

Similarly:

package.json

does not by itself prove that a repository uses Express, NestJS, or Next.js.

5.24 Unsupported Frameworks

A repository may use a framework outside the currently approved framework boundary.

StackSense must not fabricate framework-specific understanding in such cases.

Instead, it should:

perform generic language analysis where possible;
identify the unsupported or unknown framework when detectable;
preserve available evidence;
mark framework-specific analysis as limited;
continue with capabilities that remain reliable.

Unsupported framework detection must therefore degrade gracefully.

5.25 Unknown Languages

If a repository contains an unsupported programming language, StackSense should not automatically fail the entire repository analysis.

It should:

identify the unsupported language;
classify its files appropriately;
preserve metadata;
exclude unsupported files from language-specific analysis;
continue analyzing supported portions where safe.

The final analysis must communicate the limitation.

5.26 Unsupported File Types

Unsupported source formats must not be silently treated as supported code.

The artifact classification subsystem must distinguish:

supported source;
supported configuration;
supported documentation;
supported metadata;
unsupported source;
binary;
generated;
ignored;
unknown.

The detailed artifact classification rules are defined in the repository and artifact boundary sections.

5.27 Generated Code

Generated code should be identified where reliable evidence exists.

Examples may include:

generated API clients;
build output;
generated TypeScript;
compiled JavaScript;
generated schemas;
framework-generated files.

Generated code should not automatically be treated as primary architectural evidence if the source from which it is generated is available.

However, generated artifacts may still contain useful architecture evidence when no better source exists.

5.28 Build Output

Build output should generally be treated differently from source code.

Examples:

dist/;
build/;
compiled assets;
generated bundles.

These artifacts should not normally be used as primary source-analysis inputs when corresponding source files are available.

The analyzer must avoid double-counting architecture relationships from both source and generated output.

5.29 Dependencies

Dependency manifests are important architectural evidence.

Python examples may include:

requirements files;
pyproject configuration;
lockfiles.

JavaScript/TypeScript examples may include:

package.json;
package-lock;
yarn lock;
pnpm lock.

Dependency information should be represented separately from source imports where appropriate.

A declared dependency does not automatically mean that the dependency participates in a particular runtime architecture path.

5.30 Lockfiles

Lockfiles may be used for:

dependency identification;
dependency version information;
reproducibility metadata;
framework detection.

Lockfiles should not normally be treated as source code.

They are metadata/configuration artifacts.

5.31 Configuration Files

Configuration files may contain important architectural evidence.

Examples include:

framework configuration;
environment configuration;
package configuration;
build configuration;
deployment configuration;
database configuration;
routing configuration.

Configuration must be analyzed according to its format and architectural relevance.

Secrets must never be incorporated into the Architecture Model or knowledge system merely because they appear in configuration.

5.32 Environment Files

Environment files may contain architecture-relevant metadata but can also contain secrets.

The analyzer must treat them carefully.

It may detect the existence and names of configuration variables where useful, but secret values must not be stored as ordinary architecture evidence.

Examples of sensitive values include:

passwords;
API keys;
tokens;
credentials;
connection strings containing secrets.

5.33 Documentation

Documentation may provide useful architectural evidence.

Supported documentation analysis may include:

Markdown;
plain text;
project documentation;
API documentation;
architecture documentation.

Documentation should be treated as evidence rather than automatically as authoritative truth.

When documentation conflicts with deterministic source analysis, the system should preserve the distinction rather than silently treating documentation as more authoritative.

5.34 Images

Images may exist in repositories.

Examples:

architecture diagrams;
screenshots;
UI assets;
documentation images.

Images may be classified and stored as repository artifacts.

They should not automatically be treated as authoritative architecture evidence.

Image understanding may be added as a future capability if explicitly approved.

5.35 Binary Files

Binary files should generally be classified as binary artifacts and excluded from normal source analysis.

Examples:

executables;
compiled libraries;
archives after acquisition;
media files;
fonts;
unrelated binary assets.

Binary files may still contribute metadata such as:

file existence;
file size;
extension;
location.

They should not be passed to source parsers.

5.36 Frontend Architecture

When supported frontend frameworks are detected, StackSense should identify frontend-specific architecture such as:

components;
routes;
layouts;
state boundaries;
API clients;
external service calls;
shared UI libraries;
frontend-backend communication.

The frontend architecture should connect to backend architecture where evidence supports the relationship.

5.37 Backend Architecture

When supported backend frameworks are detected, StackSense should identify:

routes;
controllers/views;
services;
repositories/data access;
models;
middleware;
dependency injection;
external integrations;
background tasks;
database relationships.

Framework-specific terminology should be normalized into common architecture concepts where appropriate.

5.38 Full-Stack Applications

Some frameworks combine frontend and backend responsibilities.

Next.js is a key example.

StackSense must therefore allow a single framework to contribute to multiple architectural layers.

The analyzer should determine the role of each relevant artifact rather than assigning the entire framework to a single layer.

5.39 Runtime and Framework Are Independent Dimensions

The following must remain conceptually separate:

Language
Runtime
Framework
Application Role

For example:

TypeScript
↓
Node.js
↓
NestJS
↓
Backend Service

or:

TypeScript
↓
Browser
↓
React
↓
Frontend Application

or:

TypeScript
↓
Node.js + Browser
↓
Next.js
↓
Full-Stack Application

This separation is necessary for accurate architecture reconstruction.

5.40 Analysis Capability Levels

Each supported ecosystem may have different analysis depth.

The system may distinguish between:

Level 1:
File and language detection.

Level 2:
Generic structural analysis.

Level 3:
Dependency and relationship analysis.

Level 4:
Framework-aware architecture extraction.

Level 5:
Advanced semantic analysis.

Not every framework must immediately support every level.

The system must not pretend that an unsupported capability exists.

5.41 Framework Analyzer Interface

Framework-specific analyzers should follow a common architectural interface.

Conceptually:

FrameworkDetector
↓
FrameworkAnalyzer
↓
Common IR

Different framework analyzers may implement framework-specific logic internally.

They must emit compatible representations into the common analysis pipeline.

5.42 Language Analyzer Interface

Language-specific analysis should similarly follow a common conceptual boundary.

Conceptually:

LanguageDetector
↓
LanguageAnalyzer
↓
Common IR

Examples:

PythonAnalyzer
JavaScriptAnalyzer
TypeScriptAnalyzer

JSX and TSX analysis may use the corresponding JavaScript/TypeScript analyzers with JSX-specific parsing and semantic handling.

5.43 No Framework-Specific Source of Truth

A Django analyzer, NestJS analyzer, or Next.js analyzer must not independently define architecture truth.

Framework analyzers contribute evidence to the common analysis pipeline.

The final architecture is constructed through the approved architecture-building process.

5.44 Cross-Framework Normalization

Different frameworks often express similar concepts differently.

For example:

Django View
FastAPI Route Handler
Express Route Handler
NestJS Controller
Next.js Route Handler

may all contribute to the broader concept of an HTTP endpoint or application entry point.

StackSense should normalize such concepts where appropriate while preserving framework-specific metadata.

5.45 Framework-Specific Metadata Preservation

Normalization must not destroy useful framework information.

For example, an endpoint may be represented as:

Generic:
HTTP Endpoint

Metadata:
Framework = FastAPI
Router = users
Handler = create_user

This allows both generic architecture queries and framework-specific exploration.

5.46 Supported Ecosystem Expansion

Future language/framework support should be added through the same architecture.

Adding a new language should not require rewriting the Architecture Model.

Adding a new framework should not require changing existing framework analyzers unnecessarily.

The intended extension model is:

New Language
↓
Language Analyzer
↓
Common IR
↓
Existing Architecture Pipeline

New Framework
↓
Framework Detector/Analyzer
↓
Common IR
↓
Existing Architecture Pipeline

5.47 Initial Framework Support Is Not Exclusive Forever

The currently approved framework list defines the MVP analysis boundary.

It does not mean StackSense can never support:

additional Python frameworks;
additional JavaScript frameworks;
additional TypeScript frameworks;
additional runtimes;
additional languages.

Such additions require proper implementation and testing.

Major architectural additions require explicit approval.

5.48 Unsupported Repository Behavior

When a repository falls outside the supported ecosystem:

Repository
↓
Detect Supported Portions
↓
Analyze What Is Reliable
↓
Mark Unsupported Portions
↓
Produce Partial Result When Safe

StackSense must prefer partial reliable analysis over complete fabricated analysis.

5.49 Repository Analysis Must Remain Evidence-Based

Language and framework classification must be based on repository evidence.

The system should consider:

file extensions;
package manifests;
dependency declarations;
imports;
configuration;
framework-specific structures;
directory conventions;
runtime metadata;
lockfiles;
source patterns.

No single weak signal should automatically determine the complete architecture.

5.50 Section Summary

The initial StackSense language and framework boundary is:

Python
JavaScript
TypeScript
JSX
TSX

Approved Python framework targets:

Django
Flask
FastAPI

Approved JavaScript/TypeScript runtime:

Node.js

Approved JavaScript/TypeScript framework targets:

Express
NestJS
Next.js

The analyzer must distinguish:

language;
runtime;
framework;
application role.

Framework-specific analysis enriches generic language analysis.

All framework analyzers feed the common IR and Architecture Model.

Unsupported languages and frameworks must degrade gracefully rather than causing fabricated architecture.

Mixed-language and multi-framework repositories are valid targets.

Generated code, build output, binaries, configuration, documentation, and other non-source artifacts must be classified appropriately rather than being blindly passed through source analysis.

The central rule is:

StackSense must analyze supported ecosystems deeply where possible, normalize their architectural meaning into a common representation, preserve framework-specific evidence, and never claim architectural understanding that the available repository evidence does not support.

End of Section 5.


6. REPOSITORY & ARTIFACT ANALYSIS BOUNDARY

6.1 Purpose

This section defines what StackSense is allowed to ingest, classify, analyze, retain, index, and use as evidence when processing a software repository.

The repository boundary is intentionally broader than the programming-language boundary.

A software repository is not composed only of source code.

It may contain:

* source files;
* configuration;
* dependency manifests;
* documentation;
* tests;
* images;
* metadata;
* generated artifacts;
* build output;
* binary files;
* archives;
* infrastructure definitions;
* miscellaneous files.

StackSense must therefore classify repository artifacts before deciding how each artifact participates in analysis.

The central rule is:

> Every repository artifact must have an explicit classification and an explicit role in the analysis pipeline.

6.2 Repository Snapshot Principle

Every analysis must operate against a specific immutable repository snapshot.

The conceptual flow is:

Repository Input
↓
Acquisition
↓
Immutable Snapshot
↓
Artifact Inventory
↓
Artifact Classification
↓
Analysis

The snapshot provides the stable input boundary for the analysis.

Workers operating on the same analysis must reference the same snapshot rather than independently re-reading a changing repository.

6.3 Snapshot Immutability

Once an analysis snapshot has been created, the snapshot must be treated as immutable.

The analysis pipeline must not modify the original repository snapshot while processing it.

Temporary processing files may be created separately.

The canonical snapshot must remain available as the evidence baseline for:

* source analysis;
* evidence references;
* debugging;
* reproducibility;
* architecture version generation;
* future projection rebuilding where required.

6.4 Repository Inventory

Before source analysis begins, StackSense must construct a repository inventory.

The inventory should identify, where applicable:

* relative path;
* artifact type;
* extension;
* detected language;
* detected framework relevance;
* file size;
* binary/text classification;
* generated status;
* ignored status;
* sensitive-data status;
* analysis eligibility;
* exclusion reason where applicable.

The inventory is a structural representation of the repository.

It is not itself the Architecture Model.

6.5 Artifact Classification

Every discovered artifact must be assigned an appropriate classification.

The primary classification categories are:

1. Source Code
2. Configuration / Specification
3. Documentation
4. Tests
5. Images / Visual Assets
6. Generated / Build Artifacts
7. Binary / Non-Analyzable Artifacts
8. Archives / Containers
9. Unknown / Unsupported Artifacts

An artifact may also carry secondary metadata such as:

* language;
* framework;
* generated status;
* sensitive status;
* excluded status;
* analysis status.

6.6 Source Code

Source code is the primary architecture evidence category.

The initially supported source languages/syntaxes are:

* Python;
* JavaScript;
* TypeScript;
* JSX;
* TSX.

Source analysis may extract:

* modules;
* packages;
* classes;
* functions;
* methods;
* imports;
* exports;
* calls;
* inheritance;
* decorators;
* routes;
* framework structures;
* service relationships;
* dependency relationships;
* other architecture-relevant structures.

Source code should generally receive the highest architectural evidence weight because it directly represents implemented behavior and structure.

6.7 Configuration and Specification Artifacts

Configuration and specification files are secondary but important architectural evidence.

Examples include:

* dependency manifests;
* lockfiles;
* framework configuration;
* build configuration;
* routing configuration;
* deployment configuration;
* environment configuration;
* API specifications;
* schema definitions;
* infrastructure configuration;
* project metadata.

These artifacts may reveal:

* frameworks;
* dependencies;
* runtimes;
* service boundaries;
* external integrations;
* databases;
* queues;
* build structure;
* deployment relationships;
* environment configuration.

Configuration is evidence, not automatically architectural truth.

7.8 Dependency Manifests

Dependency manifests are particularly important because they help determine:

* language ecosystem;
* runtime;
* framework;
* external libraries;
* package relationships;
* project boundaries.

Examples include:

Python:

* pyproject.toml;
* requirements files;
* dependency configuration;
* supported Python packaging metadata.

JavaScript/TypeScript:

* package.json;
* package manager metadata;
* lockfiles.

Dependency declarations should be retained as evidence.

However, a declared dependency alone must not automatically be interpreted as an active runtime architecture relationship.

6.9 Lockfiles

Lockfiles are metadata artifacts.

They may be used to determine:

* dependency versions;
* package identity;
* reproducibility information;
* framework evidence;
* runtime ecosystem information.

They must not normally be parsed as source code.

Lockfiles should not be allowed to create duplicate source-level architecture relationships.

6.10 Documentation

Documentation is a secondary evidence category.

Examples include:

* README files;
* Markdown;
* plain text;
* architecture documentation;
* API documentation;
* design notes;
* developer documentation.

Documentation can help StackSense understand:

* intended architecture;
* terminology;
* component purpose;
* system behavior;
* external integrations;
* deployment expectations;
* domain concepts.

However:

> Documentation does not automatically override deterministic source evidence.

Documentation and implementation may disagree.

When they conflict, StackSense should preserve the distinction rather than silently modifying architectural truth to match documentation.

6.11 Tests

Tests are retained as secondary evidence.

Tests may provide valuable information about:

* expected behavior;
* component boundaries;
* API contracts;
* service interactions;
* dependencies;
* integration behavior;
* intended workflows.

Tests should not automatically become the primary source of architecture.

They can strengthen or contextualize architectural evidence discovered elsewhere.

6.12 Images and Visual Assets

Images may exist within a repository.

Examples include:

* architecture diagrams;
* screenshots;
* UI designs;
* documentation images;
* icons;
* other visual assets.

Images must be classified separately from source code.

An image may be retained as a repository artifact and associated with its original path.

However, images must not automatically be treated as authoritative architecture evidence.

Image-based architecture extraction is not part of the mandatory MVP architecture unless explicitly approved as a future capability.

6.13 Generated and Build Artifacts

Generated and build artifacts must be distinguished from primary source artifacts.

Examples include:

* compiled JavaScript;
* build directories;
* distribution directories;
* generated API clients;
* generated schemas;
* generated source;
* bundles;
* transpiled output;
* framework-generated output.

When the original source is available, generated artifacts should generally not be treated as primary architectural evidence.

This prevents duplicate or misleading relationships.

For example:

TypeScript Source
↓
Compiled JavaScript
↓
Generated Bundle

must not be interpreted as three independent implementations of the same architecture.

6.14 Generated Artifact Detection

Generated status may be inferred from:

* known directory conventions;
* build configuration;
* file headers;
* generated markers;
* package configuration;
* source/output relationships;
* known framework conventions.

Generated detection should be conservative.

If StackSense cannot reliably determine that a file is generated, it should not silently discard potentially useful evidence.

6.15 Binary and Non-Analyzable Artifacts

Binary files must be classified separately from source and text artifacts.

Examples include:

* executables;
* compiled libraries;
* fonts;
* media;
* binary assets;
* unrelated binary blobs.

Binary artifacts may still contribute inventory metadata such as:

* path;
* extension;
* size;
* classification.

They must not be passed through source parsers.

6.16 Archives

Archives may be encountered inside repository inputs.

Examples include:

* ZIP;
* TAR;
* TAR.GZ;
* other supported archive formats.

The initial repository acquisition process may extract an approved top-level repository archive into the immutable analysis snapshot.

However, arbitrary nested archives must not automatically trigger recursive repository analysis.

6.17 Nested Archive Boundary

Nested archives are treated as artifacts unless an explicitly approved analysis capability exists for them.

For example:

repository.zip
↓
extract
↓
repository contents

is part of normal repository acquisition.

But:

repository
↓
archive.zip
↓
nested-project.zip
↓
another-project.zip

must not cause unbounded recursive analysis.

This protects against:

* resource exhaustion;
* archive bombs;
* accidental recursive ingestion;
* unclear repository boundaries.

6.18 Unknown and Unsupported Artifacts

Unknown artifacts must not be silently treated as source code.

If StackSense cannot confidently classify an artifact, it should:

* retain it in the inventory;
* classify it as unknown;
* preserve metadata;
* avoid unsupported parsing;
* continue processing other eligible artifacts.

Unknown files should therefore not cause the entire repository analysis to fail.

6.19 Inventory-Only Artifacts

Some artifacts may be retained only for inventory purposes.

Examples include:

* unsupported binary files;
* unknown file formats;
* irrelevant media;
* unsupported source languages.

Inventory-only artifacts may contribute:

* file counts;
* repository structure;
* metadata;
* repository statistics.

They do not contribute unsupported semantic architecture claims.

6.20 Artifact Analysis Roles

An artifact may have one of several analysis roles:

Primary Evidence

Directly contributes to architecture extraction.

Examples:

* supported source code.

Secondary Evidence

Can support, explain, or enrich architecture findings.

Examples:

* configuration;
* dependency manifests;
* documentation;
* tests.

Metadata Evidence

Provides structural or repository-level information.

Examples:

* lockfiles;
* package metadata;
* file inventory.

Inventory Only

Retained for repository completeness but not semantically analyzed.

Examples:

* unsupported binaries;
* unknown formats.

Excluded

Not processed because it violates analysis policy, user configuration, or safety/resource constraints.

6.21 Evidence Priority

StackSense should generally prioritize evidence according to reliability.

A conceptual ordering is:

1. Deterministic source analysis
2. Explicit configuration/specification
3. Dependency metadata
4. Tests
5. Documentation
6. Other contextual evidence
7. Unsupported or inferred information

This ordering does not mean lower-priority evidence is useless.

It means lower-priority evidence should not silently override stronger evidence.

6.22 Conflicting Evidence

Different artifacts may disagree.

For example:

Source:
Service A calls Service B.

Documentation:
Service A calls Service C.

StackSense must not silently select one without preserving the conflict.

The system should distinguish:

* confirmed evidence;
* conflicting evidence;
* inferred information;
* unsupported claims.

The Architecture Model must not be modified solely to make conflicting sources appear consistent.

6.23 Evidence Provenance

Architecture evidence should retain provenance wherever practical.

A provenance reference should be able to identify information such as:

* source artifact;
* repository snapshot;
* path;
* source location;
* analyzer;
* analysis stage;
* evidence type;
* architecture version.

This allows the user to move from:

Architecture Fact

back toward:

Repository Evidence.

6.24 Sensitive Artifact Detection

Repository contents must be treated as potentially sensitive.

Sensitive information may appear in:

* environment files;
* configuration;
* source code;
* documentation;
* test fixtures;
* logs;
* connection strings;
* credentials;
* API keys.

StackSense must use content-aware detection where appropriate.

Sensitive values must not be blindly ingested into:

* knowledge indexes;
* embeddings;
* AI prompts;
* reports;
* diagrams;
* normal API responses;
* logs.

6.25 Secrets Are Never Normal Architecture Evidence

The existence of a configuration variable may be architecture-relevant.

The secret value stored in that variable is not.

For example:

DATABASE_URL exists

may be useful evidence.

A password contained inside DATABASE_URL must not become architecture knowledge.

The system should preserve useful structural information while removing or redacting sensitive values.

6.26 Secret Redaction

When sensitive content is encountered, StackSense should prefer:

Detect
↓
Classify
↓
Redact / Exclude Sensitive Value
↓
Preserve Safe Structural Information

rather than:

Detect
↓
Store Entire File in Knowledge System

Secret handling must apply consistently across:

* source analysis;
* indexing;
* embeddings;
* AI context;
* logs;
* reports;
* API responses.

6.27 User Exclusions

Users may be allowed to configure exclusions for repository analysis.

Exclusions may include:

* directories;
* files;
* patterns;
* artifact classes;
* specific analysis scopes.

However, user exclusions must remain subject to mandatory safety and system constraints.

A user exclusion must not:

* expose secrets;
* disable mandatory security controls;
* cause unsafe archive extraction;
* bypass resource limits;
* allow arbitrary code execution.

6.28 .gitignore Behavior

`.gitignore` should be treated as an advisory repository signal rather than an absolute StackSense security boundary.

A `.gitignore` entry may indicate that a file is normally excluded from version control.

However, the existence of a file in the supplied repository snapshot means StackSense must still classify it according to its actual content and safety rules.

`.gitignore` must not be treated as permission to ingest sensitive data.

6.29 Exclusion Does Not Mean Snapshot Deletion

When a file is excluded from semantic analysis, that does not mean the original immutable snapshot must be modified or destroyed.

The conceptual distinction is:

Immutable Snapshot
↓
Complete Repository Inventory
↓
Analysis Eligibility
↓
Excluded From Semantic Processing

This preserves reproducibility and allows the system to explain why an artifact was not analyzed.

6.30 Effective Analysis Configuration

Every analysis should have an effective configuration describing relevant analysis choices.

This may include:

* enabled language analyzers;
* enabled framework analyzers;
* exclusions;
* resource limits;
* analysis mode;
* relevant feature flags;
* other approved analysis settings.

The effective configuration should be associated with the analysis so that results can be reproduced or explained.

6.31 Configuration Versioning

If an analysis configuration affects the meaning of the resulting Architecture Model, the configuration must be associated with the analysis or architecture version.

This prevents:

Analysis V1

from being interpreted as though it were generated using:

Analysis Configuration V2.

6.32 Repository Structure Preservation

The original relative paths of artifacts should be preserved in the analysis snapshot.

Paths are useful evidence for:

* module boundaries;
* application boundaries;
* package structure;
* framework conventions;
* source references;
* user navigation.

Path information must be handled safely and must not permit path traversal outside the analysis sandbox.

6.33 Path Safety

Repository paths must be normalized and validated before being used.

StackSense must defend against:

* `../` traversal;
* absolute-path extraction;
* symbolic-link abuse;
* archive path traversal;
* paths escaping the analysis sandbox.

All repository processing must remain inside the intended analysis boundary.

6.34 Symbolic Links

Symbolic links must be handled carefully.

The analyzer must not blindly follow links outside the repository snapshot.

If symbolic links are supported, their targets must remain within the allowed analysis boundary.

Unsafe or external links should be classified and handled without allowing repository input to escape the sandbox.

6.35 File Size and Resource Eligibility

Individual files must be evaluated against the resource limits defined by the project.

A very large file must not be allowed to consume unlimited parser memory or worker time.

If a file exceeds its applicable limit, StackSense should:

* classify it;
* record the reason;
* exclude it from the affected analysis stage;
* continue where safe;
* expose an appropriate warning.

The exact numerical limits are defined in Section 7.

6.36 Repository Size and File Count

Repository-level limits are required to protect the analysis system.

StackSense must enforce limits on at least:

* total repository size;
* total file count;
* individual file size;
* extracted archive size;
* analysis resource consumption.

These limits are safety boundaries rather than arbitrary restrictions.

Exact approved values are defined in Section 7.

6.37 Resource Limits Apply Before Expensive Processing

Resource limits should be checked as early as practical.

The system should not:

Download an unrestricted repository
↓
Extract everything
↓
Start analysis
↓
Discover it is too large

when the limit can be detected earlier.

Where practical:

Acquisition
↓
Validation
↓
Size / Count Checks
↓
Extraction / Analysis

must occur in controlled stages.

6.38 No Unbounded Repository Processing

StackSense must never assume that a repository is small enough to process without limits.

Potentially expensive operations include:

* archive extraction;
* parsing;
* AST construction;
* dependency resolution;
* graph construction;
* indexing;
* embedding;
* diagram generation;
* AI processing.

Each must operate within defined resource boundaries.

6.39 Analysis of Large Repositories

When a repository exceeds the configured limits, StackSense should fail or reject the analysis according to the applicable resource policy rather than silently processing an arbitrary subset.

Where partial analysis is explicitly supported, the system must clearly communicate what was excluded and why.

The system must not present an incomplete analysis as a complete representation of the repository.

6.40 Repository Completeness

When an analysis is accepted, StackSense should maintain a clear distinction between:

Complete Snapshot

The full accepted repository snapshot.

Analyzed Artifacts

Artifacts successfully processed by the applicable analyzers.

Excluded Artifacts

Artifacts intentionally excluded.

Unsupported Artifacts

Artifacts outside supported analysis capability.

Failed Artifacts

Artifacts that could not be analyzed successfully.

This distinction is important for trustworthy analysis results.

6.41 Artifact Processing State

Individual artifacts may have processing states such as:

DISCOVERED
↓
CLASSIFIED
↓
ELIGIBLE
↓
ANALYZING
↓
ANALYZED

or:

EXCLUDED
UNSUPPORTED
FAILED

These states should not be confused with the overall analysis lifecycle.

6.42 Parser Failure

If one supported source file fails to parse, StackSense should not automatically fail the entire repository analysis.

Instead:

File
↓
Parser Failure
↓
Record Diagnostic
↓
Mark File Failed
↓
Continue Independent Analysis

unless the failed artifact is critical to a required architectural stage.

6.43 Framework Detection Failure

If framework-specific analysis fails but generic language analysis remains possible, StackSense should degrade to the generic analysis where safe.

For example:

FastAPI Analyzer Failure
↓
Generic Python Analysis
↓
Partial Architecture Evidence

The system must explicitly communicate that framework-specific information may be incomplete.

6.44 Unsupported Framework Handling

If an unsupported framework is detected:

* generic language analysis should continue where possible;
* framework-specific analysis should not be fabricated;
* the framework should be recorded as unsupported/unknown;
* the resulting architecture should indicate the limitation where relevant.

6.45 Multiple Applications in One Repository

The repository boundary must allow multiple applications or services within one snapshot.

Examples:

frontend/
backend/
worker/

or:

apps/
web/
api/
admin/

or:

services/
auth/
payments/
notifications/

StackSense should identify application/service boundaries where evidence supports them.

The repository itself must not automatically be treated as a single application.

6.46 Monorepo Boundary

Monorepos are valid analysis targets.

The analyzer should attempt to identify:

* applications;
* services;
* packages;
* shared libraries;
* infrastructure;
* tests;
* configuration;
* workspace boundaries.

The monorepo root remains the repository snapshot boundary.

Individual applications may become separate architectural entities within the Architecture Model.

6.47 Repository-Level Metadata

Repository-level metadata may include:

* repository name;
* snapshot identifier;
* analysis identifier;
* source type;
* detected languages;
* detected frameworks;
* artifact counts;
* analyzed/excluded counts;
* warnings;
* analysis configuration;
* analysis version.

This metadata helps users understand the scope of the generated architecture.

6.48 No Arbitrary Code Execution

Normal repository analysis must remain static.

StackSense must not execute arbitrary repository code merely to understand its architecture.

This includes avoiding automatic execution of:

* package installation scripts;
* post-install hooks;
* build scripts;
* shell scripts;
* repository executables;
* application startup commands.

Any future capability requiring execution must be explicitly isolated, sandboxed, security-reviewed, and separately approved.

6.49 Dependency Installation Boundary

Dependency manifests may be inspected for analysis.

StackSense must not automatically install arbitrary repository dependencies merely because they are declared.

Dependency installation can introduce:

* arbitrary code execution;
* network access;
* malicious packages;
* resource consumption;
* supply-chain risk.

Normal static analysis should therefore operate without executing repository installation scripts.

6.50 Network Access During Analysis

Repository analysis should not assume unrestricted outbound network access.

The analyzer should prefer information available from the repository snapshot.

External network access, if ever required by a specific analysis capability, must be explicitly controlled and security-reviewed.

This is especially important because repositories may contain configuration intended to contact external services.

6.51 Evidence Boundary

Only information that has entered the approved analysis pipeline may become architecture or knowledge evidence.

The system must not casually incorporate:

* unrelated host files;
* developer machine state;
* arbitrary environment variables;
* external credentials;
* uncontrolled network responses;
* data outside the repository snapshot.

This keeps the analysis reproducible and prevents accidental data leakage.

6.52 Source-to-Knowledge Boundary

Not every repository artifact should automatically be embedded or indexed.

The knowledge pipeline must decide which artifacts are appropriate for:

* lexical indexing;
* semantic indexing;
* graph projection;
* AI context;
* evidence storage.

For example:

Binary File
↓
Inventory

rather than:

Binary File
↓
Embedding
↓
AI Context

6.53 Source-to-Diagram Boundary

Diagrams must not be generated directly from arbitrary raw repository files.

The approved flow is:

Repository
↓
Analysis
↓
IR
↓
Architecture Model
↓
Diagram Specification
↓
Layout
↓
React Flow

This prevents inconsistent diagrams from independently interpreting raw source files.

6.54 Repository Boundary and Architecture Truth

The repository is the raw evidence source.

It is not itself the Architecture Model.

The relationship is:

Repository Snapshot
↓
Evidence
↓
IR
↓
Architecture Model

This distinction allows the analyzer to normalize different ecosystems into a common architecture representation.

6.55 Section Summary

The StackSense repository boundary follows these principles:

1. Every analysis operates against an immutable repository snapshot.
2. The repository is inventoried before semantic analysis.
3. Every artifact receives an explicit classification.
4. Source code is the primary architecture evidence.
5. Configuration and specifications provide secondary architecture evidence.
6. Documentation and tests provide contextual evidence.
7. Images are retained as artifacts but are not automatically authoritative architecture evidence.
8. Generated/build output must be distinguished from primary source.
9. Binary and unknown artifacts must not be blindly analyzed.
10. Nested archives must not trigger unbounded recursive analysis.
11. Sensitive information must be detected and excluded from normal knowledge flows.
12. Secrets must never become ordinary architecture evidence.
13. User exclusions are allowed within mandatory safety boundaries.
14. `.gitignore` is advisory rather than an absolute security boundary.
15. Exclusion does not require modifying the immutable snapshot.
16. Effective analysis configuration must be associated with the analysis.
17. Repository paths must be preserved safely.
18. Path traversal and unsafe symbolic links must be prevented.
19. Resource limits apply to repository size, file count, file size, extraction, and processing.
20. Exact resource values are defined separately in Section 7.
21. Individual parser failures should not unnecessarily fail the entire analysis.
22. Unsupported languages and frameworks should degrade gracefully.
23. Monorepos and mixed-language repositories are valid targets.
24. Normal analysis must not execute arbitrary repository code.
25. Dependency installation is not automatically performed during static analysis.
26. External network access must not be assumed.
27. Only approved repository evidence may enter architecture and knowledge pipelines.
28. Not every artifact should automatically be indexed or embedded.
29. Diagrams must originate from the Architecture Model rather than raw repository interpretation.
30. The repository is evidence, while the Architecture Model is the resulting canonical architectural representation.

The fundamental rule is:

> StackSense must preserve the complete accepted repository snapshot and distinguish what it knows, what it analyzed, what it excluded, what it does not support, and what failed. It must never turn unsupported or unsafe artifacts into fabricated architectural knowledge.

End of Section 6.



7. RESOURCE LIMITS & SAFETY CONSTRAINTS

7.1 Purpose

This section defines the resource and safety boundaries within which StackSense is allowed to acquire, store, extract, analyze, index, visualize, and process repositories.

These limits exist to protect:

* system stability;
* worker availability;
* memory;
* CPU;
* disk;
* queue capacity;
* database capacity;
* search infrastructure;
* graph infrastructure;
* AI-provider usage;
* user experience;
* operational cost.

Resource limits are architectural safety boundaries.

They are not merely performance optimizations.

7.2 Core Resource Principle

StackSense must never assume that a repository is small enough to process without limits.

Every potentially expensive operation must have a bounded resource policy.

This includes:

* repository acquisition;
* archive extraction;
* file parsing;
* AST construction;
* symbol resolution;
* dependency analysis;
* architecture construction;
* graph construction;
* indexing;
* embedding;
* diagram generation;
* report generation;
* AI processing.

The system must fail safely when a resource boundary is exceeded.

7.3 Initial MVP Resource Profile

The initial MVP resource profile is intentionally designed to support reasonably sized software projects while preventing extremely large or malicious inputs from consuming unlimited resources.

The following limits are the default architectural baseline.

These values may be tuned during implementation and benchmarking, but changing the category or intent of a limit does not require changing the architecture.

7.4 Maximum Repository Size

Maximum accepted repository snapshot size:

500 MB

This limit applies to the repository content after acquisition and before semantic analysis.

Repositories exceeding this limit should normally be rejected before expensive analysis begins.

The system must communicate that the repository exceeds the supported analysis boundary.

7.5 Maximum Extracted Repository Size

Maximum extracted size:

1 GB

This limit exists separately from the compressed repository size.

For example:

10 MB archive
↓
900 MB extracted content

may be accepted if all other limits are satisfied.

But:

10 MB archive
↓
10 GB extracted content

must be rejected.

This protects against archive bombs and extreme compression ratios.

7.6 Maximum Individual File Size

Maximum individual analyzable text/source file size:

5 MB

Files larger than this limit must not be passed blindly into source parsers.

The system should:

* classify the file;
* record that it exceeded the limit;
* exclude it from the affected semantic analysis;
* continue processing other files where safe.

7.7 Maximum File Count

Maximum repository file count:

50,000 files

This includes files discovered in the accepted repository snapshot.

The limit exists because file count can become expensive even when total repository size is relatively small.

A repository with hundreds of thousands of tiny files can still create significant:

* parsing overhead;
* metadata overhead;
* graph complexity;
* indexing cost;
* database writes.

7.8 Maximum Directory Depth

The analyzer should enforce a maximum supported directory nesting depth.

Initial baseline:

100 levels

This prevents pathological repository structures from causing excessive traversal or recursion.

Normal software repositories should remain well below this boundary.

7.9 Maximum Path Length

Repository paths must be bounded to a safe supported length.

Initial baseline:

4,096 characters

Paths exceeding the supported boundary should be rejected or classified as invalid artifacts rather than being passed into filesystem operations without validation.

7.10 Maximum Archive Nesting

Maximum nested archive extraction depth:

2 levels

Top-level repository archive extraction does not count as an unsafe recursive archive operation.

Nested archives beyond the supported depth must not be automatically extracted.

Example:

repository.zip
↓
project/
↓
archive.zip
↓
nested-project.zip

The system may analyze the repository and first-level nested archive according to policy, but must not continue recursively without an explicitly approved capability.

7.11 Maximum Compression Ratio

Archive extraction should apply a compression-ratio safety check.

A compressed archive that expands by an extreme factor must be rejected even when the compressed file itself is small.

The system should evaluate:

compressed size
+
expected extracted size
+
compression ratio

before allowing unrestricted extraction.

The exact implementation threshold may be tuned according to the archive library and deployment environment.

7.12 Maximum Total Extracted Files

The extraction process must enforce the repository file-count boundary before allowing unbounded extraction.

The system must not fully extract an archive that is already known to exceed the allowed file count.

Where the archive format permits safe inspection of entry metadata before extraction, that information should be used.

7.13 Maximum Parsing Time Per File

Individual source parsing must be bounded.

A pathological source file must not be allowed to occupy a worker indefinitely.

Initial baseline:

30 seconds per individual source-analysis operation

If the parser exceeds the allowed processing time:

* terminate the affected operation safely;
* record the failure;
* mark the artifact as failed;
* continue independent processing where possible.

7.14 Maximum Analysis Time

A single repository analysis must have a maximum execution boundary.

Initial baseline:

30 minutes

This is a safety boundary, not a guarantee that every repository will take this long.

An analysis should normally complete substantially faster.

If the analysis exceeds the configured maximum duration, it should transition into an appropriate failure or timeout state.

7.15 Analysis Stage Timeouts

The total analysis timeout should not be the only protection.

Expensive stages should also have individual timeouts where appropriate.

Potential stages include:

* acquisition;
* extraction;
* inventory;
* parsing;
* symbol resolution;
* architecture construction;
* graph projection;
* indexing;
* embedding;
* diagram generation;
* report generation.

A failure in one optional stage should not necessarily consume the entire analysis timeout.

7.16 Worker Resource Boundaries

Workers must operate within controlled resource limits.

Relevant limits include:

* memory;
* CPU;
* execution time;
* temporary storage;
* network access where applicable.

Workers must not assume unlimited host resources.

The exact container/runtime limits may vary by deployment environment, but the application must remain designed around bounded execution.

7.17 Memory Protection

Repository parsing and analysis must avoid loading the entire repository into memory unnecessarily.

Preferred behavior:

Repository
↓
Inventory
↓
Process Eligible Artifacts
↓
Release Temporary Memory
↓
Continue

rather than:

Repository
↓
Load Everything Into Memory
↓
Analyze

Large files and large collections should be processed incrementally where practical.

7.18 Temporary Storage Limit

Analysis may require temporary storage for:

* extraction;
* parser output;
* intermediate artifacts;
* generated reports;
* indexing batches;
* diagram generation.

Temporary storage must also be bounded.

Initial baseline:

2 GB temporary storage per analysis

An analysis must not be allowed to consume arbitrary host disk space.

7.19 Cleanup of Temporary Data

Temporary analysis data should be cleaned up when:

* analysis completes;
* analysis fails;
* analysis is cancelled;
* analysis times out.

Cleanup must be robust enough to prevent abandoned analyses from accumulating unlimited temporary files.

Where data is required for debugging or recovery, it must be explicitly promoted to persistent artifact storage rather than accidentally remaining in temporary directories.

7.20 Maximum Concurrent Analyses

The system must limit concurrent repository analyses.

Initial local/MVP baseline:

4 concurrent analyses per deployment

This value may be configurable depending on available CPU, memory, and worker capacity.

The architectural requirement is that concurrency must be bounded.

7.21 Per-Organization Concurrency

Organizations should have a configurable concurrency boundary for expensive operations.

Initial baseline:

2 concurrent repository analyses per organization

This prevents a single organization from consuming all available worker capacity.

The exact production quota may later become plan/deployment-specific.

7.22 Queue Capacity

The asynchronous queue must be bounded operationally.

RabbitMQ may contain queued jobs, but StackSense should not allow unlimited user-generated work to accumulate without control.

The system should monitor:

* queue depth;
* oldest queued job;
* task throughput;
* retry volume;
* failure rate.

If capacity is exhausted, new expensive jobs should be rejected or delayed explicitly rather than silently accepted into an uncontrolled backlog.

7.23 Queue Backpressure

When worker capacity is exhausted:

Client
↓
Create Analysis
↓
Capacity Check
↓
Accept / Queue / Reject

The system must not create unlimited background work.

Backpressure is required for:

* repository analysis;
* expensive AI operations;
* large indexing jobs;
* other high-cost background operations.

7.24 AI Request Limits

AI calls must have explicit resource controls.

Limits should apply to:

* requests per analysis;
* maximum context size;
* maximum output size;
* retry count;
* request timeout;
* provider-specific rate limits.

AI must not be called repeatedly without a bounded reason.

7.25 AI Call Budget

A single analysis should not automatically trigger an unbounded number of LLM requests.

AI calls should be associated with explicit purposes such as:

* architecture explanation;
* report generation;
* user question answering;
* diagram presentation assistance.

The system should prefer deterministic preprocessing and retrieval before invoking the LLM.

7.26 AI Retry Policy

AI provider failures should use bounded retries.

A reasonable pattern is:

Request
↓
Failure
↓
Retry with Backoff
↓
Failure
↓
Retry Limit
↓
Provider Failure
↓
Graceful Degradation

The system must not retry indefinitely.

7.27 AI Context Limits

The system must not send the entire repository to an LLM as the default mechanism for answering a question.

Instead:

User Question
↓
Retrieval
↓
Evidence Selection
↓
Context Construction
↓
LLM

This controls:

* token usage;
* cost;
* latency;
* irrelevant information;
* privacy exposure;
* hallucination risk.

7.28 Embedding Limits

Embedding generation must also be bounded.

The system should:

* chunk content according to approved knowledge rules;
* avoid embedding duplicate content unnecessarily;
* avoid embedding binary data;
* avoid embedding secret values;
* avoid embedding irrelevant artifacts;
* avoid generating unlimited embeddings for a single analysis.

7.29 Search Index Limits

Search indexing must be performed in bounded batches.

The system should avoid:

Repository
↓
One giant indexing operation

and prefer:

Repository
↓
Bounded Batches
↓
Elasticsearch

This reduces memory pressure and improves retry behavior.

7.30 Graph Size Limits

The Architecture Model and Neo4j projection must account for graph size.

Extremely large repositories can generate:

* huge node counts;
* huge edge counts;
* dense dependency graphs.

The system should not attempt to render an unbounded graph directly in the frontend.

Large architecture graphs must use:

* filtering;
* hierarchy;
* pagination where appropriate;
* aggregation;
* subgraph exploration;
* lazy loading.

7.31 Diagram Complexity Limits

The diagram engine must not attempt to render thousands of nodes in a single interactive diagram by default.

Initial baseline:

Maximum default diagram node count:
500 nodes

When a requested view exceeds the supported visualization size, the system should prefer:

* aggregation;
* hierarchy;
* filtering;
* component grouping;
* focused subgraphs;
* on-demand expansion.

The system should not simply create an unreadable "everything diagram."

7.32 Initial Diagram Size

Initial analysis should generate only a curated subset of high-value diagrams.

The system must not generate every possible diagram automatically.

This protects:

* analysis time;
* CPU;
* memory;
* frontend performance;
* storage;
* user experience.

Additional diagrams should be generated on demand or when justified by the architecture.

7.33 Diagram Layout Timeout

ELK layout operations must be bounded.

A highly complex graph must not block a worker indefinitely.

If layout exceeds its configured limit:

* the diagram generation should fail safely;
* the failure should be recorded;
* the Architecture Model remains valid;
* other diagrams or architecture capabilities should remain available.

7.34 Frontend Rendering Protection

The frontend must not blindly render arbitrarily large graphs.

The frontend should apply:

* graph size checks;
* lazy expansion;
* node grouping;
* filtering;
* viewport-based loading where appropriate.

A large architecture should remain explorable rather than attempting to render the entire repository at once.

7.35 API Payload Limits

REST APIs must enforce appropriate request and response size limits.

Large repository uploads and artifact transfers should use dedicated upload/storage mechanisms rather than enormous JSON request bodies.

API endpoints should reject clearly excessive payloads.

7.36 Pagination

Large collections must not be returned in unlimited API responses.

Pagination should be used for collections such as:

* analyses;
* architecture entities;
* artifacts;
* search results;
* audit logs;
* jobs;
* project resources.

The API must not assume that a collection will remain small forever.

7.37 Search Result Limits

Search operations should return bounded result sets.

The system should support:

* result limits;
* pagination;
* relevance ranking;
* filters;
* maximum context extraction.

A user query must not cause the system to retrieve the entire repository into memory or AI context.

7.38 Report Size Limits

Generated reports must also have bounded size.
