20.126 Security Request Flow
The complete protected-request flow is:
                         Browser
                            │
                         HTTPS
                            │
                            ▼
                    Reverse Proxy / TLS
                            │
                            ▼
                       API Gateway
                            │
                            ▼
                    Authentication
                            │
                            ▼
                   Identity Resolution
                            │
                            ▼
                   Authorization Check
                            │
                            ▼
                    Tenant Resolution
                            │
                            ▼
                    Resource Ownership
                            │
                            ▼
                    Application Service
                            │
                            ▼
                      Domain Policy
                            │
                            ▼
                       Repository
                            │
                            ▼
                       PostgreSQL


20.127 Multi-Tenant Data Flow
For a project resource:
User
 ↓
Organization
 ↓
Project
 ↓
Repository
 ↓
Analysis
 ↓
Architecture
 ↓
Knowledge
 ↓
Diagram / Report

Every downstream representation must retain enough context to enforce the original ownership boundary.

20.128 Secret Flow
The intended secret lifecycle is:
User/Admin
    ↓
Credential Input
    ↓
Secret Provider
    ↓
Encrypted / Protected Secret
    ↓
Secret Reference
    ↓
Domain Resource

When the credential is needed:
Resource
    ↓
Secret Reference
    ↓
Secret Provider
    ↓
Runtime Credential
    ↓
External Service

The raw secret should exist in memory only for as long as necessary.

20.129 Final Security Model
The fundamental security architecture is:
                         ZERO TRUST
                             │
              ┌──────────────┼──────────────┐
              ▼              ▼              ▼
        Authentication   Authorization   Secrets
              │              │              │
              ▼              ▼              ▼
            User          Tenant Scope    Secret Store
                             │
                             ▼
                          Project
                             │
              ┌──────────────┼──────────────┐
              ▼              ▼              ▼
          Repository     Architecture     Reports
              │              │              │
              ▼              ▼              ▼
           Analysis       Knowledge       Artifacts
                             │
                             ▼
                             AI

The critical invariant is:

No convenience mechanism—frontend checks, cache hits, graph queries, search results, background jobs, AI retrieval, or internal service calls—may bypass tenant authorization or secret-protection boundaries.


20.130 Final Principle
StackSense's security architecture can ultimately be summarized as:
Identity
    =
WHO ARE YOU?

Authorization
    =
WHAT MAY YOU DO?

Tenant Isolation
    =
WHOSE DATA MAY YOU ACCESS?

Secrets
    =
WHAT MUST NEVER BE EXPOSED?

Encryption
    =
HOW IS SENSITIVE DATA PROTECTED?

Audit
    =
WHAT HAPPENED?

Least Privilege
    =
WHAT IS THE MINIMUM ACCESS REQUIRED?

Zero Trust
    =
WHY SHOULD WE TRUST ANY REQUEST?

Therefore:

StackSense treats every user, request, repository, service, integration, and retrieved piece of content as untrusted until the appropriate security boundary explicitly establishes trust. Tenant isolation and secret protection are enforced at the backend and infrastructure layers, never delegated to the frontend or to user behavior.

End of Section 20.



21. STORAGE INFRASTRUCTURE & DEPLOYMENT
21.1 Purpose
This section defines how StackSense stores data, manages infrastructure, packages the application, and moves from local development to production deployment.
The architecture must support:

local development;
reproducible environments;
single-server deployment;
future cloud deployment;
future Kubernetes deployment;
persistent storage;
artifact storage;
database storage;
graph/search infrastructure;
background workers;
scheduled jobs;
secure configuration;
horizontal scaling where required.

The central principle is:

Application logic must remain independent from the physical deployment environment and storage implementation.


21.2 Infrastructure Philosophy
StackSense should follow an infrastructure-as-code and adapter-based deployment philosophy.
The application should not assume:
local filesystem
localhost
single process
single machine
specific cloud provider

Instead, infrastructure implementations should be replaceable.
Conceptually:
                 StackSense Application
                         │
        ┌────────────────┼────────────────┐
        ▼                ▼                ▼
     Storage          Database          Queue
        │                │                │
   ┌────┴────┐       PostgreSQL        Redis
   │         │
 Local       S3


21.3 Initial Deployment Philosophy
The first implementation should prioritize:

local reproducibility;
simple development;
Docker-based infrastructure;
modular services;
clear environment configuration.

The initial environment should run using Docker Compose or an equivalent local orchestration mechanism.

21.4 Local Development Environment
The local development stack should conceptually contain:
┌─────────────────────────────────────┐
│             Developer               │
└──────────────────┬──────────────────┘
                   │
          ┌────────▼────────┐
          │ Frontend        │
          │ Next.js         │
          └────────┬────────┘
                   │
          ┌────────▼────────┐
          │ Backend API     │
          └────────┬────────┘
                   │
       ┌───────────┼────────────┐
       ▼           ▼            ▼
 PostgreSQL      Redis        Storage
       │           │            │
       │           │         Local FS
       │           │
       └──────┬────┘
              ▼
           Workers
              │
       ┌──────┴──────┐
       ▼             ▼
    Neo4j       Elasticsearch

AI providers may be external or locally configured depending on the environment.

21.5 Docker as Local Infrastructure Boundary
Docker should be used to make infrastructure reproducible.
Infrastructure services should not require every developer to manually install:

PostgreSQL;
Redis;
Neo4j;
Elasticsearch.

Instead:
docker compose up

should be capable of bringing up the required development infrastructure.

21.6 Infrastructure Services
The initial infrastructure consists conceptually of:
Frontend
Backend API
Worker
Scheduler
PostgreSQL
Redis
Neo4j
Elasticsearch

Additional services may be introduced only when justified.

21.7 Storage Categories
StackSense has several distinct storage categories.
Transactional Storage
PostgreSQL.
Cache / Queue Storage
Redis.
Graph Projection
Neo4j.
Search Projection
Elasticsearch.
File / Artifact Storage
Local filesystem initially, S3 later.
These stores must not be treated as interchangeable.

21.8 PostgreSQL
PostgreSQL is the primary transactional database.
It should contain authoritative application state such as:

users;
organizations;
projects;
repositories;
analysis metadata;
findings;
architecture model;
jobs;
reports;
notification state;
configuration metadata.


21.9 PostgreSQL Is Canonical
The architecture must maintain the distinction:
PostgreSQL
     =
Canonical transactional state

while:
Neo4j
     =
Graph projection

Elasticsearch
     =
Search projection


21.10 PostgreSQL Persistence
Production PostgreSQL must use persistent storage.
A container restart must not destroy application data.
Conceptually:
PostgreSQL Container
        │
        ▼
Persistent Volume
        │
        ▼
Durable Storage


21.11 PostgreSQL Backups
Production PostgreSQL must have a backup strategy.
Backups should support:

scheduled backups;
retention;
restore;
integrity verification;
disaster recovery.

A backup that has never been restored/tested should not be considered a reliable recovery mechanism.

21.12 Database Migrations
Database schema changes must use controlled migrations.
Do not modify production schemas manually as the normal development workflow.
Conceptually:
Code Change
    ↓
Migration
    ↓
Test Environment
    ↓
Production


21.13 Migration Ownership
Database migrations belong to the backend persistence layer.
They should be version-controlled.
Every schema state should be reproducible from:
Base Schema
+
Migration History


21.14 Redis
Redis is infrastructure for transient/high-speed operations.
Potential uses:

background job queue;
caching;
rate limiting;
temporary coordination;
transient state.

Redis must not become the authoritative database for important business entities.

21.15 Redis Persistence
Redis persistence requirements depend on the workload.
For queue state, durability requirements should be selected based on the queue implementation and failure model.
For cache data:
Cache loss
    ≠
Data loss

The application must be able to reconstruct cached data.

21.16 Queue Infrastructure
The initial queue architecture uses Redis-based queue infrastructure.
The queue abstraction should remain replaceable.
Conceptually:
Job Producer
     ↓
Queue Abstraction
     ↓
Redis Queue
     ↓
Worker

The domain must not depend directly on Redis queue APIs.

21.17 Future Queue Evolution
If scale or system-design requirements justify it, the queue can later be replaced with:

RabbitMQ;
Kafka;
another distributed messaging platform.

This should require changing infrastructure adapters rather than rewriting domain logic.

21.18 Kafka Boundary
Kafka should not be introduced simply because it is technologically impressive.
Kafka becomes relevant if StackSense later requires:

high-throughput event streaming;
durable event history;
multiple independent consumers;
replayable event streams;
large-scale distributed event processing.

Until those requirements exist, Redis-based job infrastructure remains the simpler initial choice.

21.19 Neo4j
Neo4j stores graph projections derived from canonical architecture data.
It is used for:

dependency traversal;
impact analysis;
relationship exploration;
graph-oriented queries.


21.20 Neo4j Is Rebuildable
The system must be designed so that Neo4j can be rebuilt from canonical data.
Conceptually:
PostgreSQL Architecture
          ↓
Projection Job
          ↓
Neo4j

Therefore corruption/loss of the graph projection should not permanently destroy the architecture model.

21.21 Elasticsearch
Elasticsearch stores search/retrieval projections.
Potential indexed content includes:

architecture entities;
relationships;
source evidence;
findings;
documentation;
repository metadata.


21.22 Elasticsearch Is Rebuildable
Like Neo4j:
Canonical Data
      ↓
Projection
      ↓
Elasticsearch

Search index loss should result in degraded search, not loss of canonical application data.

21.23 Artifact Storage
Artifacts include:

generated reports;
exported diagrams;
potentially architecture snapshots;
generated files;
future analysis bundles.

The initial implementation uses local storage.

21.24 Local Artifact Storage
Development may use:
./storage/

or an equivalent configured directory.
The application must not hard-code the filesystem path.

21.25 Storage Abstraction
The backend should expose an abstraction such as:
ArtifactStorage

with operations conceptually including:
put()
get()
delete()
exists()
generate_access()

The exact API can evolve.

21.26 Local Storage Adapter
Initial implementation:
ArtifactStorage
      ↑
LocalArtifactStorage


21.27 S3 Adapter
Future implementation:
ArtifactStorage
      ↑
S3ArtifactStorage

The Report module should not know whether the artifact is stored locally or in S3.

21.28 S3 Migration
Moving from local storage to S3 should primarily involve:
Configuration
+
Storage Adapter

rather than rewriting Report/Diagram/business logic.

21.29 Object Storage Keys
Artifact paths/keys must be generated by the backend.
Example:
organizations/{organization_id}/
projects/{project_id}/
reports/{report_id}/
artifact

Users must not control arbitrary object-storage paths.

21.30 Artifact Metadata
PostgreSQL should store artifact metadata such as:
artifact_id
project_id
report_id
storage_provider
storage_key
content_type
size
created_at
checksum

The binary content itself may live in filesystem/S3.

21.31 Artifact Integrity
Generated artifacts should optionally include checksums.
For example:
SHA-256

This helps detect corruption and verify downloaded content.

21.32 Artifact Access
Artifacts must not be publicly accessible by default.
Access should follow:
User
 ↓
Authentication
 ↓
Authorization
 ↓
Artifact Endpoint
 ↓
Storage Adapter


21.33 Presigned URLs
When using S3, presigned URLs may be used for large artifact downloads.
The backend should generate them only after authorization.

21.34 Local Storage Security
Local storage must also enforce access control.
A user must not be able to guess:
storage/other-project/report.pdf

and retrieve another project's artifact.
The backend controls the mapping between artifact ID and storage location.

21.35 Storage Encryption
Sensitive artifacts should support encryption at rest.
For local deployments this depends on host/disk encryption.
For cloud object storage, server-side encryption should be enabled.
Application-level encryption may be added for particularly sensitive data.

21.36 Encryption Abstraction
Where application-level encryption is required:
EncryptionService
       ↓
Encrypt / Decrypt

The storage implementation should not own business encryption policy.

21.37 Configuration Architecture
Configuration must be environment-specific.
Conceptually:
Application
    ↑
Configuration
    ↑
Environment

Examples:
development
test
staging
production


21.38 Configuration Categories
Configuration includes:
Application
APP_ENV
DEBUG
LOG_LEVEL

Database
DATABASE_URL

Queue
REDIS_URL

Storage
STORAGE_PROVIDER
STORAGE_PATH
S3_BUCKET

AI
AI_PROVIDER

Secrets themselves should be provided through the secret-management mechanism defined in Section 20.

21.39 Configuration Validation
The application should validate required configuration during startup.
Bad:
Application starts successfully
    ↓
fails randomly when database is first used

Preferred:
Application startup
    ↓
Configuration validation
    ↓
Invalid
    ↓
Fail fast


21.40 Environment Separation
Development, test, staging, and production must use separate configuration.
Never accidentally point local development at production databases.

21.41 Infrastructure Naming
Infrastructure resources should use predictable names.
Conceptually:
stacksense-postgres
stacksense-redis
stacksense-neo4j
stacksense-elasticsearch

Environment-specific prefixes/suffixes may be used.

21.42 Docker Compose
The local environment should have a Compose configuration that describes infrastructure dependencies.
Conceptually:
compose/
    postgres
    redis
    neo4j
    elasticsearch

The exact structure may evolve.

21.43 Application Containers
The backend should be containerizable.
The frontend should also be containerizable where deployment requires it.
Workers and scheduler processes may use the same backend image with different commands.
Example:
Backend Image
├── API command
├── Worker command
└── Scheduler command

This avoids unnecessary duplicate images.

21.44 API Deployment
Production API deployment may look like:
Internet
    ↓
Load Balancer / Nginx
    ↓
Backend API

Multiple API instances can later be added.

21.45 Worker Deployment
Workers should be independently scalable.
Example:
Queue
 ├── Worker 1
 ├── Worker 2
 └── Worker 3

This is especially important for expensive repository analysis.

21.46 Scheduler Deployment
The scheduler should generally run as a controlled singleton or use distributed locking where multiple scheduler instances are deployed.
The architecture must avoid accidentally scheduling the same task multiple times due to duplicate scheduler instances.

21.47 Scheduler and Workers
Scheduler:
decides WHEN

Worker:
performs WHAT

Queue:
transports HOW

This separation must remain.

21.48 Horizontal Scaling
The architecture should support scaling stateless components horizontally.
Potentially scalable:
Frontend
API
Workers

Stateful systems require persistent/distributed infrastructure:
PostgreSQL
Redis
Neo4j
Elasticsearch


21.49 Stateless API
API instances should avoid storing important session/business state only in local memory.
Preferred:
API 1 ─┐
API 2 ─┼── PostgreSQL / Redis
API 3 ─┘

This allows load balancing.

21.50 Local In-Memory State
In-memory state may be used for:

short-lived caches;
request-local state;
performance optimizations.

It must not become the only copy of important business data.

21.51 Frontend Deployment
The Next.js frontend can be deployed as:

a Node.js application;
a container;
a platform-specific Next.js deployment.

The architecture must preserve API separation.

21.52 Reverse Proxy
A reverse proxy/load balancer may handle:

TLS;
routing;
compression;
request limits;
static assets;
load balancing.

Example:
Internet
   ↓
Nginx / Load Balancer
   ├── Frontend
   └── Backend API


21.53 Production Topology: Single Server
The first production-capable deployment can use a single server.
Conceptually:
                    SERVER
┌─────────────────────────────────────────┐
│ Nginx                                    │
│   │                                      │
│   ├── Next.js                            │
│   │                                      │
│   └── Backend API                        │
│                                          │
│ Worker                                   │
│ Scheduler                                │
│                                          │
│ PostgreSQL                               │
│ Redis                                    │
│ Neo4j                                    │
│ Elasticsearch                            │
└─────────────────────────────────────────┘

This is appropriate for early deployment and demonstration.

21.54 Production Topology: Scaled Server
As workload grows:
                 Load Balancer
                       │
          ┌────────────┼────────────┐
          ▼            ▼            ▼
       API 1        API 2        API 3
          │            │            │
          └────────────┼────────────┘
                       ▼
                 PostgreSQL
                       │
                 ┌─────┴─────┐
                 ▼           ▼
               Redis       Storage
                 │
          ┌──────┼──────┐
          ▼      ▼      ▼
       Worker  Worker  Worker


21.55 Cloud Deployment
Future cloud deployment can map existing abstractions to managed services.
For example:
PostgreSQL → Managed PostgreSQL
Redis → Managed Redis
S3 → Object Storage
Workers → Containers
Frontend → Managed/Container Hosting

The application architecture should not depend on a specific cloud vendor.

21.56 AWS Compatibility
The system can later map to AWS services such as:
RDS PostgreSQL
ElastiCache Redis
S3
ECS
ECR
ALB
Secrets Manager
CloudWatch

These are deployment choices, not domain dependencies.

21.57 Kubernetes
Kubernetes is a future deployment option.
Conceptually:
Kubernetes
├── Frontend
├── API
├── Workers
├── Scheduler
└── Supporting Services

Stateful services may be:

managed externally;
deployed using operators;
or hosted using appropriate persistent storage.


21.58 Kubernetes Boundary
Application code must not require Kubernetes-specific APIs.
Kubernetes should provide:

scheduling;
scaling;
service discovery;
health management;
rollout.


21.59 Health Checks
Every deployable service should expose appropriate health information.
Conceptually:
Liveness
    =
Is process alive?

Readiness
    =
Can this instance serve requests?


21.60 Readiness
The API should not receive production traffic until required dependencies/configuration are ready.
However, optional services should not necessarily make the entire application permanently unavailable.

21.61 Liveness
A temporary dependency failure should not necessarily cause the container to be restarted endlessly.
Health checks must distinguish:
Application dead

from:
Dependency temporarily unavailable


21.62 Graceful Shutdown
Services should handle shutdown signals.
The backend should:

stop accepting new work;
finish safe in-flight work;
acknowledge/close connections;
stop workers gracefully.


21.63 Worker Graceful Shutdown
Workers should not terminate halfway through a critical operation without handling job state correctly.
Jobs must support:
running
    ↓
retry / failed / completed

rather than becoming permanently stuck.

21.64 Job Durability
Important jobs should persist their lifecycle state.
Example:
Job
├── created
├── queued
├── running
├── completed
└── failed

This state belongs to the Jobs system, not only to Redis memory.

21.65 Deployment Configuration
Deployment should be reproducible.
A deployment should specify:

image version;
environment;
configuration;
migrations;
infrastructure dependencies;
secret references.


21.66 Versioned Images
Container images should use immutable/versioned tags where practical.
Avoid relying exclusively on:
latest

for production.

21.67 Deployment Process
A conceptual deployment pipeline is:
Git Commit
    ↓
CI
    ↓
Tests
    ↓
Security Checks
    ↓
Build Images
    ↓
Push Registry
    ↓
Deploy
    ↓
Run Migrations
    ↓
Health Checks
    ↓
Traffic


21.68 Migration Deployment Ordering
Schema changes must be compatible with the deployment sequence.
For breaking changes, use an expand/contract approach where required.
Example:
Expand schema
    ↓
Deploy compatible application
    ↓
Migrate data
    ↓
Remove old schema


21.69 Rollback
Deployment should support rollback of application versions.
However, database migrations require special care.
A rollback should not blindly reverse a destructive migration.

21.70 Database Migration Compatibility
Prefer backward-compatible migrations when deploying multiple API/worker versions.
This is particularly important when:
API V1
API V2

may temporarily coexist during rolling deployment.

21.71 Artifact Deployment
Application images should not contain user-generated reports or project artifacts.
Those belong in persistent artifact storage.

21.72 Container Immutability
Containers should be treated as disposable.
Important state must live in:

PostgreSQL;
Redis where appropriate;
persistent volumes;
object storage;
graph/search persistence.


21.73 Persistent Volume Rules
Persistent volumes are required for stateful local services.
For example:
PostgreSQL → postgres_data
Neo4j → neo4j_data
Elasticsearch → elastic_data

The exact volume names are implementation details.

21.74 Development vs Production Storage
Development:
Docker volumes
Local filesystem

Production:
Managed database
Durable disks
Object storage

The application storage interface remains consistent.

21.75 Storage Migration Contract
Changing storage provider must not change the domain API.
Example:
ReportService
      ↓
ArtifactStorage
      ↓
Local filesystem

Later:

ReportService
      ↓
ArtifactStorage
      ↓
S3


21.76 Storage Failure Handling
Storage failures should produce explicit states.
Example:
Report generated
      ↓
Artifact upload failed
      ↓
Report = STORAGE_FAILED

The system must not claim:
Report ready

when the artifact is unavailable.

21.77 Storage Retry
Transient storage failures may be retried.
Retries should be:

bounded;
observable;
idempotent where possible.


21.78 Artifact Idempotency
Repeated artifact-generation jobs should not unintentionally create uncontrolled duplicates.
Use stable identifiers or idempotency keys where appropriate.

21.79 Backup Scope
Backups should cover all required canonical state.
At minimum:
PostgreSQL

and required artifact storage.
Graph/search projections may be rebuildable and therefore can have different backup requirements.

21.80 Recovery Hierarchy
The system should be recoverable in this order:
Infrastructure
    ↓
PostgreSQL
    ↓
Application
    ↓
Graph/Search projections
    ↓
Caches

Caches should be the least critical recovery layer.

21.81 Recovery From Graph Loss
If Neo4j is lost:
PostgreSQL
    ↓
Projection Jobs
    ↓
Neo4j rebuilt

The application may temporarily provide degraded graph features.

21.82 Recovery From Search Loss
If Elasticsearch is lost:
Canonical Data
    ↓
Reindex
    ↓
Elasticsearch

Search functionality may be temporarily unavailable.

21.83 Recovery From Redis Loss
If Redis queue state is lost, job durability must determine what can be safely reconstructed.
Important business state must not exist only in Redis.

21.84 Disaster Recovery Goals
Future production deployment should define:
RPO
How much data loss is acceptable?
RTO
How quickly must the system recover?
Exact values are deployment-level decisions, not hard-coded application assumptions.

21.85 Observability Infrastructure
Production infrastructure should provide:

logs;
metrics;
traces;
health checks;
alerts.

These should integrate with the broader observability architecture.

21.86 Infrastructure Metrics
Useful infrastructure metrics include:
CPU
Memory
Disk
Network
PostgreSQL connections
Redis memory
Queue depth
Worker utilization
Elasticsearch health
Neo4j health
Artifact storage usage


21.87 Application Metrics
Application metrics include:
API latency
Analysis duration
Job latency
Queue wait time
Report generation time
AI latency
Search latency
Projection lag


21.88 Scaling Signals
Worker scaling may use:
Queue depth
Job wait time
CPU

API scaling may use:
Request rate
Latency
CPU
Memory


21.89 Infrastructure Cost Awareness
Infrastructure should scale according to actual requirements.
Do not deploy expensive managed services prematurely.
The initial architecture should remain affordable while preserving the correct boundaries.

21.90 Local-to-Production Parity
The local environment should resemble production conceptually:
Local:
Docker PostgreSQL
Docker Redis
Local storage

Production:
Managed PostgreSQL
Managed Redis
S3

The interfaces remain equivalent.

21.91 Development Convenience
Developers should be able to run StackSense without manually recreating the entire production infrastructure.
The goal is:
Clone
 ↓
Configure local environment
 ↓
docker compose up
 ↓
Run migrations
 ↓
Start application


21.92 Infrastructure Repository Structure
A conceptual repository structure is:
infra/
├── docker/
│   ├── backend/
│   ├── frontend/
│   └── worker/
│
├── compose/
│   ├── docker-compose.yml
│   └── docker-compose.dev.yml
│
├── deployment/
│   ├── local/
│   ├── server/
│   ├── cloud/
│   └── kubernetes/
│
└── scripts/
    ├── bootstrap
    ├── migrate
    └── healthcheck

This is a conceptual target rather than a requirement to create every directory immediately.

21.93 Infrastructure as Code
Production infrastructure should eventually be defined declaratively.
Potential technologies include:

Terraform;
cloud-native infrastructure definitions;
Kubernetes manifests;
Helm.

The specific tool may be selected later.

21.94 Infrastructure Version Control
Infrastructure configuration must be version-controlled.
Changes to:

deployment;
network;
storage;
environment configuration;
service definitions

should be reviewable.
Secrets themselves must not be committed.

21.95 Deployment Environments
StackSense should conceptually support:
Development
     ↓
Test
     ↓
Staging
     ↓
Production

Not every environment must have identical infrastructure scale.

21.96 Development
Purpose:

rapid development;
debugging;
local integration.

Characteristics:
Docker Compose
Local storage
Development credentials
Verbose logging


21.97 Test
Purpose:

automated tests;
integration tests;
contract tests.

Test data must remain isolated from development/production.

21.98 Staging
Purpose:

production-like validation;
deployment verification;
migration testing;
end-to-end validation.


21.99 Production
Purpose:

real users;
durable data;
high availability requirements where applicable;
strict security;
monitoring;
backups.


21.100 Deployment Strategy
The initial production deployment can use:
Single Server
+
Docker Compose
+
Persistent Volumes
+
Reverse Proxy
+
Backups

This provides a realistic production deployment without requiring Kubernetes immediately.

21.101 Future Deployment Strategy
As StackSense grows:
Single Server
      ↓
Multiple Containers
      ↓
Multiple Servers
      ↓
Managed Services
      ↓
Kubernetes / Cloud

The application architecture should remain stable throughout this evolution.

21.102 Zero-Downtime Goal
Future scaled deployments should target minimal downtime.
Mechanisms may include:

rolling deployments;
multiple API instances;
health checks;
load balancer draining;
backward-compatible migrations.


21.103 Worker Deployment Updates
Workers should be updated carefully because jobs may be in progress.
The deployment process should ensure:
Old Worker
   ↓
Finish / safely stop
   ↓
New Worker

without corrupting job state.

21.104 Scheduler Deployment Updates
Only one logical scheduler should execute scheduled tasks.
If multiple scheduler instances exist, distributed locking/leader election must prevent duplicate execution.

21.109 Infrastructure Rules
The following rules are mandatory:

Application logic must remain independent of deployment topology.
Local development must be reproducible.
Docker should provide the initial local infrastructure environment.
PostgreSQL is the primary transactional database.
PostgreSQL is the canonical persistence layer for application state.
Redis is used for queue/cache/transient infrastructure.
Redis must not become canonical business storage.
Neo4j is a rebuildable graph projection.
Elasticsearch is a rebuildable search projection.
Artifact storage initially uses local filesystem storage.
Artifact storage must be abstracted behind ArtifactStorage.
S3 must be supported as a future storage implementation.
Business modules must not know whether artifacts are stored locally or in S3.
Storage paths/keys must be generated by the backend.
Artifact metadata belongs in PostgreSQL.
Artifacts must be access-controlled.
Sensitive artifacts should use encryption at rest.
PostgreSQL must use persistent storage in production.
PostgreSQL must have a tested backup strategy.
Database changes must use version-controlled migrations.
Redis may provide queue infrastructure but queue access must be abstracted.
RabbitMQ/Kafka may be considered later without changing domain logic.
Kafka must not be introduced without a concrete scaling/event-streaming requirement.
Infrastructure services must not be unnecessarily publicly exposed.
APIs should be stateless where practical.
Workers must be independently scalable.
Scheduler must prevent duplicate scheduled execution.
Containers should be disposable.
Important state must live outside disposable containers.
Configuration must be environment-specific.
Secrets must use the secret-management architecture from Section 20.
Production images must be versioned/immutable where practical.
Health checks must distinguish liveness from readiness.
Services must support graceful shutdown.
Job state must survive worker restarts.
Deployment must support controlled migrations.
Database migrations must be compatible with deployment strategy.
Application rollback must not blindly reverse destructive database changes.
Development, test, staging, and production data must remain isolated.
Infrastructure configuration must be version-controlled.
Infrastructure-as-code should be introduced for production infrastructure.
Monitoring must cover both application and infrastructure health.
Queue depth and worker health must be observable.
Graph/search projection lag must be observable.
Storage failures must result in explicit application states.
Storage retries must be bounded and observable.
Artifact generation must be idempotent where appropriate.
Backups must include required canonical state.
Rebuildable projections may have different backup requirements.
Recovery procedures must preserve tenant isolation and security.
The initial production deployment may use a single server.
The architecture must support future horizontal scaling.
Kubernetes is a future deployment option, not an initial requirement.
Cloud-specific services must remain infrastructure implementations rather than domain dependencies.
Local-to-production storage implementations must preserve the same application contracts.


21.110 Final Infrastructure Architecture
The complete infrastructure model is:
                         INTERNET
                            │
                            ▼
                  ┌──────────────────┐
                  │ Reverse Proxy /  │
                  │ Load Balancer    │
                  └────────┬─────────┘
                           │
             ┌─────────────┴─────────────┐
             ▼                           ▼
        ┌───────────┐              ┌───────────┐
        │ Next.js   │              │ API       │
        │ Frontend  │              │ Backend   │
        └───────────┘              └─────┬─────┘
                                         │
                    ┌────────────────────┼────────────────────┐
                    │                    │                    │
                    ▼                    ▼                    ▼
              PostgreSQL              Redis             ArtifactStorage
                    │                    │                    │
                    │                    ▼                    │
                    │                 Queue                  │
                    │                    │                    │
                    │          ┌─────────┼─────────┐          │
                    │          ▼         ▼         ▼          │
                    │       Worker    Worker    Worker        │
                    │          │         │         │          │
                    └──────────┼─────────┼─────────┼──────────┘
                               │         │         │
                               ▼         ▼         ▼
                            Analysis  Knowledge  Reports
                               │         │
                               │         ├──────────► Elasticsearch
                               │         │
                               │         └──────────► Neo4j
                               │
                               ▼
                           Architecture


21.111 Future Cloud Architecture
The future cloud architecture can become:
                         INTERNET
                            │
                            ▼
                    Load Balancer / CDN
                       │          │
                       ▼          ▼
                   Next.js       API
                                  │
              ┌───────────────────┼────────────────────┐
              │                   │                    │
              ▼                   ▼                    ▼
        Managed PostgreSQL   Managed Redis        S3 Storage
                                  │
                                  ▼
                              Job Queue
                                  │
                       ┌──────────┼──────────┐
                       ▼          ▼          ▼
                    Worker     Worker     Worker
                       │
              ┌────────┴────────┐
              ▼                 ▼
           Neo4j           Elasticsearch

The domain architecture remains unchanged.
Only infrastructure implementations change.

21.112 Final Storage Principle
The complete storage hierarchy is:
                    CANONICAL
                       │
                       ▼
                  PostgreSQL
                       │
            ┌──────────┴──────────┐
            ▼                     ▼
      Derived Projection      Derived Projection
            │                     │
            ▼                     ▼
          Neo4j             Elasticsearch

                    Artifacts
                       │
                       ▼
                ArtifactStorage
                 /           \
                /             \
        Local Filesystem       S3

Therefore:

PostgreSQL remains the source of truth for durable application state. Neo4j and Elasticsearch remain rebuildable projections. ArtifactStorage abstracts generated binary content, beginning with local storage and later supporting S3. Redis provides queue/cache infrastructure rather than canonical business storage.


21.113 Final Deployment Principle
StackSense's deployment evolution is:
LOCAL
Docker Compose
    ↓
SINGLE SERVER
Docker + Reverse Proxy
    ↓
SCALED DEPLOYMENT
Multiple API + Worker Instances
    ↓
CLOUD
Managed Stateful Infrastructure
    ↓
KUBERNETES
Independent Scaling / Orchestration

The important architectural invariant is:

Deployment topology may evolve without requiring the domain architecture to be rewritten.


21.114 Final Infrastructure Contract
The infrastructure boundary can ultimately be summarized as:
PostgreSQL
    =
CANONICAL STATE

Redis
    =
QUEUE + CACHE

Neo4j
    =
GRAPH PROJECTION

Elasticsearch
    =
SEARCH PROJECTION

ArtifactStorage
    =
BINARY ARTIFACTS

SecretProvider
    =
SECRET MATERIAL

Docker
    =
LOCAL REPRODUCIBILITY

Single Server
    =
INITIAL PRODUCTION

Cloud / Kubernetes
    =
FUTURE SCALE


21.115 Final Principle

StackSense must be deployable as a simple local Docker-based system while preserving the architectural boundaries necessary for production deployment, horizontal scaling, managed infrastructure, and eventual Kubernetes adoption. Storage implementations must remain replaceable, canonical state must remain distinguishable from derived projections, and no deployment decision should leak into business logic.

End of Section 21.



22. OBSERVABILITY, RELIABILITY & GRACEFUL DEGRADATION
22.1 Purpose
Observability and reliability are cross-cutting architectural concerns in StackSense.
The system must not only perform its intended operations, but also make it possible to determine:

what is happening;
what happened;
why something failed;
which component failed;
which tenant/resource was affected;
whether the system is recovering;
whether a failure is isolated or systemic;
what functionality can continue operating despite the failure.

The central principle is:

StackSense must be observable enough to diagnose failures and resilient enough to preserve useful functionality when non-critical components fail.


22.2 Reliability Philosophy
StackSense follows four fundamental reliability principles:
Detect
  ↓
Understand
  ↓
Recover
  ↓
Degrade Safely

The system should avoid both extremes:
Failure
  ↓
Everything stops

and:
Failure
  ↓
System silently continues with incorrect data

Instead:

When a dependency fails, StackSense should preserve correctness first, then availability where possible.


22.3 Observability vs Monitoring
These terms must remain distinct.
Monitoring
Monitoring answers:

Is the system healthy?

Examples:
CPU
Memory
API latency
Error rate
Queue depth
Database connections

Observability
Observability answers:

Why is the system behaving this way?

It is built primarily around:
Logs
Metrics
Traces


22.4 Three Pillars
StackSense observability follows:
                 OBSERVABILITY
                      │
          ┌───────────┼───────────┐
          ▼           ▼           ▼
        Logs       Metrics      Traces

These must work together rather than existing as unrelated telemetry.

22.5 Logging
Logs describe discrete events.
Examples:
Analysis started
Analysis failed
Repository ingestion completed
Projection published
Report generated
AI provider timeout
Database connection failed

Logs should be structured rather than relying exclusively on free-form text.

22.6 Structured Logging
Preferred:
{
    "event": "analysis_started",
    "analysis_id": "...",
    "project_id": "...",
    "organization_id": "...",
    "request_id": "...",
    "timestamp": "..."
}

rather than:
"Analysis started for project xyz"

Structured logs allow automated search and correlation.

22.7 Logging Levels
The system should support standard log levels such as:
DEBUG
INFO
WARNING
ERROR
CRITICAL

Use them intentionally.
DEBUG
Detailed development diagnostics.
INFO
Normal significant application events.
WARNING
Unexpected but recoverable conditions.
ERROR
Operation failed.
CRITICAL
Severe system-level failure requiring immediate attention.

22.8 Production Logging
Production should avoid excessive DEBUG logging.
Production logs should prioritize:

important lifecycle events;
failures;
security events;
performance anomalies;
operational state.


22.9 Sensitive Data in Logs
Logs must never contain:

passwords;
API keys;
database credentials;
authentication tokens;
private keys;
raw secrets.

This follows the security contract established in Section 20.

22.10 Log Correlation
Every request should have a correlation/request identifier.
Conceptually:
Request
  │
  ├── API log
  ├── Service log
  ├── Database operation log
  ├── Job event
  └── Worker log

All relevant logs should be searchable using the same identifier.

22.11 Request ID
Example:
request_id = req_8f32...

The request ID should propagate through synchronous operations.

22.12 Correlation ID Across Async Boundaries
When a request creates a background job:
HTTP Request
    ↓
Job Created
    ↓
Queue
    ↓
Worker

the job should retain the relevant correlation context.
Conceptually:
request_id
analysis_id
job_id
organization_id
project_id

This allows an operator to trace an analysis from API request to final result.

22.13 Job Observability
Background jobs must expose lifecycle state.
At minimum:
QUEUED
RUNNING
COMPLETED
FAILED

Where appropriate:
RETRYING
CANCELLED


22.14 Job Metrics
Important metrics include:
job_created_total
job_completed_total
job_failed_total
job_retry_total
job_duration
job_queue_wait_time


22.15 Queue Observability
Redis/queue infrastructure should expose:

queue depth;
oldest waiting job;
processing rate;
failure rate;
retry count;
worker utilization.

Example:
Queue depth: 42
Oldest job: 3m 17s
Workers: 4
Processing rate: 8 jobs/min


22.16 Queue Backlog
A growing queue is an early reliability signal.
Conceptually:
Queue depth
    ↑
    │
    │        /
    │       /
    │      /
    └─────/────────── Time

Persistent growth indicates:

insufficient workers;
slow jobs;
dependency failure;
unexpected workload.


22.17 Worker Observability
Workers should expose:

current status;
jobs processed;
jobs failed;
jobs retried;
execution duration;
resource consumption where useful.


22.18 Worker Failure
A worker crash must not permanently lose the job.
The queue/job system should support retry/recovery semantics.
Conceptually:
Job
 ↓
Worker crashes
 ↓
Job becomes retryable
 ↓
Another worker
 ↓
Retry


22.19 Retry Policy
Retries should be controlled.
Every retry policy should define:
Maximum attempts
Backoff
Retryable failures
Non-retryable failures


22.20 Exponential Backoff
Transient failures should generally use increasing delays.
Conceptually:
Attempt 1 → immediate
Attempt 2 → short delay
Attempt 3 → longer delay
Attempt 4 → longer delay

This prevents a failing dependency from being overwhelmed.

22.21 Retryable Errors
Examples may include:

temporary network failure;
connection timeout;
temporary storage failure;
transient external provider failure.


22.22 Non-Retryable Errors
Examples:

invalid repository;
malformed configuration;
unauthorized credentials;
invalid request;
unsupported file type.

Retrying these indefinitely wastes resources.

22.23 Dead-Letter Handling
Jobs that repeatedly fail should eventually stop retrying.
Conceptually:
Job
 ↓
Retry 1
 ↓
Retry 2
 ↓
Retry 3
 ↓
Permanent Failure / Dead Letter

The failed job should remain inspectable.

22.24 Failure Classification
Failures should be classified rather than represented only as:
FAILED

Useful categories include:
VALIDATION_FAILURE
AUTHENTICATION_FAILURE
AUTHORIZATION_FAILURE
DEPENDENCY_FAILURE
TIMEOUT
RESOURCE_EXHAUSTION
INTERNAL_ERROR
EXTERNAL_PROVIDER_FAILURE
STORAGE_FAILURE


22.25 Error Codes
Backend failures should expose stable machine-readable error codes.
Example:
ANALYSIS_TIMEOUT
REPOSITORY_ACCESS_DENIED
STORAGE_UNAVAILABLE
AI_PROVIDER_TIMEOUT

The frontend can then present appropriate UX without parsing human-readable messages.

22.26 Metrics
Metrics measure numerical system behavior.
StackSense metrics should cover:
Application

request count;
latency;
error rate;
throughput.

Analysis

analysis count;
analysis duration;
failure rate;
queue wait.

AI

request count;
latency;
provider failure rate;
token usage where available.

Infrastructure

CPU;
memory;
disk;
network;
database connections.


22.27 Metric Naming
Metrics should use consistent naming.
Conceptually:
api_requests_total
api_request_duration_seconds
analysis_duration_seconds
analysis_failures_total
queue_depth
ai_request_duration_seconds

The exact naming convention may be standardized during implementation.

22.28 Metric Labels
Metrics may use labels such as:
operation
status
provider
environment

Avoid unbounded labels such as:
user_id
repository_name
request_id

because they can create excessive metric cardinality.

22.29 High-Cardinality Data
Identifiers such as:
request_id
analysis_id
project_id

belong primarily in logs/traces, not as unrestricted metric labels.

22.30 API Reliability Metrics
The API should expose:
Request Rate
Error Rate
P50 Latency
P95 Latency
P99 Latency

The previously defined target remains:
P95 API latency < 200 ms

for normal API operations where applicable.
Long-running operations such as analysis should not be forced into this target.

22.31 Long-Running Operations
Analysis, report generation, and other expensive operations must not block normal HTTP requests unnecessarily.
Preferred:
POST /analysis
      ↓
202 Accepted
      ↓
job_id
      ↓
background processing

rather than holding an HTTP request open for the entire operation.

22.32 Analysis Observability
Analysis should expose its major lifecycle stages.
Conceptually:
QUEUED
  ↓
INGESTING
  ↓
PARSING
  ↓
ANALYZING
  ↓
BUILDING_ARCHITECTURE
  ↓
PROJECTING
  ↓
FINALIZING
  ↓
COMPLETED

The exact stages must follow the analysis lifecycle defined elsewhere in this document.

22.33 Analysis Timing
The system should record timings for major phases.
Example:
Repository ingestion: 12s
Parsing: 21s
Architecture extraction: 18s
Graph projection: 4s
Search projection: 6s
Total: 61s

This helps identify bottlenecks.

22.34 Projection Lag
Because Neo4j and Elasticsearch are derived projections, their freshness must be observable.
Example:
Canonical architecture:
Version 15

Graph:
Version 15

Search:
Version 14

The system should be able to identify that search projection is stale.

22.35 Projection Health
Projection status may include:
CURRENT
UPDATING
STALE
FAILED


22.36 Projection Recovery
If projection fails:
Canonical Data
     │
     ├── Neo4j projection failed
     │
     └── Elasticsearch projection succeeded

The system should preserve the successful projection while retrying the failed one.

22.37 Projection Retry
Projection jobs should use the same controlled retry architecture:
Projection
 ↓
Failure
 ↓
Retry
 ↓
Backoff
 ↓
Retry
 ↓
Dead Letter


22.38 Projection Rebuild
The system must support rebuilding derived stores.
Conceptually:
PostgreSQL
    ↓
Rebuild Graph Projection
    ↓
Neo4j

and:
PostgreSQL
    ↓
Rebuild Search Index
    ↓
Elasticsearch


22.39 Database Reliability
PostgreSQL is a critical dependency.
The system should monitor:

connection pool usage;
query latency;
connection failures;
transaction failures;
disk usage;
replication/backup health where applicable.


22.40 Database Connection Pool
The API and workers should use controlled connection pools.
Unbounded connection creation can exhaust PostgreSQL.

22.41 Database Backpressure
When PostgreSQL is overloaded, the system should avoid blindly increasing concurrency.
Instead:
Database saturation
      ↓
Reduce / control concurrency
      ↓
Queue work
      ↓
Recover gradually


22.42 Redis Reliability
Redis failure should be observable.
Potential consequences:
Queue unavailable
Cache unavailable
Rate limiting unavailable

These should be handled according to the importance of each Redis usage.

22.43 Redis Cache Failure
If Redis is being used purely as cache:
Redis unavailable
      ↓
Cache miss
      ↓
Fetch canonical data

The application may continue operating with reduced performance.

22.44 Redis Queue Failure
If Redis is being used for job delivery:
Redis unavailable
      ↓
Cannot enqueue new job
      ↓
Return controlled error

The system must not pretend that a job was successfully queued.

22.45 Queue Backpressure
When queue capacity is exhausted or workers cannot keep up, the API may:

reject new expensive jobs;
throttle requests;
place jobs into controlled backlog;
inform the user.

The system must avoid unbounded memory growth.

22.46 Elasticsearch Failure
If Elasticsearch becomes unavailable:
Search
   ↓
Unavailable / degraded

but:
Canonical PostgreSQL data
   ↓
Still available

The failure must not corrupt canonical state.

22.47 Neo4j Failure
If Neo4j becomes unavailable:
Graph traversal
   ↓
Unavailable / degraded

but the architecture model stored canonically remains available.

22.48 AI Provider Failure
AI is an enhancement layer rather than the source of truth.
Therefore:
AI Provider unavailable
       ↓
AI explanation unavailable
       ↓
Deterministic architecture / analysis remains available

This is a mandatory graceful-degradation behavior.

22.49 AI Provider Timeout
If an AI provider exceeds the configured timeout:
AI Request
   ↓
Timeout
   ↓
Controlled failure
   ↓
Retry/fallback if configured
   ↓
Otherwise explain unavailable

The frontend must not wait indefinitely.

22.50 AI Provider Fallback
The AI provider abstraction may support fallback providers.
Conceptually:
AI Service
    ↓
Provider Factory
    ↓
Primary Provider
    ↓
Failure
    ↓
Fallback Provider

Fallback must respect:

provider availability;
configuration;
cost;
security;
data-handling requirements.


22.51 AI Failure Boundary
AI failure must never cause:
Architecture unavailable
Analysis unavailable
Database state unavailable

AI is optional from the core correctness perspective.

22.52 Storage Failure
Artifact storage failure should not falsely mark an artifact as available.
Example:
Report generation
     ↓
Successful
     ↓
Storage upload fails
     ↓
Report status = STORAGE_FAILED

The user should receive a meaningful retry/recovery option.

22.53 Storage Recovery
Transient storage failure:
Generate Artifact
      ↓
Upload fails
      ↓
Retry
      ↓
Success

Permanent failure:
Generate Artifact
      ↓
Upload repeatedly fails
      ↓
Mark failed
      ↓
Preserve diagnostic information


22.54 External Repository Failure
Repository access may fail because:

repository unavailable;
credentials expired;
network failure;
repository deleted;
permission revoked.

The system should classify the failure.
It should not mark the analysis as successful.

22.55 Repository Retry
Network failures may be retried.
Invalid credentials should not be repeatedly retried indefinitely.

22.56 Dependency Timeout
Every external dependency call should have an explicit timeout.
No external call should be allowed to block indefinitely.
Examples:
Database timeout
Repository timeout
AI timeout
Storage timeout
Search timeout
Graph timeout


22.57 Timeout Budget
Operations should have bounded time budgets.
Conceptually:
Request
 ↓
Dependency A
 ↓ timeout
Dependency B
 ↓ timeout
Final response

The total operation must remain bounded.

22.58 Circuit Breaker
Frequently failing external dependencies may use circuit-breaker behavior.
Conceptually:
Healthy
  ↓
Repeated failures
  ↓
OPEN
  ↓
Reject quickly
  ↓
Cooldown
  ↓
HALF-OPEN
  ↓
Test
  ↓
Healthy / Open

This prevents repeatedly hammering an unhealthy dependency.

22.59 Circuit Breaker Candidates
Potential candidates:

AI providers;
external Git providers;
external storage;
remote services.

Internal databases may use different failure-handling strategies.

22.60 Graceful Degradation Levels
StackSense should distinguish levels of functionality.
Level 0 — Fully Operational
Everything works.
Level 1 — Minor Degradation
Optional optimizations unavailable.
Level 2 — Feature Degradation
Search/graph/AI may be unavailable.
Level 3 — Core Processing Degradation
Analysis or report processing unavailable.
Level 4 — Core System Failure
Authentication/API/database unavailable.

22.61 Degradation Matrix



Failure
Impact
System Behavior




AI unavailable
AI explanation
Continue deterministic features


Elasticsearch unavailable
Search
Disable/degrade search


Neo4j unavailable
Graph traversal
Preserve architecture


Redis cache unavailable
Performance
Fetch canonical data


Redis queue unavailable
Background work
Reject/hold new jobs safely


Artifact storage unavailable
Downloads/reports
Retry / mark unavailable


Repository unavailable
Analysis
Fail analysis safely


PostgreSQL unavailable
Core state
Controlled outage


Auth unavailable
Access control
Fail closed


Frontend unavailable
UI
Backend remains protected




22.62 Core vs Optional Dependencies
Dependencies should be explicitly classified.
Core
PostgreSQL
Identity

Operationally Important
Redis Queue
Artifact Storage

Derived / Optional
Neo4j
Elasticsearch
AI Provider

This classification determines degradation behavior.

22.63 Correctness Over Availability
StackSense must never preserve availability by serving incorrect architecture information.
For example:
Search index stale

must not be presented as:
Search index current

Similarly:
Graph projection stale

must not silently masquerade as the latest architecture.

22.64 Stale Data Contract
If stale data is served intentionally, it should be identifiable.
Example:
Architecture data is current.
Search index updated 2 minutes ago.

or:
Graph view may be stale.


22.65 Read vs Write Degradation
Read operations and write operations should degrade differently.
Read
May sometimes use:

cache;
stale projection;
fallback source.

Write
Must preserve transactional correctness.
A write should not be reported successful unless the authoritative operation succeeds.

22.66 Idempotency
Retryable operations should be idempotent where possible.
Example:
Create Projection

should not create duplicate graph nodes simply because the worker retried.

22.67 Idempotency Keys
For sensitive/expensive requests, idempotency keys may be used.
Potential examples:
Start Analysis
Generate Report
Create Integration


22.68 Duplicate Job Prevention
The same analysis should not accidentally execute multiple times because of:

client retries;
worker retries;
network timeouts;
duplicate queue messages.

The system should use analysis/job identity to detect duplicates.

22.69 Exactly-Once vs At-Least-Once
The queue architecture should not assume perfect exactly-once execution.
The safer model is:

Assume jobs may be delivered more than once and design operations to be idempotent.


22.70 Transactional Boundaries
Database changes that establish canonical state should be transactional.
Example:
Create Analysis
    +
Create Job Record

should be designed so the system does not leave impossible states such as:
Job exists
but
Analysis does not exist

where that relationship is required.

22.71 Transaction + Queue Boundary
If an operation requires:
Database transaction
+
Queue message

the architecture should avoid unreliable dual writes.
An outbox/event mechanism may be introduced where necessary.
Conceptually:
Transaction
 ├── Business State
 └── Outbox Event
        ↓
     Dispatcher
        ↓
       Queue


22.72 Outbox Pattern
The Outbox Pattern may be used for reliable asynchronous event publication.
It ensures:
Database state committed
        +
Event persisted

before attempting external delivery.
This is especially useful for critical domain events.

22.73 Event Delivery
Events should be considered at-least-once unless the infrastructure explicitly guarantees otherwise.
Consumers should therefore be idempotent.

22.74 Event Deduplication
Consumers may use:
event_id

to detect previously processed events.

22.75 Reliability of Projections
Projection consumers should record enough state to determine:
last processed event
current projection version
projection status

This makes recovery and replay possible.

22.76 Health Endpoint
The API should expose health information through controlled endpoints.
Conceptually:
/health/live
/health/ready

The exact routes may evolve.

22.77 Health Check Design
Health checks should avoid causing additional load.
Do not perform expensive operations every time a load balancer asks:
"Are you healthy?"


22.78 Dependency Health
Readiness may check critical dependencies.
Example:
API
 ↓
PostgreSQL reachable
 ↓
Ready

Optional dependency failure should be represented separately when possible.

22.79 Health Status Model
A component can be:
HEALTHY
DEGRADED
UNAVAILABLE

This is more useful operationally than a binary healthy/unhealthy model.

22.80 System Health
Overall StackSense health should be derived from component health.
Example:
API          HEALTHY
PostgreSQL   HEALTHY
Redis        HEALTHY
Neo4j        DEGRADED
Search       UNAVAILABLE
AI           UNAVAILABLE

Overall:
DEGRADED

not necessarily:
DOWN


22.81 Operational Dashboard
The system should eventually provide an operations view showing:
API
Database
Queue
Workers
Analysis
Search
Graph
Storage
AI

with:

status;
latency;
recent errors;
backlog;
dependency health.


22.82 Alerting
Alerts should focus on actionable conditions.
Good examples:
API error rate > threshold
Queue backlog continuously increasing
Database connection pool exhausted
Analysis failure rate unusually high
Storage unavailable
Repeated AI provider failures
Projection stale for too long

Avoid alerting on every isolated minor error.

22.83 Alert Severity
Alerts may use:
INFO
WARNING
CRITICAL

Critical alerts should indicate conditions requiring immediate attention.

22.84 Alert Fatigue
Reliability systems must avoid generating so many alerts that operators ignore them.
Every alert should have:
Condition
Impact
Likely Cause
Action

where practical.

22.85 SLO / SLA Boundary
StackSense may eventually define SLOs.
Examples:
API availability
Analysis completion success rate
Report generation success rate
Search availability

SLA commitments should not be hard-coded into application logic.

22.86 Recovery Objectives
The infrastructure should eventually define:
RPO
RTO

for critical data and services.
These are deployment/environment-specific.

22.87 Incident Lifecycle
A reliability incident should conceptually follow:
Detect
 ↓
Alert
 ↓
Investigate
 ↓
Mitigate
 ↓
Recover
 ↓
Verify
 ↓
Document


22.88 Incident Correlation
During an incident, operators should be able to correlate:
Metric spike
    ↓
Trace
    ↓
Request
    ↓
Job
    ↓
Logs
    ↓
Dependency failure

This is the core purpose of distributed observability.

22.89 Distributed Tracing
Tracing should be introduced for cross-service operations.
Example:
HTTP Request
    │
    ├── API
    │
    ├── PostgreSQL
    │
    └── Queue
          │
          └── Worker
                │
                ├── Repository
                ├── Neo4j
                ├── Elasticsearch
                └── AI


22.90 Trace Context
Trace context should propagate across:

HTTP;
internal service calls;
queue jobs;
external calls where supported.


22.91 Trace Sampling
High-volume systems may use trace sampling.
Not every request necessarily needs a complete trace.
Errors and slow requests should receive higher observability priority.

22.92 Performance Diagnostics
Tracing should help identify:
API slow
    ↓
Database slow

or:

API slow
    ↓
AI provider slow

or:

Analysis slow
    ↓
Repository parser slow


22.93 Slow Query Observability
PostgreSQL slow queries should be observable.
Metrics/logging should help identify:

query duration;
frequency;
database load;
affected operation.

Sensitive query parameters should not be logged blindly.

22.94 Analysis Resource Observability
Analysis workloads should track:
CPU
Memory
Disk
Execution time
Repository size
File count

This allows abnormal repositories to be detected.

22.95 Resource Exhaustion
If an analysis exceeds resource limits:
Analysis
 ↓
Resource limit reached
 ↓
Terminate safely
 ↓
Mark RESOURCE_EXHAUSTION
 ↓
Record diagnostics

The worker should remain healthy where possible.

22.96 Dependency Isolation
One failing analysis should not crash every worker.
Potential strategies:

process isolation;
task-level timeouts;
resource limits;
separate worker pools for expensive workloads.


22.97 Worker Pool Separation
Future architecture may use:
General Worker Pool
        +
Analysis Worker Pool
        +
Report Worker Pool

This prevents one expensive workload from starving unrelated jobs.

22.98 Backpressure
Backpressure is mandatory for expensive operations.
Example:
User requests
       ↓
100 analysis jobs
       ↓
Queue
       ↓
Limited workers

The system must process at a controlled rate rather than spawning unlimited tasks.

22.99 Concurrency Limits
Limits should exist for expensive operations such as:

repository analysis;
report generation;
AI calls;
large graph queries.

Limits may be:

global;
per organization;
per project;
per worker.


22.100 Tenant Fairness
One organization must not be able to monopolize shared resources.
For example:
Organization A
    500 analysis jobs

should not automatically prevent:
Organization B
    1 analysis job

from being processed.
Fair scheduling/quotas may be introduced as scale requires.

22.101 Resource Quotas
Potential quotas include:
Repository size
Analysis frequency
Concurrent analyses
Report generation rate
AI requests
Storage usage

Exact limits are environment/configuration dependent.

22.102 Graceful Shutdown
During deployment or maintenance:
SIGTERM
 ↓
Stop accepting new work
 ↓
Finish/hand off safe work
 ↓
Close connections
 ↓
Exit

Workers should not abandon jobs without updating job state.

22.103 Maintenance Mode
Future deployments may support controlled maintenance mode.
The frontend could show:
StackSense is temporarily undergoing maintenance.

Existing analysis jobs may continue.


22.104 Dependency Maintenance
Optional dependencies can be disabled independently where possible.
Example:
Neo4j maintenance
 ↓
Graph disabled
 ↓
Core application remains operational


22.105 Graceful Degradation UX
The frontend must communicate degradation clearly.
Bad:
Graph button

does nothing.
Good:
Graph view is temporarily unavailable.

Architecture data is still available.


22.106 AI Degradation UX
Example:
AI explanations are temporarily unavailable.

You can still explore the architecture and deterministic findings.


22.107 Search Degradation UX
Example:
Search is temporarily unavailable.

Browse architecture directly instead.

where the fallback exists.

22.108 Graph Degradation UX
Example:
Dependency graph is temporarily unavailable.

Entity details remain accessible.


22.109 Report Degradation UX
If report storage is unavailable:
Report generation completed, but the artifact could not be stored.

[Retry Storage]

where supported.

22.110 Reliability State Propagation
Backend states should propagate accurately to the frontend.
Example:
Backend:
PROJECTION_STALE

Frontend:
"Architecture graph may be out of date."

The frontend must not convert:
STALE

into:
READY


22.111 Reliability and Source of Truth
The system must preserve this hierarchy:
PostgreSQL
    ↓
Truth

Neo4j / Elasticsearch
    ↓
Derived Views

Redis
    ↓
Transient Infrastructure

Cache
    ↓
Performance Optimization

Failure of a lower layer must not overwrite the truth of a higher layer.

22.112 Data Consistency
StackSense should distinguish:
Strongly consistent

from:
Eventually consistent

Stronger consistency
Transactional application state.
Eventual consistency
Graph/search projections.
This distinction must be visible in the architecture.

22.113 Projection Consistency Example
After an analysis completes:
PostgreSQL
Version 15

may become available before:
Neo4j
Version 15

and:
Elasticsearch
Version 15

The UI should handle this transitional state.

22.114 Eventual Consistency UX
Example:
Architecture generated successfully.

Graph and search indexes are still updating.

This is preferable to pretending everything is immediately synchronized.

22.115 Reliability Invariant
A fundamental invariant is:

A derived-system failure must never corrupt canonical application state.

Examples:
Neo4j failure
    ≠
Architecture loss

Elasticsearch failure
    ≠
Finding loss

AI failure
    ≠
Analysis loss

Redis cache failure
    ≠
Database loss


22.116 Observability Invariant
Another fundamental invariant:

Every important asynchronous or distributed operation must be traceable from initiation to final outcome.

For example:
User
 ↓
API Request ID
 ↓
Analysis ID
 ↓
Job ID
 ↓
Worker
 ↓
Projection
 ↓
Report


22.117 Reliability Invariant
Another mandatory invariant:

Every failure must result in an explicit, recoverable state whenever possible.

Avoid:
Unknown state

Examples:
STORAGE_FAILED
ANALYSIS_FAILED
PROJECTION_FAILED
AI_UNAVAILABLE

are preferable to silent failure.

22.118 Observability Infrastructure
The observability stack may eventually include:
Application
   ↓
Logs ───────────────► Log Storage
Metrics ────────────► Metrics System
Traces ─────────────► Trace System
   │
   └────────────────► Dashboards / Alerts

The exact products are deployment choices.
The project should not hard-code one observability vendor into domain logic.

22.119 ELK Compatibility
The previously selected observability direction may use Elasticsearch/Kibana for centralized logs where appropriate.
Conceptually:
Application
    ↓
Structured Logs
    ↓
Log Pipeline
    ↓
Elasticsearch
    ↓
Kibana

However:

Elasticsearch used for observability logs must remain conceptually separate from Elasticsearch used for application search/retrieval.

They may eventually use separate indexes or clusters depending on deployment requirements.

22.120 Log Retention
Logs should have retention policies.
Retention depends on:

environment;
volume;
operational requirements;
security requirements.

Logs should not grow indefinitely.

22.121 Metrics Retention
Metrics retention should support:

immediate operational debugging;
trend analysis;
capacity planning.

Long-term retention may use downsampling or separate storage.

22.122 Trace Retention
Traces are typically higher-volume.
Retention should prioritize:

errors;
slow requests;
important workflows.


22.123 Observability Cost
Observability itself consumes:

CPU;
storage;
network;
memory.

Instrumentation should therefore be useful and controlled.

22.124 Self-Observability
The observability system itself should be observable.
Monitor:
Log ingestion
Metric collection
Trace ingestion
Storage capacity
Dropped telemetry


22.125 Failure of Observability
If observability infrastructure fails:
Application
   ↓
continues operating

where possible.
Observability should not become a mandatory dependency for normal business operations.
However, severe telemetry loss should be visible when monitoring recovers.

22.126 Reliability Testing
Reliability must be tested deliberately.
Tests should include:

database unavailable;
Redis unavailable;
Neo4j unavailable;
Elasticsearch unavailable;
storage unavailable;
AI provider unavailable;
worker crash;
queue backlog;
timeout;
malformed repository;
resource exhaustion.


22.127 Failure Injection
Future environments may use controlled failure injection.
Example:
Kill worker
 ↓
Observe job recovery

or:
Disable Elasticsearch
 ↓
Observe search degradation


22.128 Recovery Testing
Recovery tests should verify:
Failure
 ↓
Detection
 ↓
Correct state
 ↓
Retry / rebuild
 ↓
Recovery


22.129 Backup Recovery Testing
Backups must periodically be restored into a test environment.
The goal is to verify:
Backup
 ↓
Restore
 ↓
Application starts
 ↓
Data accessible


22.130 Disaster Recovery
Disaster recovery should eventually cover:

database loss;
storage loss;
infrastructure loss;
region/server loss where applicable.

The exact DR architecture depends on deployment scale.

22.131 Reliability Runbooks
Important operational failures should have runbooks.
Example:
Redis unavailable
1. Check Redis health.
2. Check connection errors.
3. Verify queue backlog.
4. Restore/restart Redis if appropriate.
5. Verify workers reconnect.
6. Verify queued jobs recover.


22.132 Incident Documentation
After significant incidents, document:
What happened?
Why?
Impact?
How detected?
How recovered?
What prevents recurrence?


22.133 Post-Incident Principle
The goal is not merely:

"Fix the bug."

The goal is:

Reduce the probability and impact of the same failure happening again.


22.134 Reliability Rules
The following rules are mandatory:

StackSense must be observable through logs, metrics, and traces.
Logs must be structured where practical.
Production logs must not contain secrets.
Requests must have correlation/request IDs.
Correlation context should cross asynchronous boundaries.
Important jobs must have explicit lifecycle states.
Queue depth must be observable.
Worker health must be observable.
Retry policies must be explicit.
Retries must be bounded.
Retries should use backoff for transient failures.
Non-retryable errors must not be retried indefinitely.
Failed jobs must become inspectable.
Long-running operations must be asynchronous.
Expensive operations must have timeouts.
External dependencies must not block indefinitely.
Circuit breakers may protect repeatedly failing external providers.
Database connection pools must be bounded.
Expensive workloads must have concurrency limits.
Backpressure must prevent unbounded resource consumption.
Tenant fairness must be considered for shared resources.
Important operations should be idempotent.
The system must assume asynchronous messages may be delivered more than once.
Critical database/event combinations should use an outbox pattern where required.
PostgreSQL remains the canonical source of truth.
Neo4j remains a rebuildable projection.
Elasticsearch remains a rebuildable projection.
Redis cache failure must not cause canonical data loss.
AI failure must not prevent deterministic functionality.
Search failure must not destroy architecture data.
Graph failure must not destroy architecture data.
Storage failure must result in an explicit state.
Projection failures must be retryable/rebuildable.
Stale projections must be detectable.
Eventual consistency must be explicitly represented.
The frontend must not present stale/failed data as current.
Health checks must distinguish liveness and readiness.
Services must support graceful shutdown.
Workers must safely handle shutdown and restart.
Deployment must not silently abandon active jobs.
Alerts must be actionable.
Alert fatigue must be avoided.
Metrics must avoid uncontrolled high-cardinality labels.
Distributed traces should cover important cross-service workflows.
Observability infrastructure should not become a hard dependency for business correctness.
Infrastructure failures must degrade gracefully where possible.
Core security failures must fail closed.
Reliability must prioritize correctness over availability.
Recovery procedures must be tested.
Backups must be tested through restoration.
Major infrastructure failures should have operational runbooks.
Significant incidents should result in documented corrective actions.
Resource exhaustion must result in controlled failure rather than uncontrolled system collapse.
Every important asynchronous operation must be traceable from initiation to final outcome.
Every important failure must produce an explicit state.
Derived-system failure must never corrupt canonical application state.
