The phases are sequential at the architectural level.
Individual implementation tasks inside a phase may run in parallel where dependencies permit.

25.10 Phase 1 — Engineering Foundation
Objective
Build the technical foundation required by all later phases.
P1 establishes the environment in which the rest of StackSense can safely be implemented.

25.10.1 Backend Responsibilities
P1 includes the foundational backend structure:
Application bootstrap
Configuration
Environment handling
Dependency management
Base module structure
Error handling
Logging foundation
Database foundation
Migration foundation
API foundation


25.10.2 Infrastructure Responsibilities
Initial infrastructure should be established according to the frozen technology decisions.
This includes the required local development infrastructure.
The goal is:
Clone Repository
      ↓
Install / Start Infrastructure
      ↓
Run StackSense
      ↓
Execute Tests


25.10.3 Frontend Responsibilities
The frontend is delivered with P1.
It should establish:
Frontend application
Routing
Application shell
Layout
Navigation foundation
API client foundation
Error handling foundation
Loading-state foundation
Design-system foundation

It does not need the complete product UI yet.

25.10.4 P1 Vertical Slice
The phase should produce a basic working slice:
Browser
   ↓
Frontend
   ↓
Backend API
   ↓
Database

The complete infrastructure does not need every future feature, but the basic application must work end-to-end.

25.10.5 P1 Testing
P1 must establish:

backend test framework;
frontend test framework;
integration test foundation;
CI foundation;
linting;
formatting;
type checking;
basic architecture validation.


25.10.6 P1 Deliverable
At the end of P1:

StackSense can be run, tested, and developed as a real application.

25.12 Evaluation 1 — Source Understanding
Evaluation 1 should be supported by the capabilities produced by P1 + P2 and the source-understanding capabilities implemented around this stage.

25.13 Phase 3 — Analysis Engine & Architecture Model
Objective
Build the deterministic analysis core.
This is one of the most important phases of StackSense.

      ↓

      ↓
Findings

The Intermediate Representation provides a normalized representation of source information.
It should allow different languages/frameworks to eventually converge into a common architecture understanding.
Conceptually:

JavaScript

       ↓

       ↓

       ↓

This is important for:

It should capture the relationships necessary to understand:

according to the frozen architecture.

25.13.6 Deterministic Analysis
The deterministic engine remains the source of truth.
It must not depend on the LLM for basic architectural facts.

25.13.7 Frontend Responsibilities
The frontend is delivered with P3.
It should provide:
Start Analysis
Analysis Status

25.14 Phase 4 — Architecture Graph & Exploration
Objective
Transform the architecture model into an explorable graph representation.

25.14.1 Backend Responsibilities
P4 includes:

Graph nodes
Graph relationships

Graph traversal
Architecture exploration
Dependency exploration
Relationship queries
Graph synchronization/rebuild


25.14.2 Graph Philosophy
The graph is not the canonical source of truth.
The architecture/data ownership remains governed by the frozen architecture.
Conceptually:
Canonical State
      ↓
Projection
      ↓
Graph


25.14.3 Graph Rebuild
The architecture must support rebuilding the graph when required.
Canonical State
      ↓
Delete/Recreate Projection
      ↓
Graph


25.14.4 Exploration
Users should be able to explore relationships such as:
What depends on X?
What does X depend on?
Which module contains X?
Which components communicate?

The exact query capabilities follow the finalized graph/retrieval contracts.

25.14.5 Frontend Responsibilities
The frontend is delivered with P4.

 ↓

25.15 Evaluation 2 — Architecture Reconstruction & Exploration
Evaluation 2 should demonstrate that StackSense has progressed from source understanding to architecture reconstruction.
The evaluator should be able to see:
Source
 ↓
Entities
 ↓
Relationships
 ↓
Architecture Model
 ↓
Graph
 ↓
Exploration

The key question at this stage is no longer simply:

"What files exist?"

but:

"How is this software architecturally organized, and how can I explore those relationships?"


25.16 Phase 5 — Knowledge, Search & Diagram Intelligence
Objective
Build the knowledge and retrieval layer around the deterministic architecture model.

25.16.1 Backend Responsibilities
P5 includes:
Knowledge projection
Knowledge representation

Retrieval

Context building
Knowledge queries

Diagram data models
Diagram rendering pipeline


25.16.2 Knowledge Architecture
The knowledge layer should follow the frozen architecture.
Conceptually:

        ↓

        ↓
Knowledge / Graph / Search
        ↓
Retriever
        ↓
Evidence


25.16.3 Search
Search should allow users to locate architecture information efficiently.
Examples:
Find authentication service
Find database access
Find dependencies of X
Find files containing Y
Find architecture components


25.16.4 Retrieval
Retrieval is not simply:
Search
 ↓
Return random documents

It is an evidence-planning process.
The system should retrieve the information necessary to answer the requested architectural question.

25.16.5 Diagram Engine
P5 also delivers the deterministic diagram engine.
It should produce architecture visualizations from structured architecture information.
The diagram engine must not require an LLM to understand the architecture.

25.16.6 Frontend Responsibilities
The frontend is delivered with P5.
It should provide:

Knowledge exploration
Architecture queries

25.17 Phase 6 — AI Architecture Intelligence
Objective
Add the AI layer while preserving the deterministic architecture boundary.

25.17.1 Backend Responsibilities
P6 includes:
AI provider abstraction
Provider factory
Provider implementations
Prompt builders
Context builders
Explanation engine
AI response handling
Streaming/SSE
AI failure handling
AI evaluation


25.17.2 AI Responsibility Boundary
The core rule remains:
Deterministic Engine
       ↓
Source of Truth

AI
       ↓
Explanation / Communication

AI does not silently become the architecture analyzer.

25.17.3 AI Provider Architecture
The provider system should use the agreed abstraction/factory approach.
Conceptually:
AI Service
    ↓
Provider Factory
    ↓
Provider Interface
    ├── Provider A
    ├── Provider B
    └── Provider C

This prevents provider-specific logic from leaking throughout the application.

25.17.4 AI Context
AI receives structured evidence rather than arbitrary uncontrolled repository content.
Conceptually:
Question
   +
Retrieved Evidence
   +
Architecture Context
   ↓
Prompt
   ↓
AI Provider
   ↓
Explanation


25.17.5 AI Capabilities
The final intelligence layer may answer questions such as:
Why does this component depend on X?

Where is authentication implemented?

What are the major architectural boundaries?

What is the impact of changing this component?

Why is this architecture structured this way?

Answers must remain grounded in available evidence.

25.17.6 SSE
Where real-time AI output is required, the agreed SSE mechanism should be used.
Conceptually:
Frontend
   ↓
SSE
   ↓
Backend
   ↓
AI Provider
   ↓
Streaming Response


25.17.7 Frontend Responsibilities
The frontend is delivered with P6.
It should provide:
Architecture assistant
Question interface
Streaming responses
Evidence display
Context display
AI explanations
AI error states
Provider-independent UX


25.17.8 P6 Vertical Slice

      ↓

      ↓

      ↓

25.20 Frontend Delivery Rule
This rule is mandatory and applies to every phase:

A backend phase is not considered complete until its corresponding frontend capability has also been implemented, integrated, tested, and demonstrated as a working vertical slice.

Therefore:
Backend Module
      +
Frontend Feature
      +
Integration
      +
Tests
      ↓
Phase Complete


25.21 No Backend-Only Phase Completion
The following is explicitly prohibited:
Backend P3 complete
Frontend P3 postponed

Instead:
P3 Backend
   +
P3 Frontend
   +
P3 Integration
   +
P3 Tests
   =
P3 Complete


25.22 Frontend Work Can Start Before Backend Completion
Although frontend must be delivered with the corresponding backend phase, frontend implementation does not have to wait for every backend endpoint to be completed.
The team may use:
API contracts
mock responses
fixtures
typed interfaces

to develop frontend components in parallel.

25.23 Contract-First Frontend Development
For larger features:
Requirement
 ↓
API Contract
 ↓
Frontend + Backend in Parallel
 ↓
Integration
 ↓
E2E

This reduces late-stage integration problems.

25.24 Vertical Slice Definition
A vertical slice is a user-visible capability that crosses the necessary system boundaries.
Example:
Frontend
   ↓
API
   ↓
Application Service
   ↓
Domain
   ↓
Infrastructure
   ↓
Database / Queue / Storage

It must work as one coherent flow.

25.25 Phase Completion Contract
Every phase must satisfy:
1. Backend implementation
2. Frontend implementation
3. API contract
4. Infrastructure integration
5. Unit tests
6. Integration tests
7. Frontend tests
8. End-to-end validation where applicable
9. Observability
10. Security validation
11. Documentation
12. Architecture compliance
13. Working vertical slice


25.26 Roadmap Does Not Mean Waterfall
The seven phases define architectural progression, not a requirement that every developer work sequentially on every file.
Within a phase:
Backend
Frontend
Tests
Infrastructure
Documentation

may progress concurrently.
The phase boundary exists to control architecture and deliverables.

25.27 Phase Dependencies
Each phase should consume stable outputs from previous phases.
Example:
P2 Repository Platform
        ↓
P3 Analysis Engine
        ↓
P4 Graph
        ↓
P5 Knowledge/Search/Diagram
        ↓
P6 AI
        ↓
P7 Product Hardening

AI should not become the foundation for deterministic analysis.

25.28 No Premature AI
AI is intentionally late in the roadmap.
The system first establishes:
Source Understanding
 ↓
Deterministic Analysis
 ↓
Architecture Model
 ↓
Graph
 ↓
Knowledge
 ↓
Retrieval

Only then does:
AI Explanation

become meaningful.

25.29 No Premature Graph Dependency
The deterministic architecture model should exist before the graph becomes a major exploration layer.
The graph is a projection/exploration mechanism, not the reason the architecture model exists.

25.30 No Premature Search Dependency
Search should be built around meaningful architecture/knowledge representations rather than being introduced before the system understands what it is indexing.

25.31 No Premature Report Dependency
Reports should consume validated analysis/architecture information.
They should not become an independent source of architectural truth.

25.32 Final Phase Relationship
The roadmap should be understood as:
P1
Foundation
   ↓
P2
Repository Understanding
   ↓
P3
Architecture Understanding
   ↓
P4
Architecture Exploration
   ↓
P5
Architecture Knowledge
   ↓
P6
Architecture Intelligence
   ↓
P7
Complete Product

The evaluations align with this progression:
                    STACKSENSE MATURITY

Every phase ends with:

25.36 Phase Handoff Rule
The next phase should not assume that the previous phase is merely "mostly working."
The previous phase must provide a stable contract.
For example:
P3 → P4

means P4 can rely on the defined architecture model rather than rebuilding analysis logic.

25.37 No Reimplementation Across Phases
A later phase must not duplicate functionality already established by an earlier phase.
Example:
P4 should consume P3's architecture model rather than creating another independent architecture representation.

25.38 Phase Refactoring
Refactoring across phase boundaries is allowed when required.
However:
Existing Contract
      ↓
Refactor
      ↓
Same Contract

is preferred.
If the contract itself must change, follow Section 24 change-control rules.

25.39 Phase Documentation
At the end of every phase, update the relevant documentation.
At minimum:
Implementation status
API changes
Architecture changes
Known limitations
Testing status
Phase acceptance


25.40 Phase Demonstration
Each phase should be demonstrable independently.
A phase demonstration should show:
What was built
Why it exists
How it connects
What the user can do
What the backend does
What the frontend does
How it was tested


25.41 Evaluation Demonstration Strategy
The three evaluations should show progression rather than unrelated features.
Evaluation 1
"StackSense understands source code."

Evaluation 2
"StackSense reconstructs and lets us explore architecture."

Evaluation 3
"StackSense provides complete architecture intelligence."

                  Retrieval
                     │
                     ▼
                 AI Context
                     │
                     ▼
                AI Provider
                     │
                     ▼
                Explanation
                     │
                     ▼
                   Report
                     │
                     ▼
                  FRONTEND


25.43 Roadmap Invariant
The following must remain true:
P1 → P2 → P3 → P4 → P5 → P6 → P7

and:
Every Phase
 =
Backend
+
Frontend
+
Tests
+
Integration
+
Working Vertical Slice


25.44 What "Phase Complete" Means
A phase is not complete because:
✓ backend code exists

A phase is complete only when:
✓ backend capability exists
✓ frontend capability exists
✓ contracts are integrated
✓ tests pass
✓ architecture rules pass
✓ security is considered
✓ observability exists where required
✓ documentation is updated
✓ vertical slice works
✓ phase can be demonstrated


25.45 Final Roadmap Contract
The StackSense implementation roadmap is therefore:
PHASE 1
Engineering Foundation
        ↓
PHASE 2
Project & Repository Platform
        ↓
EVALUATION 1
Source Understanding
        ↓
PHASE 3
Analysis Engine & Architecture Model
        ↓
PHASE 4
Architecture Graph & Exploration
        ↓
EVALUATION 2
Architecture Reconstruction & Exploration
        ↓
PHASE 5
Knowledge, Search & Diagram Intelligence
        ↓
PHASE 6
AI Architecture Intelligence
        ↓
PHASE 7
Final Product & Hardening
        ↓
EVALUATION 3
Complete Architecture Intelligence


25.46 Final Frontend Delivery Contract
This is an explicit master-rulebook requirement:

Frontend development is distributed across all seven phases. It is never postponed until the backend is finished.

The implementation model is:
P1 Backend + P1 Frontend
              ↓
        Working Slice

P2 Backend + P2 Frontend
              ↓
        Working Slice

P3 Backend + P3 Frontend
              ↓
        Working Slice

P4 Backend + P4 Frontend
              ↓
        Working Slice

P5 Backend + P5 Frontend
              ↓
        Working Slice

P6 Backend + P6 Frontend
              ↓
        Working Slice

P7 Backend + P7 Frontend
              ↓
       Complete Product


25.47 Final Principle

StackSense will be built as seven progressively complete vertical slices, not as a backend project followed by a frontend project.

Every phase must move the entire product forward.
The backend provides the capability.
The frontend exposes that capability.
Infrastructure makes it executable.
Tests prove it works.
Observability makes it understandable.
Security makes it trustworthy.
And the phase is complete only when all of those pieces form a working slice.
End of Section 25.


26. EVALUATION & ACADEMIC MILESTONES
26.1 Purpose
This section defines the academic evaluation strategy for StackSense.
The academic evaluation process must demonstrate the progressive development of the system, rather than presenting three disconnected prototypes.
The three evaluations represent three increasing levels of capability:
Evaluation 1
    ↓
Source Understanding

Evaluation 2
    ↓
Architecture Reconstruction & Exploration

Evaluation 3
    ↓
Complete Architecture Intelligence

Each evaluation must demonstrate:

what has been implemented;
what architectural capability has been achieved;
what the frontend can demonstrate;
what backend components support it;
what deterministic analysis is available;
what tests validate the capability;
what remains for the next milestone.


26.2 Academic Evaluation Philosophy
The evaluations should communicate the evolution of StackSense as an engineering system.
The progression is:
Repository
    ↓
Understand Source
    ↓
Understand Structure
    ↓
Understand Architecture
    ↓
Explore Architecture
    ↓
Retrieve Knowledge
    ↓
Explain Architecture
    ↓
Generate Reports

The project should therefore avoid presenting AI as the main achievement.
The primary achievement is:

Building a deterministic architecture-understanding platform and progressively adding graph, retrieval, visualization, and AI capabilities around it.


26.3 Three Evaluation Milestones
StackSense has exactly three major backend academic evaluations.
┌─────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│ Evaluation 1                               │
│ Source Understanding                       │
└──────────────────────┬──────────────────────┘
                       ↓
┌─────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│ Evaluation 2                               │
│ Architecture Reconstruction & Exploration  │
└──────────────────────┬──────────────────────┘
                       ↓
┌─────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│ Evaluation 3                               │
│ Complete Architecture Intelligence         │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────┘


26.4 Evaluation 1 — Source Understanding
Objective
Demonstrate that StackSense can ingest a software repository and understand its source-level structure.
The evaluation should establish that the project is already more than a file-upload system.

26.5 Evaluation 1 Core Question
The evaluator should be able to ask:

"Can StackSense understand what is present inside this repository?"

The answer should be demonstrated through the implemented source-analysis pipeline.

26.6 Evaluation 1 Expected Pipeline
Repository
    ↓
Ingestion
    ↓
File Discovery
    ↓
File Classification
    ↓
Language Detection
    ↓
Framework Detection
    ↓
Parsing
    ↓
Source-Level Entities
    ↓
Basic Relationships


26.7 Evaluation 1 Backend Demonstration
The backend should demonstrate the relevant capabilities from:
Foundation

application startup;
configuration;
database;
API;
logging;
error handling.

Repository Platform

project;
repository;
repository ingestion;
repository metadata;
source storage.

Source Analysis

file discovery;
supported file detection;
language detection;
framework detection;
parsing;
source entity extraction.


26.8 Evaluation 1 Frontend Demonstration
The frontend must be demonstrated alongside the backend.
The evaluator should be able to:
Create/Open Project
      ↓
Add Repository
      ↓
Start Ingestion
      ↓
View Repository
      ↓
Start Analysis
      ↓
View Analysis Status
      ↓
Explore Source-Level Results

The frontend should make the backend capability visible rather than requiring the evaluator to inspect API responses manually.

26.9 Evaluation 1 UI Expectations
The UI should demonstrate at minimum:
Project
Repository
Repository Status
Analysis Status
Files / Source Overview
Detected Languages
Detected Frameworks
Basic Analysis Results

The exact visual design can evolve later.
The important requirement is that the capability is understandable.

26.10 Evaluation 1 Deterministic Boundary
Evaluation 1 should emphasize deterministic analysis.
The system should not require an LLM to answer:
What files exist?
What language is this file?
What framework is detected?
What entities were extracted?

These should come from deterministic processing.

26.11 Evaluation 1 AI Position
AI may be demonstrated only if useful, but it is not the primary evaluation capability.
The evaluator should understand that AI is intentionally deferred because:
Reliable Architecture Evidence
        ↓
must exist first

before meaningful AI explanations can be generated.

26.12 Evaluation 1 Academic Value
Evaluation 1 demonstrates:

repository processing;
software parsing;
language/framework recognition;
backend engineering;
data modeling;
asynchronous processing where applicable;
API design;
frontend integration;
deterministic source understanding.

This establishes the technical foundation of StackSense.

26.13 Evaluation 1 Success Criteria
Evaluation 1 is successful when the evaluator can see:
Repository
   ↓
StackSense
   ↓
Structured Source Understanding

and the result is:

reproducible;
deterministic;
explainable;
visible through the frontend.


26.14 Transition After Evaluation 1
After Evaluation 1:
Source Understanding
        ↓
Architecture Understanding

becomes the next objective.
The system should not simply add more file-level features indefinitely.
The next milestone must move toward relationships and architecture.

26.15 Evaluation 2 — Architecture Reconstruction & Exploration
Objective
Demonstrate that StackSense can reconstruct a meaningful architecture model from the analyzed repository and allow users to explore it.

26.16 Evaluation 2 Core Question
The evaluator should be able to ask:

"Can StackSense understand how the software is organized and how its components relate to each other?"

This is a major conceptual progression from Evaluation 1.

26.17 Evaluation 2 Expected Pipeline

    ↓

    ↓

    ↓

stable identities;
entities;
relationships.

components;

dependencies;
architectural relationships.

Graph

graph projection;

graph relationships;
graph traversal;
graph rebuildability.


26.19 Evaluation 2 Frontend Demonstration
The frontend must demonstrate the architecture model visually.
The evaluator should be able to:

26.26 Transition After Evaluation 2
After Evaluation 2, StackSense already understands and represents architecture.
The next question becomes:

"How can StackSense help a user query, understand, visualize, explain, and communicate that architecture?"

This leads into Knowledge, Search, Diagram, AI, and Reporting capabilities.

26.27 Evaluation 3 — Complete Architecture Intelligence

Demonstrate the complete StackSense system as an integrated architecture-intelligence platform.

26.28 Evaluation 3 Core Question
The evaluator should be able to ask:

"Can StackSense analyze a repository, reconstruct its architecture, let me explore it, answer architecture questions using evidence, visualize it, and generate useful reports?"

The final evaluation answers this question.

The system should show evidence/context where appropriate.

26.63 Final Academic Principle

Each evaluation must demonstrate a meaningful architectural progression, not merely an increase in the number of features.

The progression is:
"I can understand the code."

        ↓

"I can reconstruct and explore the architecture."

        ↓

"I can use that architecture knowledge
to search, visualize, explain and report
on the system."


26.64 Final Evaluation Contract
The following rules are mandatory:
1. StackSense has exactly three major backend evaluations.
2. Evaluation 1 focuses on source understanding.
3. Evaluation 2 focuses on architecture reconstruction and exploration.
4. Evaluation 3 focuses on complete architecture intelligence.
5. Evaluations are cumulative.
6. Previous evaluation capabilities must remain functional.
7. Each evaluation must demonstrate a working vertical slice.
8. Frontend must be demonstrated alongside backend capabilities.
9. Evaluation 1 must not depend on AI for deterministic source facts.
10. Evaluation 2 must demonstrate architecture relationships.
11. Evaluation 2 must demonstrate graph-based exploration.
12. Evaluation 3 must demonstrate knowledge/search/retrieval.
13. Evaluation 3 must demonstrate diagrams.
14. Evaluation 3 must demonstrate grounded AI explanation.
15. Evaluation 3 must demonstrate reporting.
16. AI remains an explanation/communication layer.
17. Deterministic analysis remains the source of truth.
18. Evaluation repositories must be reproducible.
19. Major evaluation changes should be stabilized before presentation.
20. Architecture changes immediately before evaluation should be avoided.
21. Evaluation evidence must include both implementation and testing evidence.
22. HLD and LLD decisions should be explainable during evaluation.
23. Evaluation demonstrations must show why the architecture exists, not only what the UI looks like.
24. If time is constrained, core architecture takes priority over cosmetic features.
25. Evaluation milestones must remain aligned with the master roadmap.

26.66 Final Principle
The three evaluations are checkpoints in one continuous product journey.

27. DEFINITION OF DONE
27.1 Purpose
This section defines the formal Definition of Done (DoD) for StackSense.
The purpose is to establish a strict and objective standard for determining whether:

a task is complete;
a feature is complete;
a module is complete;
a phase is complete;
an evaluation milestone is complete;
a release is complete.

The central principle is:

Code being written does not mean work is done. Work is done only when the implementation, contracts, tests, security, integration, documentation, and required validation are complete.


27.2 Definition of Done Hierarchy
StackSense uses multiple levels of completion:
Task
 ↓
Feature
 ↓
Module
 ↓
Phase
 ↓
Evaluation Milestone
 ↓
Release

Each level inherits the requirements of the level below it.

27.3 Universal Definition of Done
A change is considered complete only when:
Implementation
+
Architecture Compliance
+
Contract Compliance
+
Testing
+
Security
+
Observability
+
Integration
+
Documentation
+
Validation

have been satisfied to the degree required by the change.

27.4 Task-Level Definition of Done
A small implementation task is Done when:
□ Requirement understood
□ Correct existing code inspected
□ Correct module identified
□ Implementation completed
□ No unnecessary files created
□ No duplicate responsibility introduced
□ Architecture boundaries respected
□ Relevant tests pass
□ Existing tests still pass
□ No obvious regression introduced


27.5 Feature-Level Definition of Done
A feature is Done when:
□ Backend capability implemented
□ Frontend capability implemented where applicable
□ API contract implemented
□ Validation implemented
□ Error handling implemented
□ Loading states implemented
□ Empty states implemented where applicable
□ Permission checks implemented
□ Tests implemented
□ Integration verified
□ Observability considered
□ Security considered
□ Documentation updated


27.6 Backend Definition of Done
A backend feature is Done when:
□ Domain responsibility identified
□ Application service implemented
□ Infrastructure boundary respected
□ Persistence implemented where required
□ API endpoint implemented where required
□ Request validation implemented
□ Response contract implemented
□ Error contract implemented
□ Authentication/authorization considered
□ Tenant isolation verified
□ Logging implemented where appropriate
□ Metrics/tracing considered
□ Tests implemented
□ Integration tests pass


27.7 Frontend Definition of Done
A frontend feature is Done when:
□ UI implemented
□ API integration implemented
□ Loading state implemented
□ Error state implemented
□ Empty state implemented where applicable
□ Permission state handled
□ Success state handled
□ API failures handled
□ Responsive behavior considered
□ Type safety maintained where applicable
□ Frontend tests added where appropriate
□ Integration verified
□ UX is consistent with existing application


27.8 API Definition of Done
An API endpoint is Done when:
□ Correct route
□ Correct HTTP method
□ Authentication requirement defined
□ Authorization requirement defined
□ Tenant boundary enforced
□ Request schema defined
□ Request validation implemented
□ Response schema defined
□ Error responses defined
□ Pagination implemented where required
□ Filtering implemented where required
□ Sorting implemented where required
□ Documentation/OpenAPI updated
□ Tests implemented


27.9 Database Definition of Done
A database change is Done when:
□ Schema change implemented
□ Migration created
□ Migration tested
□ Existing data impact considered
□ Indexing considered
□ Constraints considered
□ Transaction behavior considered
□ Rollback/recovery strategy considered
□ Repository/data-access layer updated
□ Tests updated
□ Production impact considered


27.10 Database Migration Definition of Done
A migration is Done when:
□ Migration is version-controlled
□ Migration runs from a clean database
□ Migration runs against representative existing data
□ Application remains compatible where required
□ Data integrity verified
□ Indexes/constraints verified
□ Failure behavior understood
□ Recovery strategy documented


27.11 Queue/Job Definition of Done
A background job is Done when:
□ Job contract defined
□ Job lifecycle defined
□ Queue integration implemented
□ Worker implementation completed
□ Retry behavior defined
□ Failure behavior defined
□ Idempotency considered
□ Timeout defined where applicable
□ Job status persisted where required
□ Logging implemented
□ Observability implemented
□ Tests implemented


27.12 Storage Definition of Done
A storage feature is Done when:
□ Storage abstraction respected
□ Correct storage implementation used
□ Metadata persisted correctly
□ File/artifact lifecycle defined
□ Error handling implemented
□ Security considered
□ Access control enforced
□ Cleanup behavior defined
□ Tests implemented


27.13 Analysis Engine Definition of Done
An analysis capability is Done when:
□ Input defined
□ Output defined
□ Deterministic behavior defined
□ Relevant parsing implemented
□ IR updated if necessary
□ Identity handling implemented
□ Architecture model updated if necessary
□ Findings generated where applicable
□ Errors handled
□ Results persisted
□ Tests implemented
□ Representative repositories tested


27.14 Deterministic Analysis Rule
The deterministic analysis engine must be considered complete independently of AI.
The following must not be required for deterministic analysis to be Done:
LLM availability
AI provider availability
AI response generation
AI explanation

AI is a separate capability.

27.15 IR Definition of Done
An IR change is Done when:
□ Entity semantics defined
□ Relationship semantics defined
□ Identity semantics defined
□ Source mapping preserved where required
□ Language-specific information normalized correctly
□ Existing consumers remain compatible
□ Tests cover the new representation
□ Architecture model remains consistent


27.16 Identity Definition of Done
An identity change is Done when:
□ Identity format defined
□ Stability requirements defined
□ Collision behavior considered
□ Repository/revision context considered
□ Entity ownership clear
□ Graph compatibility verified
□ Versioning implications considered
□ Tests implemented


27.17 Architecture Model Definition of Done
An architecture-model capability is Done when:
□ Entity types defined
□ Relationship types defined
□ Ownership defined
□ Dependency direction defined
□ Canonical source identified
□ Versioning handled
□ Serialization/API representation defined where needed
□ Tests implemented


27.18 Graph Definition of Done
A graph feature is Done when:
□ Projection source identified
□ Node mapping defined
□ Relationship mapping defined
□ Identity mapping verified
□ Projection implemented
□ Query/traversal implemented
□ Rebuild behavior supported where required
□ Synchronization behavior defined
□ Tests implemented


27.19 Search Definition of Done
A search feature is Done when:
□ Indexed source defined
□ Indexing process implemented
□ Query semantics defined
□ Filtering implemented where required
□ Ranking/relevance considered
□ Tenant isolation enforced
□ Failure behavior defined
□ Index rebuild strategy defined
□ Tests implemented


27.20 Retrieval Definition of Done
Retrieval is Done when:
□ Query interpretation defined
□ Evidence sources defined
□ Retrieval strategy implemented
□ Relevant context selected
□ Tenant boundaries preserved
□ Evidence traceability preserved
□ Failure/empty-result behavior handled
□ Tests implemented


27.21 RAG Definition of Done
The RAG pipeline is Done when:
Question
 ↓
Retrieval
 ↓
Evidence
 ↓
Context
 ↓
Prompt
 ↓
AI
 ↓
Grounded Response

works end-to-end.
The system must not simply send the entire repository to an LLM and call that RAG.

27.22 AI Provider Definition of Done
An AI provider implementation is Done when:
□ Provider interface implemented
□ Factory integration implemented
□ Configuration implemented
□ Authentication/credentials handled securely
□ Timeout implemented
□ Error handling implemented
□ Rate-limit handling considered
□ Retry behavior defined
□ Streaming supported where required
□ Provider-specific code isolated
□ Tests implemented


27.23 AI Feature Definition of Done
An AI feature is Done when:
□ Deterministic evidence exists
□ Retrieval implemented
□ Context builder implemented
□ Prompt builder implemented
□ Provider abstraction used
□ Response validation implemented where required
□ Failure state handled
□ Streaming handled where applicable
□ Hallucination/grounding risk considered
□ Tests/evaluation performed


27.24 AI Grounding Requirement
For architecture questions, AI output must be grounded in available StackSense evidence wherever the feature claims to provide architecture-aware answers.
The system must not present unsupported speculation as verified architecture.

27.25 Diagram Definition of Done
A diagram feature is Done when:
□ Diagram input model defined
□ Architecture data mapped correctly
□ Relationships represented correctly
□ Layout/rendering implemented
□ Large graph behavior considered
□ Filtering/navigation implemented where required
□ Diagram is derived from actual architecture data
□ Tests/validation implemented


27.26 Report Definition of Done
A report feature is Done when:
□ Report schema defined
□ Required analysis information included
□ Architecture information included where required
□ Findings included
□ Evidence included where required
□ AI explanations identified appropriately
□ Report generation implemented
□ Artifact stored correctly
□ Metadata recorded
□ Tests implemented


27.27 Security Definition of Done
A feature is not Done until its security impact has been considered.
At minimum:
□ Authentication considered
□ Authorization considered
□ Tenant isolation verified
□ Input validation implemented
□ Sensitive data handling reviewed
□ Secrets handling reviewed
□ Logging reviewed for sensitive information
□ Access control tested


27.28 Multi-Tenancy Definition of Done
Any tenant-scoped functionality must ensure:
Tenant A
   ↓
Can access only A's data

Tenant B
   ↓
Can access only B's data

Cross-tenant access must be prevented at the appropriate application/data boundaries.

27.29 Secrets Definition of Done
A feature involving credentials is Done only when:
□ No credentials hard-coded
□ Environment/configuration mechanism used
□ Secrets excluded from source control
□ Logs do not expose secrets
□ Access scope minimized
□ Rotation strategy considered


27.30 Observability Definition of Done
A production-relevant feature must provide appropriate observability.
Depending on the feature:
□ Structured logs
□ Metrics
□ Traces
□ Job status
□ Error information
□ Latency information

must be available.
Not every trivial UI change requires new metrics.

27.31 Reliability Definition of Done
A feature involving external systems or asynchronous work must define:
□ Timeout
□ Retry behavior
□ Failure behavior
□ Recovery behavior
□ Idempotency where required
□ User-visible failure state


27.32 Graceful Degradation Definition
Optional infrastructure failures must not unnecessarily destroy unrelated core functionality.
Example:
AI unavailable
      ↓
Architecture analysis still works
Graph still works
Search still works where possible


27.33 Testing Definition of Done
A feature is not Done merely because one happy-path test passes.
Testing should cover the appropriate combination of:
Unit
Integration
API
Database
Queue
Frontend
End-to-End
Architecture
Security


27.34 Unit Testing
Unit tests should validate isolated business behavior.
Examples:
Rule evaluation
Entity extraction
Identity generation
Service logic
Validation
Transformation


27.35 Integration Testing
Integration tests should verify boundaries between components.
Examples:
API → Service
Service → Database
Job → Worker
Analysis → Storage
Projection → Graph
Retrieval → Search
AI Service → Provider


27.36 End-to-End Testing
Critical user journeys should be tested end-to-end.
Examples:
Create Project
 ↓
Add Repository
 ↓
Analyze
 ↓
View Architecture

and eventually:
Ask Question
 ↓
Retrieve Evidence
 ↓
AI Response


27.37 Regression Testing
Every important bug fix should add a regression test when practical.
The target is:
Bug
 ↓
Regression Test
 ↓
Fix
 ↓
Test remains permanently


27.38 Architecture Testing
Architecture rules should be tested where possible.
Examples:
Forbidden imports
Module dependency rules
Layer boundaries
Security boundaries


27.39 Frontend Testing
Frontend testing should cover important user behavior rather than only rendering snapshots.
Examples:
Create project
Start analysis
Display job status
Display errors
Navigate architecture
Search
Ask AI


27.40 CI Definition of Done
A change is not merge-ready until required CI checks pass.
Depending on the repository configuration:
□ Formatting
□ Linting
□ Type checking
□ Unit tests
□ Integration tests
□ Frontend tests
□ Architecture checks
□ Security checks
□ Build


27.41 No Test Weakening
The following is explicitly prohibited:
Test fails
    ↓
Delete test

or:
Test fails
    ↓
Weaken assertion

solely to make CI pass.
The implementation must be corrected unless the expected behavior itself has intentionally changed.

27.42 Documentation Definition of Done
Documentation must be updated when a change affects:

architecture;
public APIs;
developer workflows;
deployment;
security;
configuration;
user-facing behavior.


27.43 ADR Definition of Done
If a feature changes a frozen architectural decision:
□ Change identified
□ ADR reviewed
□ New ADR created/updated
□ Previous decision marked appropriately
□ Master architecture updated
□ Implementation aligned

The implementation is not Done until documentation and architecture are synchronized.

27.44 Diagram Documentation Definition
When architecture relationships materially change:
□ HLD updated
□ Relevant LLD updated
□ Architecture diagrams updated


27.45 Frontend + Backend Completion Rule
A backend feature that requires frontend exposure is not considered complete until the frontend portion is integrated.
Backend
   +
Frontend
   +
API
   +
Tests
   =
Done

This directly follows the roadmap rule established in Section 25.

27.46 Vertical Slice Definition of Done
A vertical slice is Done when a real user can complete the intended workflow through the actual system.
For example:
User
 ↓
Frontend
 ↓
API
 ↓
Application
 ↓
Infrastructure
 ↓
Persistence

works without manually bypassing application boundaries.

27.47 Module Definition of Done
A module is Done when:
□ All assigned responsibilities implemented
□ Public interfaces defined
□ Internal boundaries respected
□ Tests complete
□ Integration complete
□ Frontend capability delivered where applicable
□ Documentation complete
□ Observability complete where applicable
□ Security verified
□ No known blocking defects


27.48 Phase Definition of Done
A phase is Done when all phase responsibilities from Section 25 have been delivered.
Minimum requirements:
□ Backend complete
□ Frontend complete
□ API contracts complete
□ Infrastructure integrated
□ Tests complete
□ Security reviewed
□ Observability implemented
□ Documentation updated
□ Architecture compliance verified
□ Vertical slice working
□ Phase demonstration possible


27.49 Phase Acceptance
The phase owner/team must be able to demonstrate:
What was built
Why it exists
How it works
How frontend and backend interact
How it is tested
What infrastructure it uses
What architectural decisions support it


27.50 Evaluation Definition of Done
An academic evaluation milestone is Done when:
□ Required phase capabilities implemented
□ Frontend demonstration ready
□ Backend demonstration ready
□ End-to-end flow works
□ Evaluation repository works
□ Tests pass
□ Architecture explanation prepared
□ HLD explanation prepared
□ Relevant LLD explanation prepared
□ Known limitations documented
□ Demo flow validated


27.51 Evaluation 1 Definition of Done
Evaluation 1 is Done when the system can demonstrate:
Repository
 ↓
Ingestion
 ↓
Source Analysis
 ↓
Language/Framework Understanding
 ↓
Source-Level Results

through a working frontend/backend vertical slice.

27.52 Evaluation 2 Definition of Done
Evaluation 2 is Done when the system can demonstrate:
Repository
 ↓
Analysis
 ↓
IR
 ↓
Architecture Model
 ↓
Graph
 ↓
Architecture Exploration

through a working frontend/backend vertical slice.

27.53 Evaluation 3 Definition of Done
Evaluation 3 is Done when the system can demonstrate:
Repository
 ↓
Analysis
 ↓
Architecture
 ↓
Graph
 ↓
Knowledge
 ↓
Retrieval
 ↓
Diagram
 ↓
AI Explanation
 ↓
Report

through the complete integrated product.

27.54 Release Definition of Done
A release is Done when:
□ Intended features complete
□ Tests pass
□ CI passes
□ Security checks pass
□ Database migrations verified
□ Deployment verified
□ Configuration verified
□ Observability verified
□ Rollback/recovery considered
□ Release version assigned
□ Release notes prepared
□ Documentation synchronized


27.55 Production Definition of Done
A feature intended for production is Done when it can be safely operated.
This means:
Correctness
+
Security
+
Observability
+
Reliability
+
Recoverability
+
Documentation

are satisfied.

27.56 AI-Assisted Development Definition of Done
When AI assists implementation, the resulting code is subject to the exact same Definition of Done as human-written code.
AI assistance does not reduce requirements.
AI-generated code
        =
Code

and therefore must pass the same:
Architecture
Testing
Security
CI
Review

requirements.

27.57 AI Implementation Verification
Before accepting AI-generated code:
□ Existing repository inspected
□ Architecture source consulted
□ Code manually reviewed
□ Generated assumptions verified
□ Imports verified
□ APIs verified
□ Dependencies verified
□ Tests reviewed
□ Security reviewed


27.58 No Hallucination Acceptance
The following are not acceptable:
Invented files
Invented APIs
Invented framework behavior
Invented database fields
Invented configuration
Invented architecture

If AI is uncertain, repository inspection must occur.

27.59 Performance Definition of Done
Performance-sensitive features should be validated against the relevant NFRs.
Where applicable:
API latency
Database query performance
Analysis duration
Search latency
Diagram rendering
AI latency
Frontend load performance

must be measured rather than assumed.

27.60 Scalability Definition of Done
A feature that affects scalability must consider:
Concurrent users
Concurrent jobs
Database load
Queue depth
Worker concurrency
Storage growth
Search index growth
Graph growth


27.61 Resource Management
Long-running operations must not leak:

memory;
database connections;
file handles;
worker processes;
temporary artifacts.


27.62 Error-State Definition of Done
Every user-facing operation should have an understandable failure state.
For example:
Loading
   ↓
Success

or:
Loading
   ↓
Failure
   ↓
Recover / Retry / Explain

The UI must not silently remain in an infinite loading state.

27.63 Empty-State Definition of Done
Where a feature can legitimately contain no data, the UI should distinguish:
No data exists

from:
Data failed to load


27.64 Permission-State Definition of Done
If a user lacks permission:
Unauthorized

must not be confused with:
Not found

unless intentionally required by the security model.

27.65 Accessibility / UX Definition
The frontend should satisfy the project's agreed UX/accessibility expectations.
At minimum:
Readable UI
Clear states
Usable navigation
Meaningful labels
Keyboard usability where applicable


27.66 Code Quality Definition of Done
Code should:
□ Have clear responsibility
□ Use meaningful names
□ Avoid unnecessary complexity
□ Avoid duplicate logic
□ Follow repository conventions
□ Respect SOLID/DDD boundaries where applicable
□ Be understandable to another developer


27.67 No Premature Optimization
A feature is not expected to be maximally optimized before correctness is established.
Preferred:
Correct
 ↓
Measured
 ↓
Identify bottleneck
 ↓
Optimize
 ↓
Measure again


27.68 No Cosmetic Completion
A UI should not be considered complete simply because it looks finished.
The underlying workflow must work.
Beautiful UI
+
Broken API
=
NOT DONE


27.69 No Backend-Only Completion
Likewise:
Working Backend
+
Missing Required Frontend
=
NOT DONE

when the feature is intended to be user-facing.

27.70 No Test-Only Completion
Tests pass
+
Feature not actually implemented
=
NOT DONE

Tests are evidence, not a substitute for implementation.

27.71 No Documentation-Only Completion
Architecture documented
+
Implementation absent
=
NOT DONE

Documentation must describe reality.

27.72 No Demo-Only Completion
A manually staged demo that bypasses the actual system does not satisfy Definition of Done.
The demonstrated path should use the real implementation.

27.73 Known Limitations
A feature may still be considered Done when known limitations exist if:

they are explicitly documented;
they do not violate the acceptance criteria;
they are not security/correctness blockers;
they are tracked for future work.


27.74 Blocking Defects
The following normally prevent completion:
Critical security issue
Data corruption
Cross-tenant access
Major correctness failure
Broken core workflow
Unrecoverable production failure
Architecture violation
Failing required tests
Broken migration


27.75 Non-Blocking Defects
Examples may include:
Minor UI spacing issue
Non-critical cosmetic bug
Optional optimization
Minor documentation wording

provided they do not affect acceptance criteria.

27.76 Final Completion Checklist
Before marking any major work Done:
IMPLEMENTATION
□ Correct code exists
□ Correct responsibility
□ No duplication

ARCHITECTURE
□ ADRs respected
□ Module boundaries respected
□ Canonical/derived boundaries respected
□ AI boundary respected

BACKEND
□ API complete
□ Validation complete
□ Errors handled
□ Persistence complete

FRONTEND
□ UI complete
□ API integrated
□ Loading state
□ Error state
□ Empty state
□ Permission state

DATA
□ Schema correct
□ Migration complete
□ Integrity verified

ASYNC
□ Job lifecycle defined
□ Retry behavior defined
□ Idempotency considered

SECURITY
□ Authentication
□ Authorization
□ Tenant isolation
□ Secrets
□ Input validation

OBSERVABILITY
□ Logs
□ Metrics/traces where required
□ Failure visibility

TESTING
□ Unit
□ Integration
□ API
□ Frontend
□ E2E where required
□ Regression

DOCUMENTATION
□ API
□ Architecture
□ ADR
□ Diagrams
□ User/developer documentation where required

DELIVERY
□ CI passes
□ Build passes
□ Deployment validated
□ Rollback/recovery considered

FINAL
□ Vertical slice works
□ Demonstrable
□ No blocking defects

27.78 The StackSense Completion Equation
The fundamental rule is:

27.79 Final Definition

A StackSense task, feature, module, phase, evaluation, or release is Done only when it satisfies its functional requirements, respects the frozen architecture, integrates with the rest of the system, passes the required tests and validation, handles security and failure appropriately, provides the required frontend experience, and is documented sufficiently to be maintained by another developer.


27.80 Final Non-Negotiable Rules
1. "Code written" does not mean Done.

2. Backend-only work is not Done when frontend delivery is required.

3. Passing tests alone does not mean Done.

4. A demo workaround does not mean Done.

5. AI-generated code follows the same DoD as human code.

6. Architecture violations prevent Done.

7. Security violations prevent Done.

8. Cross-tenant access prevents Done.

9. Broken core workflows prevent Done.

10. Required migrations must be validated before Done.

11. Significant asynchronous operations require failure/retry handling.

12. User-facing operations require appropriate loading/error/empty states.

13. Deterministic analysis must remain independently functional.

14. AI must respect the established responsibility boundary.

15. Documentation must reflect the actual implementation.

16. ADRs must be synchronized with architectural changes.

17. Every phase must produce a working vertical slice.

18. Every evaluation must be demonstrable through the frontend and backend.

19. Known non-blocking limitations must be documented.

20. Final completion requires validation, not merely implementation.

                         │

                         │

                         │
                         ▼
                       DONE


If any mandatory stage fails, the work is not Done.

End of Section 27.



28. EXPLICIT DO-NOT RULES
28.1 Purpose
This section defines the explicit prohibitions for StackSense implementation.
These rules exist to prevent:

architectural drift;
hallucinated implementation;
accidental technology changes;
duplicated responsibilities;
security vulnerabilities;
inconsistent contracts;
unnecessary complexity;
poor engineering practices;
AI-assisted implementation errors.

These rules apply to all contributors and all AI coding agents working on StackSense.

If another instruction conflicts with this section, the master architecture document and its approved ADRs take precedence according to the change-control rules in Section 24.


28.2 DO NOT Violate Frozen Architecture
Do not change a frozen architectural decision during implementation without following the approved change-control process.
Frozen Decision
      ↓
DO NOT silently replace it

If the decision appears incorrect:
Identify Problem
      ↓
Propose Change
      ↓
Review
      ↓
ADR Update
      ↓
Implement


28.3 DO NOT Invent Architecture
Do not assume StackSense uses a technology, pattern, service, or infrastructure component simply because it is common.
Examples:
"Most systems use Kafka."
"Let's add Kubernetes."
"RAG usually uses Pinecone."
"Let's use microservices."

These are not valid reasons to introduce technology.
The architecture document is authoritative.

28.4 DO NOT Introduce Technology Without Approval
Do not add:

databases;
message brokers;
queues;
frameworks;
ORMs;
search engines;
vector databases;
cloud services;
AI providers;
infrastructure platforms;

without determining whether they are already approved by the architecture.

28.5 DO NOT Replace Technology Casually
Do not replace:
Redis → RabbitMQ
PostgreSQL → another database
Local Storage → S3
AI Provider A → Provider B
Framework A → Framework B

merely because the alternative is easier.
Technology replacement follows Section 24.

28.6 DO NOT Add Kafka Just Because It Is Impressive
Do not introduce Kafka merely to make the architecture appear more sophisticated.
The selected messaging/queue architecture must be justified by actual system requirements.

28.7 DO NOT Add Microservices Without a Requirement
StackSense must not be split into microservices merely because:

"This is a system-design project."

A modular monolith or other approved architecture must not be unnecessarily converted into microservices.

28.8 DO NOT Create Distributed Systems Complexity Without Need
Do not add:

service discovery;
distributed transactions;
API gateways;
service meshes;
complex event buses;

unless the frozen architecture explicitly requires them.

28.9 DO NOT Turn Every Component Into a Service
A class, module, worker, repository, or engine does not automatically need its own network service.

28.10 DO NOT Duplicate Responsibilities
Do not create multiple components that perform the same responsibility.
Bad:
AnalysisService
AnalysisManager
AnalysisHelper
AnalysisProcessor
AnalysisEngine

all implementing overlapping analysis logic.

28.11 DO NOT Create utils.py for Everything
Do not use generic utility files as dumping grounds for unrelated logic.
Avoid:
utils.py
helpers.py
misc.py
common.py
manager.py

when a more precise ownership exists.

28.12 DO NOT Create Duplicate Abstractions
Before creating:
RepositoryService
RepositoryManager
RepositoryHandler

inspect whether an existing repository/application abstraction already owns that responsibility.

28.13 DO NOT Bypass Module Boundaries
Do not directly access another module's internal implementation.
Use its defined public interface.
Bad:
Module A
   ↓
Module B private repository

Preferred:
Module A
   ↓
Module B public contract


28.14 DO NOT Bypass Domain/Application Boundaries
Do not place business logic inside:

controllers;
routers;
repositories;
database models;
infrastructure adapters;
UI components.

Business responsibility belongs in the appropriate application/domain layer.

28.15 DO NOT Put Business Logic in Controllers
Controllers/routes should coordinate requests and responses.
Do not turn them into giant business-logic files.

28.16 DO NOT Put Business Logic in Repositories
Repositories handle persistence concerns.
They must not determine architectural/business decisions unrelated to persistence.

28.17 DO NOT Put Business Logic in Database Models
Database models should not become the application's entire domain layer.

28.18 DO NOT Let Infrastructure Define Domain Rules
Infrastructure should implement technical mechanisms.
It must not become the source of business truth.

28.19 DO NOT Leak Infrastructure Into Domain Logic
Domain/application logic should not unnecessarily depend directly on:
Redis
Neo4j
Elasticsearch
S3 SDK
Specific AI SDK

Use the established abstraction boundaries.

28.20 DO NOT Make PostgreSQL a General-Purpose Dump
PostgreSQL is not a dumping ground for every piece of data.
Respect the ownership defined by the architecture.

28.21 DO NOT Treat Derived Stores as Canonical
Do not make:
Graph
Search Index
Cache
Vector Index

the authoritative source merely because querying them is convenient.

28.22 DO NOT Treat the Graph as the Source of Truth
The graph is a derived representation/projection according to the frozen architecture.
Do not modify graph data independently in a way that creates architectural truth separate from the canonical model.

28.23 DO NOT Treat Search Indexes as Canonical
Search indexes must be rebuildable from their authoritative source where the architecture requires.
Do not treat indexed documents as the only copy of important canonical state.

28.24 DO NOT Make Caches Authoritative
Do not design business correctness around cached state when the cache is not the canonical source.

28.25 DO NOT Store Canonical State Only in Redis
Redis may provide infrastructure capabilities such as:

queues;
caching;
temporary state;

but do not use it as the sole canonical store unless explicitly approved.

28.26 DO NOT Scatter Raw Database Access
Do not place arbitrary database queries throughout:
controllers
services
workers
utilities
frontend

Use the established persistence boundary.

28.27 DO NOT Let Frontend Access Infrastructure Directly
The frontend must not directly access:
PostgreSQL
Redis
Neo4j
Elasticsearch
S3

The frontend communicates through the approved application interfaces.

28.28 DO NOT Hard-Code Secrets
Never commit:
API keys
Passwords
Tokens
Private keys
Database credentials
Cloud credentials
AI provider credentials

into source code.

28.29 DO NOT Put Secrets in Git
Do not commit secrets even temporarily.
Deleting them later does not necessarily remove them from Git history.

28.30 DO NOT Log Secrets
Do not log:
Authorization headers
API keys
Passwords
Tokens
Connection strings containing credentials


28.31 DO NOT Expose Sensitive Data in Errors
Error responses must not accidentally expose:

credentials;
internal secrets;
stack traces;
database connection details;
sensitive tenant data.


28.32 DO NOT Trust User Input
Do not assume:
IDs are valid
paths are safe
file names are safe
queries are safe
repository contents are trustworthy

Validate and sanitize input according to the relevant boundary.

28.33 DO NOT Trust Repository Code
StackSense analyzes external repositories.
Therefore repository source code must be treated as input, not trusted application code.
Do not execute arbitrary repository code merely to analyze it unless explicitly required and safely sandboxed by the architecture.

28.34 DO NOT Execute Arbitrary Repository Code
Do not:
import arbitrary uploaded Python modules
execute repository scripts
run package installation blindly
execute repository build scripts

as part of ordinary analysis.
Analysis should be performed through controlled parsing and inspection mechanisms.

28.35 DO NOT Install Repository Dependencies Blindly
Do not automatically execute:
pip install -r requirements.txt
npm install
npm run build

against an untrusted repository merely to analyze it.
Such actions can execute arbitrary code.

28.36 DO NOT Treat File Extensions as Proof of Content
Do not assume:
.py = valid Python
.js = valid JavaScript
.ts = valid TypeScript

without appropriate validation/parsing.

28.37 DO NOT Assume Framework Detection Is Perfect
Framework detection must be treated as an analysis result with defined confidence/limitations where appropriate.
Do not fabricate framework information.

28.38 DO NOT Invent Source Relationships
If the parser cannot establish a relationship, do not create one merely because it seems likely.
Deterministic architecture information must be evidence-based.

28.39 DO NOT Invent Architecture From Naming Alone
Do not assume:
UserService → microservice
Repository → repository pattern
Controller → MVC
Manager → service layer

solely from names.
Actual source structure and relationships must support the conclusion.

28.40 DO NOT Let AI Invent Architecture
AI-generated explanations must not become architectural facts.
If the deterministic engine says:
A → B

the AI must not claim:
A → C

without supporting evidence.

28.41 DO NOT Use AI as the Deterministic Analyzer
Do not replace deterministic source analysis with:
Send repository to LLM
      ↓
Ask LLM "What is the architecture?"

and treat the result as canonical architecture.

28.42 DO NOT Make the LLM the Source of Truth
AI output is not canonical StackSense state.
The authoritative information comes from the appropriate deterministic/canonical systems.

28.43 DO NOT Give AI Unlimited Repository Context
Do not automatically send the entire repository to the AI provider for every question.
Use:
Question
 ↓
Retrieval
 ↓
Evidence
 ↓
Context
 ↓
AI


28.44 DO NOT Skip Retrieval for Architecture Questions
When the architecture-intelligence flow requires evidence retrieval, do not bypass it and directly ask the model.

28.45 DO NOT Hide Evidence From Users Where Evidence Is Required
When the product promises grounded architecture explanations, provide appropriate evidence/context visibility.
The user should be able to understand why an answer was generated.

28.46 DO NOT Couple Business Logic to One AI Provider
Do not scatter:
Gemini SDK calls
OpenAI SDK calls
Anthropic SDK calls

throughout application/domain code.
Use the approved provider abstraction.

28.47 DO NOT Instantiate AI Providers Everywhere
Do not repeatedly do:
provider = Gemini(...)

throughout unrelated modules.
Provider creation belongs behind the established factory/provider boundary.

28.48 DO NOT Assume AI Is Always Available
AI features must handle:
timeout
rate limit
provider failure
network failure
invalid response
service unavailable

gracefully.

28.49 DO NOT Make Core Features Depend on AI Availability
If AI is unavailable, unrelated deterministic capabilities should continue operating whenever possible.

28.50 DO NOT Silently Retry AI Forever
AI calls must have bounded retry behavior.
Never create an infinite retry loop.

28.51 DO NOT Ignore AI Output Validation
Do not assume an AI response is valid simply because it was returned successfully.
Validate structured output where required.

28.52 DO NOT Use AI to Hide Missing Implementation
Do not implement a missing deterministic feature by asking an LLM to simulate its output.

28.53 DO NOT Generate Fake Data for Production Logic
Mocks and fixtures are allowed for testing.
They must not silently become production data sources.

28.54 DO NOT Hard-Code Demo Results
Do not hard-code architecture results merely to make an academic demonstration look successful.
The evaluation must use the actual analysis pipeline.

28.55 DO NOT Create Demo-Only Shortcuts
Do not build:
if demo_mode:
    return fake_architecture

to bypass actual functionality.

28.56 DO NOT Delete Tests to Make CI Pass
Never solve:
Failing Test

by deleting the test.

28.57 DO NOT Weaken Assertions Without Reason
Do not change:
assert expected == actual

to something meaningless simply because the implementation currently fails.

28.58 DO NOT Ignore Failing Tests
A failing test must be:
fixed

or:
intentionally changed because the contract changed

with the appropriate documentation.

28.59 DO NOT Skip Regression Tests for Important Bugs
Important bug fixes should preserve a test that prevents recurrence where practical.

28.60 DO NOT Test Only the Happy Path
Important workflows must also test appropriate failure cases.
Examples:
invalid repository
missing project
unauthorized user
duplicate job
provider timeout
database failure
empty search


28.61 DO NOT Swallow Exceptions
Avoid patterns that silently ignore failures.
Bad:
try:
    operation()
except:
    pass


28.62 DO NOT Use Bare Exception Handling Without Reason
Do not broadly catch every exception unless there is a deliberate boundary-level reason and the failure is handled appropriately.

28.63 DO NOT Use print() as Production Observability
Use the project's structured logging system.

28.64 DO NOT Log Everything
Logging every object, request, response, or repository file can:

leak sensitive data;
create huge logs;
increase costs;
make debugging harder.

Log meaningful operational information.

28.65 DO NOT Create Infinite Background Jobs
Every job must have defined:
lifecycle
retry limit
timeout
failure state

where applicable.

28.66 DO NOT Create Non-Idempotent Retryable Jobs
If a job can be retried, do not assume it runs only once.
Consider:
job executes
 ↓
network timeout
 ↓
worker retries
 ↓
job executes again

The implementation must handle this safely where required.

28.67 DO NOT Assume Queue Delivery Means Exactly Once
Do not design critical behavior around an unverified exactly-once guarantee.
Assume duplicate delivery may occur where the infrastructure contract permits it.

28.68 DO NOT Block HTTP With Long Analysis
Do not make large repository analysis execute synchronously inside a normal request if the architecture defines it as asynchronous work.

28.69 DO NOT Use Infinite HTTP Requests
Long-running requests must have appropriate timeout and lifecycle handling.

28.70 DO NOT Poll Aggressively
Do not implement frontend polling that continuously hammers the backend.
Use the approved status/update mechanism.

28.71 DO NOT Use SSE as a Generic Replacement for Everything
SSE should be used where real-time server-to-client streaming is appropriate.
Do not force every API interaction through SSE.

28.72 DO NOT Use WebSockets Without Architectural Need
Do not replace the agreed SSE approach with WebSockets simply because they appear more advanced.

28.73 DO NOT Create Unbounded Concurrency
Do not allow unlimited:
analysis jobs
workers
AI requests
database connections
repository ingestion tasks

Concurrency must be controlled.

28.74 DO NOT Ignore Resource Limits
Repository analysis can involve large codebases.
Do not assume:
files are small
repositories are small
graphs are small
AI contexts are unlimited
memory is unlimited


28.75 DO NOT Load Entire Repositories Into Memory Unnecessarily
Prefer streaming, batching, or controlled processing where appropriate.

28.76 DO NOT Build Giant In-Memory Graphs Without Need
Architecture analysis should account for repository size and resource constraints.

28.77 DO NOT Create Unbounded Search Results
Search APIs must use appropriate pagination/limits.

28.78 DO NOT Return Unbounded API Collections
Large collections must use pagination or another controlled retrieval strategy where appropriate.

28.79 DO NOT Ignore Tenant Boundaries
Never trust a client-provided:
organization_id
project_id
repository_id
analysis_id

without verifying that the authenticated user has access.

28.80 DO NOT Use IDs as Authorization
Knowing an object's ID must never automatically grant access to it.

28.81 DO NOT Assume "Not Found" Means "Unauthorized"
Authorization must be implemented intentionally.
Do not accidentally expose whether another tenant's resource exists.

28.82 DO NOT Leak Cross-Tenant Search Results
Search/retrieval must enforce tenant boundaries.
A search query from Tenant A must not return Tenant B's information.

28.83 DO NOT Leak Cross-Tenant Graph Data
Graph queries must enforce the same isolation rules.

28.84 DO NOT Leak Cross-Tenant Artifacts
Artifact URLs/download mechanisms must verify authorization.
Do not assume possession of a URL is sufficient authorization unless explicitly designed and secured.

28.85 DO NOT Trust Client-Side Authorization
Frontend checks improve UX.
They do not replace backend authorization.

28.86 DO NOT Store Authorization Logic Only in the Frontend
The backend remains authoritative.

28.87 DO NOT Expose Internal IDs Unnecessarily
Do not expose internal identifiers simply because they exist.
Expose identifiers according to the API contract.

28.88 DO NOT Skip Input Validation
Validate:

request fields;
IDs;
paths;
repository metadata;
uploaded artifacts;
configuration;
AI structured output.


28.89 DO NOT Trust File Paths
Repository file paths can contain:
../
absolute paths
unexpected encodings
symlinks

Path handling must prevent traversal outside the intended repository boundary.

28.90 DO NOT Allow Arbitrary File Access
A repository analysis endpoint must not accidentally become:
GET /files?path=/etc/passwd


28.91 DO NOT Expose the Host Filesystem
Repository storage boundaries must be enforced.

28.92 DO NOT Treat Uploaded Files as Trusted
Uploaded content must be validated and handled safely.

28.93 DO NOT Commit Generated Artifacts Without Reason
Do not clutter Git with:
temporary analysis outputs
logs
cache files
generated build directories
local databases

unless explicitly required.

28.94 DO NOT Commit Local Environment Files
Do not commit:
.env
local secrets
IDE metadata
machine-specific configuration

unless explicitly safe and intended.

28.95 DO NOT Modify Unrelated Files
When implementing a task, do not perform unrelated cleanup throughout the repository.

28.96 DO NOT Reformat the Entire Repository Unnecessarily
Large formatting-only diffs make review and debugging harder.

28.97 DO NOT Mix Unrelated Refactors
Avoid:
Feature implementation
+
massive rename
+
folder restructuring
+
dependency upgrade

in one change unless the task is specifically a migration.

28.98 DO NOT Rename Things Without Reason
Renaming public classes, endpoints, database fields, or modules can create unnecessary compatibility work.

28.99 DO NOT Create "V2" Everything
Avoid names like:
ServiceV2
ServiceV3
UtilsNew
ManagerFinal
RepositoryNew

unless they represent an intentional versioned contract.

28.100 DO NOT Use Temporary Names as Permanent Architecture
Names such as:
temp
new
old
backup
final
final2

must not become permanent architecture.

28.101 DO NOT Copy-Paste Large Blocks of Logic
Reuse or abstract shared responsibility where appropriate.

28.102 DO NOT Over-Abstract
Do not create interfaces, factories, strategies, or abstractions purely to make the architecture appear sophisticated.
Use abstractions when they protect a real boundary or enable a meaningful variation.

28.103 DO NOT Under-Abstraction
Conversely, do not directly couple core logic to infrastructure when the architecture explicitly requires an abstraction.

28.104 DO NOT Use Design Patterns for Their Own Sake
Do not add:
Factory
Builder
Strategy
Observer
Adapter
Repository

simply because a design-pattern list says they are useful.
Use patterns where they solve an actual design problem.

28.105 DO NOT Create Generic "Manager" Classes
A class called:
Manager

without a precise responsibility is usually a sign that ownership has not been defined.

28.106 DO NOT Put Everything in One Service
Avoid giant services that own:
analysis
storage
AI
search
reports
authentication

at once.

28.107 DO NOT Create Giant Files
Avoid files containing unrelated responsibilities or enormous monolithic classes/functions.
The project's agreed file-size guidance must be respected.

28.108 DO NOT Split Files Artificially
Do not create dozens of tiny files simply to make individual files smaller.
File boundaries should represent meaningful responsibilities.

28.109 DO NOT Ignore the Framework Boundary
When implementing framework-specific behavior, follow the selected framework's conventions and the project's framework boundaries.
Do not invent hybrid architectures without justification.

28.110 DO NOT Mix Frameworks Unnecessarily
Do not combine:
Django + FastAPI + Flask

inside one application simply because all three are approved technologies.
Approved does not mean every framework must be used simultaneously.

28.111 DO NOT Assume Every Approved Framework Must Be Used
The framework boundary defines what StackSense may support/use where appropriate.
It does not require every framework to appear in the core implementation.

28.112 DO NOT Introduce TypeScript Just for Decoration
If TypeScript is used, it must provide meaningful type safety and maintainability.
Do not convert files purely to claim TypeScript usage.

28.113 DO NOT Ignore Type Safety
Where TypeScript is used, do not defeat its purpose with excessive:
any

or unsafe casts.

28.114 DO NOT Mix JS/TS Conventions Randomly
Follow the repository's established conventions for:
.js
.jsx
.ts
.tsx

Do not create arbitrary combinations without reason.

28.115 DO NOT Put Backend Logic in Next.js UI
Next.js frontend code must not become an unstructured second backend unless explicitly required by the architecture.

28.116 DO NOT Bypass the API Contract
Frontend developers must not invent request/response structures independently of the backend contract.

28.117 DO NOT Hard-Code API URLs Throughout the Frontend
Use the established API client/configuration boundary.

28.118 DO NOT Duplicate Backend Validation in a Way That Creates Conflicting Rules
Frontend validation may improve UX.
Backend validation remains authoritative.

28.119 DO NOT Trust Frontend State as Backend Truth
The backend must validate important state transitions.

28.120 DO NOT Create UI That Cannot Represent Failure
Every meaningful asynchronous operation should have a failure state.

28.121 DO NOT Hide Long-Running Operations
Analysis jobs should expose meaningful progress/status where the architecture supports it.

28.122 DO NOT Fake Progress
Do not display:
10%
20%
30%
...
100%

if the backend has no basis for those values.
Use genuine job state/progress where available.

28.123 DO NOT Claim Real-Time Updates Without Real-Time Infrastructure
Do not label periodic polling as real-time unless the product definition intentionally uses that terminology.

28.124 DO NOT Treat a Successful HTTP Request as Successful Background Work
For asynchronous jobs:
202 Accepted

or equivalent acknowledgement does not mean the job itself succeeded.
The UI must follow the job lifecycle.

28.125 DO NOT Ignore Job State Transitions
Do not let frontend or backend code assume:
queued → completed

without handling appropriate intermediate/failure states.

28.126 DO NOT Allow Orphaned Jobs
Jobs must have ownership and lifecycle tracking according to the architecture.

28.127 DO NOT Create Untracked Background Work
Do not launch background work that the system cannot observe, retry, cancel, or otherwise manage where such control is required.

28.128 DO NOT Make Schedulers Responsible for Business Logic
Schedulers trigger work.
They should not become giant business-logic containers.

28.129 DO NOT Confuse Scheduler With Queue
Scheduling determines when work should happen.
Queueing determines how work is dispatched/executed.
Do not collapse these responsibilities without architectural justification.

28.130 DO NOT Confuse Graph With Search
Graph:
relationships
traversal
architecture structure

Search:
discovery
retrieval
querying indexed information

Do not use one as an unexplained replacement for the other.

28.131 DO NOT Confuse Retrieval With AI
Retrieval determines evidence.
AI generates an explanation from the provided context.
They are separate responsibilities.

28.132 DO NOT Confuse Reports With Canonical Analysis
Reports are outputs.
They must not become the source of truth for architecture findings.

28.133 DO NOT Generate Reports From Unverified AI Claims
Reports must rely on appropriate deterministic/verified information.
AI explanations must be clearly treated according to their responsibility boundary.

28.134 DO NOT Create Circular Dependencies
Avoid module relationships such as:
A → B
B → C
C → A

unless explicitly justified by the architecture.

28.135 DO NOT Import Across Layers Arbitrarily
Follow the established dependency direction.

28.136 DO NOT Let Infrastructure Become the Domain
Infrastructure adapters must not dictate business/domain abstractions merely because the SDK exposes a convenient API.

28.137 DO NOT Let External Libraries Dictate Architecture
The project architecture comes first.
Libraries are implementation tools.

28.138 DO NOT Choose Libraries Before Understanding the Requirement
Do not start with:

"Which library should we use?"

Start with:

"What responsibility must this component provide?"

Then select the appropriate implementation.

28.139 DO NOT Add Dependencies Without Evaluating Them
Before adding a package, consider:
maintenance
security
license
size
compatibility
operational complexity


28.140 DO NOT Ignore Dependency Security
Known vulnerable dependencies must be reviewed and addressed according to project policy.

28.141 DO NOT Upgrade Dependencies Blindly
Do not run a massive dependency upgrade without understanding compatibility impact.

28.142 DO NOT Change Framework Versions During Unrelated Features
Keep dependency/version changes isolated where practical.

28.143 DO NOT Make Database Changes Without Migrations
Never manually modify the expected schema without recording the change through the migration system.

28.144 DO NOT Make Destructive Migrations Casually
Do not casually:
DROP TABLE
DROP COLUMN
DELETE DATA

without impact analysis and recovery planning.

28.145 DO NOT Assume Database Rollback Is Always Safe
A schema/data migration may not be reversible.
Plan recovery before deployment.

28.146 DO NOT Perform Large Data Migrations Inside Ordinary Requests
Large migrations should use controlled background/operational processes where appropriate.

28.147 DO NOT Ignore Transaction Boundaries
Do not allow partially completed critical operations when atomicity is required.

28.148 DO NOT Assume External Services Never Fail
Design for:
timeout
unavailability
rate limiting
partial failure
network failure


28.149 DO NOT Use Infinite Retries
All retry policies must be bounded.

28.150 DO NOT Retry Non-Retryable Errors
Do not repeatedly retry:
invalid credentials
invalid input
authorization failure
permanent validation failure

unless there is a deliberate reason.

28.151 DO NOT Ignore Timeouts
External calls and expensive operations need appropriate time limits.

28.152 DO NOT Make Timeouts Arbitrary
Timeouts should reflect the expected operation and infrastructure behavior.

28.153 DO NOT Assume Local Development Equals Production
Local Docker configuration must not be assumed to represent production deployment automatically.

28.154 DO NOT Hard-Code Local Paths
Avoid machine-specific paths such as:
/home/pr0xius/...
C:\Users\...

in project code.

28.155 DO NOT Depend on Developer-Specific Environment State
The project must be reproducible on another developer's environment according to the documented setup.

28.156 DO NOT Commit IDE-Specific Configuration Without Reason
Avoid unnecessary:
.idea
.vscode
editor caches
OS-specific metadata

unless intentionally standardized.

28.157 DO NOT Commit Build Artifacts Unnecessarily
Do not commit:
dist
build
__pycache__
node_modules
coverage
temporary generated files

unless explicitly required.

28.158 DO NOT Use Different Package Managers Randomly
Follow the repository's chosen package-management strategy.

28.159 DO NOT Create Multiple Lockfiles Without Reason
Avoid:
package-lock.json
yarn.lock
pnpm-lock.yaml

simultaneously unless intentionally required.

28.160 DO NOT Mix Python Environment Strategies Randomly
Follow the repository's agreed Python dependency/environment approach.

28.161 DO NOT Commit Virtual Environments
Do not commit:
venv/
.venv/

or equivalent local environments.

28.162 DO NOT Assume Absolute Paths
Code should not depend on the developer's current working directory unless explicitly designed.

28.163 DO NOT Use Relative Import Workarounds Against the Frozen Convention
If the project has established absolute-import rules, do not introduce ad-hoc import hacks simply to make one test or script run.

28.164 DO NOT Modify sys.path as a General Architecture Solution
Do not use runtime path manipulation to hide incorrect package/module structure.

28.165 DO NOT Ignore Packaging Problems
If imports fail because the repository structure is incorrect, fix the underlying packaging/configuration rather than accumulating path hacks.

28.166 DO NOT Create Hidden Global State
Avoid unnecessary:
global mutable variables
singleton state
module-level caches

when dependency injection/configuration can provide controlled behavior.

28.167 DO NOT Create Hidden Side Effects
Functions should not unexpectedly:
modify global state
write files
send network requests
create jobs

without their responsibility making such behavior clear.

28.168 DO NOT Make Constructors Perform Expensive Work
Avoid constructors that unexpectedly:
connect to databases
call AI providers
scan repositories
run analysis

unless explicitly required by the architecture.

28.169 DO NOT Create God Objects
Avoid classes that know everything about:
repository
analysis
graph
AI
storage
reports
users


28.170 DO NOT Create God Functions
Avoid functions that perform an entire pipeline without meaningful decomposition.

28.171 DO NOT Hide Complexity Behind Poor Names
A function called:
process()
handle()
execute()
run()

should have enough contextual ownership to make its responsibility clear.

28.172 DO NOT Overuse Boolean Flags
Avoid APIs such as:
process(data, true, false, true, false)

when named options or distinct operations are clearer.

28.173 DO NOT Create Unclear State Machines
Job/analysis states must have explicit semantics.
Do not invent states that overlap or contradict each other.

28.174 DO NOT Allow Invalid State Transitions
For example, if:
completed

is terminal, do not casually allow:
completed → running

without an explicitly defined operation.

28.175 DO NOT Lose Historical Information Unnecessarily
Analysis results, architecture versions, and important artifacts should remain traceable according to the versioning architecture.

28.176 DO NOT Overwrite Historical Analysis Blindly
