30.66 Final Architecture Contract
The following is the final compact contract for StackSense:
STACKSENSE ARCHITECTURE CONTRACT

1. StackSense is an architecture-intelligence platform.

2. Deterministic analysis is the primary source of architectural truth.

3. AI is an explanation/reasoning layer, not the canonical architecture engine.

4. Repository contents are untrusted input.

5. Repository code must not be blindly executed.

6. IR normalizes language-specific analysis.

7. Identity provides stable and traceable architectural entities.

8. Architecture Model represents the interpreted system structure.

9. Knowledge Graph is a derived projection.

10. Search is for discovery and retrieval.

11. Graph is for relationships and traversal.

12. Retrieval is an evidence-planning layer.

13. RAG provides relevant evidence/context to AI.

14. AI providers are interchangeable through an abstraction.

15. Provider-specific SDK details remain isolated.

16. Diagram Engine visualizes architecture.

17. Report Engine produces derived artifacts.

18. Long-running analysis is asynchronous.

19. Background jobs require lifecycle, failure, retry, and observability handling.

20. SSE provides approved server-to-client real-time updates where appropriate.

21. Local storage is the initial storage strategy.

22. Storage must be abstracted sufficiently for future S3 migration.

23. Security is cross-cutting.

24. Multi-tenancy is mandatory wherever resources are tenant-scoped.

25. Backend authorization is authoritative.

26. Secrets must never be hard-coded, committed, logged, or exposed to the frontend.

27. APIs use the established versioned contract.

28. Frontend and backend are developed and delivered together by phase.

29. Every major phase should produce a working vertical slice.

30. HLD defines major architecture.

31. LLD defines component-level design.

32. SOLID, low coupling, high cohesion, DI, and appropriate design patterns guide implementation.

33. Patterns must solve actual problems.

34. Over-engineering is prohibited.

35. Under-engineering security/correctness is prohibited.

36. All project imports use absolute imports.

37. Runtime path hacks must not be used to hide structural problems.

38. Existing code must be inspected before modifying it.

39. Existing files, classes, methods, APIs, schemas, and configurations must never be guessed.

40. If a required file is unavailable, ASK FOR THE FILE.

41. If requirements are genuinely ambiguous, ASK rather than invent.

42. Tests validate behavior and contracts.

43. Tests must not be deleted/weakened merely to achieve CI success.

44. Important bugs should receive regression tests.

45. Architecture changes require change control.

46. Frozen decisions cannot be silently replaced.

47. Documentation must reflect actual architecture.

48. Derived systems must remain derived.

49. Historical analysis must remain traceable where required.

50. Performance claims require measurement.

51. AI claims require appropriate evaluation.

52. Evaluation demonstrations must use the actual system.

53. Fake results, fake progress, and demo-only shortcuts are prohibited.

54. Security, reliability, observability, and graceful degradation are part of the architecture.

55. A feature is Done only when implementation, integration, testing, security, documentation, and required validation are complete.


30.67 Final Rule of StackSense

When in doubt, do not invent.

CHECK THE ARCHITECTURE.
CHECK THE ADR.
CHECK THE CONTRACT.
CHECK THE REPOSITORY.
CHECK THE FILE.

If the information exists → use it.

If the information does not exist → ask.

If the architecture needs to change → propose it and follow change control.

Never silently guess.


30.68 Final Statement
This section marks the end of the StackSense architecture specification.
Sections 1–30 together form the complete architectural foundation of the project.
The project should now transition from:
Architecture Definition
        ↓
Design Decisions
        ↓
Contracts
        ↓
Rules

into:
Implementation
        ↓
Integration
        ↓
Testing
        ↓
Evaluation
        ↓
Productization

The architecture is now the boundary within which implementation takes place.

Build inside the architecture. Do not let implementation accidentally redefine it.

APPENDICES
The appendices provide supporting reference material for the StackSense architecture specification. They do not introduce new architectural decisions or override Sections 1–30. Instead, they consolidate detailed lookup information such as technology references, structural conventions, contracts, terminology, diagrams, supported frameworks, configuration references, and other implementation-oriented material. Developers and AI coding agents should use the appendices alongside the main architecture document when they need a precise reference during implementation. Any conflict between an appendix and the main architecture must be resolved in favor of the approved architecture and change-control process defined in Sections 24 and 30.


APPENDIX A — CANONICAL TERMINOLOGY
A.1 Purpose
This appendix defines the canonical terminology used throughout StackSense.
The purpose is to ensure that developers, documentation, diagrams, APIs, database models, frontend components, and AI coding agents use the same terminology for the same concepts.
A term defined here should not be casually replaced with synonyms when referring to the same architectural concept.
For example, if StackSense defines Analysis as the canonical term for a repository-analysis execution, documentation should not randomly refer to it as a scan, inspection, job, or run when those terms could create ambiguity.

A.2 Terminology Rules
The following rules apply to terminology throughout StackSense:

Use the canonical term when referring to a defined StackSense concept.
Do not create multiple names for the same concept.
Do not use an implementation-specific name as a domain concept.
Avoid ambiguous terms such as data, manager, processor, or handler when a more precise term exists.
API names, database entities, domain objects, documentation, diagrams, and frontend terminology should remain aligned.
If a new concept genuinely requires a new term, define it before introducing it broadly.
If two concepts are different, do not use the same term for both.
When uncertain about terminology, check this appendix before creating a new name.


A.3 Canonical Product Terms



Canonical Term
Definition




StackSense
The complete software architecture intelligence platform.


Architecture Intelligence
The capability of deriving, representing, exploring, and explaining software architecture from source repositories.


Repository
The source-code project being analyzed by StackSense.


Repository Revision
A specific version/state of a repository being analyzed, such as a Git commit or equivalent revision identifier.


Ingestion
The process of receiving, validating, storing, and preparing a repository for analysis.


Analysis
A specific execution of StackSense's deterministic repository-analysis pipeline.


Analysis Engine
The subsystem responsible for deterministic analysis of repository contents.


Analysis Lifecycle
The state progression of an Analysis from creation through completion, failure, or cancellation.


Analysis Job
The background execution unit responsible for performing an Analysis.


Finding
A deterministic observation produced by the analysis engine.


Architecture Model
The structured representation of the architecture reconstructed from analyzed repository evidence.


Architecture Entity
A modeled architectural object such as a module, class, service, endpoint, or component.


Architecture Relationship
A modeled relationship between architecture entities.


Evidence
Source-derived information supporting an architectural observation or explanation.


Knowledge Graph
The derived graph representation of architecture entities and relationships.


Retrieval
The process of identifying relevant evidence and knowledge for a question or task.


Evidence Planner
The component responsible for determining what evidence should be retrieved for a request.


Context
The structured information assembled for downstream reasoning or explanation.


Context Builder
The component responsible for organizing retrieved evidence into usable reasoning context.


AI Provider
An implementation capable of generating AI-assisted explanations through the defined provider contract.


AI Provider Factory
The component responsible for selecting/creating the appropriate AI provider implementation.


Explanation
Natural-language reasoning generated from retrieved evidence and context.


Diagram
A visual representation of the Architecture Model.


Diagram Engine
The subsystem responsible for transforming architecture information into diagrams.


Report
A generated artifact presenting analysis, architecture, findings, evidence, and/or explanations.


Report Engine
The subsystem responsible for generating reports.


Artifact
A persisted/generated file or object produced or managed by StackSense.




A.4 Repository Terminology
Repository
A Repository is the software project submitted to StackSense for analysis.
Do not use:
codebase
project
source
application

interchangeably with Repository when referring specifically to the analyzed source repository.
They may describe related concepts but are not automatically equivalent.

Repository Revision
A Repository Revision identifies the specific version of a Repository used for an Analysis.
Example:
Repository
    ↓
Revision: abc123
    ↓
Analysis

This is important for reproducibility and historical traceability.

Repository File
A Repository File is an individual file contained within the analyzed Repository revision.
Examples:
main.py
src/api/routes.ts
components/Dashboard.tsx


File Type
A File Type represents the technical classification of a file.
Examples:
Python
JavaScript
TypeScript
Markdown
JSON
YAML
Image


Source Artifact
A Source Artifact refers to a repository-provided file or source object used as input to analysis.

A.5 Analysis Terminology
Analysis
An Analysis represents one logical execution of StackSense's analysis process against a specific Repository Revision.
Conceptually:
Repository
    +
Revision
    ↓
Analysis

An Analysis should be distinguishable from the background job that executes it.

Analysis Job
An Analysis Job is the asynchronous execution mechanism responsible for carrying out an Analysis.
Therefore:
Analysis
    ≠
Analysis Job

The Analysis represents the logical operation.
The Analysis Job represents its execution.

Analysis Lifecycle
The Analysis Lifecycle describes the states through which an Analysis progresses.
Typical states include:
QUEUED
RUNNING
COMPLETED
FAILED
CANCELLED

The exact state machine is defined by the relevant architecture/contracts.

Analysis Finding
A Finding is an observation produced by deterministic analysis.
Examples:
Detected dependency
Detected architectural layer
Detected framework
Detected circular dependency
Detected architectural violation

A Finding should be distinguishable from an AI-generated explanation.

Analysis Evidence
Evidence is information that supports a Finding or architectural interpretation.
Evidence should remain traceable to its source where required.

A.6 IR Terminology
IR
IR means Intermediate Representation.
It is the normalized representation produced from language/framework-specific source analysis.
Source
   ↓
Parser / Analyzer
   ↓
IR


IR Entity
An IR Entity represents a normalized source-level object.
Examples:
File
Module
Class
Function
Variable
Import
Endpoint

The exact entity taxonomy is defined by the analysis architecture.

IR Relationship
An IR Relationship represents a relationship extracted during deterministic analysis.
Examples:
imports
calls
extends
implements
contains
references


A.7 Identity Terminology
Identity
Identity is the mechanism used to determine the stable identity of an entity across analysis operations and versions where possible.

Entity Identity
Entity Identity uniquely identifies an architecture/source entity within the appropriate scope.
Identity should not rely unnecessarily on unstable properties.

Identity Resolution
Identity Resolution is the process of determining whether an observed entity corresponds to an existing known entity.
Conceptually:
Observed Entity
      ↓
Identity Resolution
      ↓
Known Identity


A.8 Architecture Terminology
Architecture Model
The Architecture Model is the canonical structured representation of the interpreted software architecture.
It is built from deterministic analysis and represents entities and their relationships.

Architecture Entity
An Architecture Entity is a meaningful unit in the Architecture Model.
Examples may include:
Application
Service
Module
Component
Class
Function
Endpoint

The exact taxonomy depends on the supported architecture model.

Architecture Relationship
An Architecture Relationship describes how two architecture entities relate.
Examples:
depends_on
contains
calls
imports
exposes
implements


Architecture Boundary
An Architecture Boundary defines a separation between responsibilities, modules, layers, or systems.
Boundaries exist to control coupling and ownership.

Architecture Layer
An Architecture Layer is a logical grouping of components based on responsibility.
Examples:
API
Application
Domain
Infrastructure


A.9 Knowledge Terminology
Knowledge Graph
The Knowledge Graph is a derived graph representation of architectural knowledge.
It consists conceptually of:
Nodes
+
Relationships
+
Metadata


Graph Node
A Graph Node represents an entity within the Knowledge Graph.

Graph Edge
A Graph Edge represents a relationship between Graph Nodes.

Graph Projection
Graph Projection is the process of transforming canonical architecture information into the Knowledge Graph.
Architecture Model
       ↓
Graph Projection
       ↓
Knowledge Graph


Projection
A Projection is a derived representation of canonical data optimized for a particular use case.
The Knowledge Graph and search index are examples.

A.10 Search and Retrieval Terminology
Search
Search is the process of finding relevant indexed information based on a query.
Search is primarily concerned with discovery.

Retrieval
Retrieval is the broader process of selecting relevant information/evidence for a specific task or question.
Search
  ↓
Candidate Results
  ↓
Retrieval
  ↓
Relevant Evidence

Search and Retrieval should not automatically be treated as synonyms.

Evidence Planner
The Evidence Planner determines what information is required to answer a request effectively.
It may use:
Search
Graph traversal
Direct lookup
Metadata
Relationships


Retrieved Context
Retrieved Context is the relevant information selected for downstream reasoning or explanation.

Context Builder
The Context Builder transforms retrieved information into structured context suitable for the next processing stage.

A.11 RAG Terminology
RAG
RAG means Retrieval-Augmented Generation.
Within StackSense:
Question
   ↓
Retrieval
   ↓
Evidence
   ↓
Context
   ↓
Generation


Retrieval Context
The Retrieval Context is the information provided to the AI generation stage based on retrieved evidence.

Prompt Builder
The Prompt Builder constructs the structured AI request from:
System requirements
+
Question
+
Retrieved context
+
Relevant instructions


A.12 AI Terminology
AI Provider
An AI Provider is an implementation of the StackSense AI-provider contract.
The provider abstracts the underlying model/vendor.

AI Model
An AI Model is the specific model used by an AI Provider.
Provider and Model are not the same concept.
AI Provider
    ↓
AI Model


AI Explanation
An AI Explanation is a natural-language explanation generated from approved context/evidence.
It is not automatically canonical architecture data.

AI Responsibility Boundary
The AI Responsibility Boundary defines what AI is allowed to perform.
AI is primarily used for:
Explanation
Summarization
Natural-language reasoning
Communication

It is not the canonical deterministic architecture analyzer.

A.13 Diagram Terminology
Diagram
A Diagram is a visual representation of architecture information.

Diagram Engine
The Diagram Engine transforms architecture information into a visual representation.
Architecture Model
       ↓
Diagram Engine
       ↓
Diagram


Diagram Layout
Diagram Layout describes the visual arrangement of entities and relationships.
Layout must not modify architectural truth.

A.14 Report Terminology
Report
A Report is a generated presentation of StackSense results.
It may contain:
Analysis Summary
Architecture
Findings
Evidence
Recommendations
AI Explanations
Diagrams

depending on the report type.

Report Engine
The Report Engine transforms approved information into a report artifact.

Report Artifact
A Report Artifact is the persisted/generated output file or object representing a Report.

A.15 Background Processing Terminology
Job
A Job represents a unit of asynchronous work.

Queue
A Queue is the mechanism used to hold work awaiting processing.

Worker
A Worker is a process/runtime responsible for executing queued Jobs.

Scheduler
A Scheduler determines when scheduled work should be created or triggered.
Important distinction:
Scheduler
    = determines WHEN

Queue
    = determines HOW work is dispatched

Worker
    = performs the work


Job Retry
A Job Retry is another execution attempt following a failure where retry is permitted.
Retries must be bounded.

Idempotent Job
An Idempotent Job can safely be executed more than once without producing an incorrect duplicated outcome.

A.16 Real-Time Terminology
SSE
SSE means Server-Sent Events.
It provides server-to-client streaming over an HTTP connection.

Event Stream
An Event Stream is a sequence of server-generated events delivered to a client.

Real-Time Update
A Real-Time Update is a server-originated state/event update delivered to the frontend through the approved real-time mechanism.

A.17 Storage Terminology
Storage Provider
A Storage Provider implements the application's storage contract.
Examples:
Local Storage Provider
S3 Storage Provider


Local Storage
The initial StackSense storage implementation.

Object Storage
Storage designed around objects/files and metadata, such as S3-compatible systems.

Artifact Storage
The storage mechanism used for generated/persisted artifacts such as:
Reports
Diagrams
Repository archives
Generated files


A.18 Security Terminology
Tenant
A Tenant is an isolated organizational boundary within StackSense.

Organization
An Organization represents the primary tenant/business boundary defined by the product architecture.

Project
A Project is a logical grouping of StackSense resources within an Organization.

Environment
An Environment represents a contextual deployment/runtime environment associated with a Project where defined by the product architecture.

Resource
A Resource is an object managed by StackSense and subject to ownership/authorization rules.
Examples:
Project
Repository
Analysis
Report
Artifact


Authentication
Authentication determines:

Who is the user?


Authorization
Authorization determines:

What is the user allowed to access or perform?


RBAC
RBAC means Role-Based Access Control.
Permissions are associated with roles and assigned according to the product's authorization model.

Tenant Isolation
Tenant Isolation ensures that resources belonging to one tenant cannot be improperly accessed by another tenant.

A.19 Security/Secret Terminology
Secret
A Secret is sensitive authentication/configuration material such as:
API Key
Password
Token
Private Key
Credential


Secret Management
Secret Management is the controlled lifecycle of storing, accessing, rotating, and protecting secrets.

Credential
A Credential is information used to authenticate or authorize access to a system.

A.20 Observability Terminology
Observability
Observability is the system's ability to understand its internal behavior through externally visible telemetry.

Log
A structured record describing an operational event.

Metric
A numerical measurement representing system behavior.

Trace
A representation of a request/operation's journey across system components.

Health Check
A mechanism for determining whether a component satisfies its defined health/readiness condition.

A.21 Reliability Terminology
Failure
A condition in which an operation cannot successfully complete according to its contract.

Retry
A subsequent attempt to perform an operation after a failure.

Timeout
A bounded maximum duration after which an operation is considered unsuccessful or requires cancellation/fallback.

Graceful Degradation
The ability of the system to continue providing useful functionality when an optional subsystem is unavailable.

Recovery
The process of restoring expected operation after a failure.

A.22 API Terminology
API
The application interface exposed to clients and other approved consumers.

Endpoint
A specific API operation exposed at a route/method combination.

Request
Data submitted by a client to an API operation.

Response
Data returned by the API.

DTO
DTO means Data Transfer Object.
A structured representation used to transfer data across a defined boundary.

API Contract
The formal definition of an API's:
Request
Response
Validation
Errors
Authentication
Authorization

and related behavior.

A.23 Frontend Terminology
Frontend
The user-facing web application.

UI
UI means User Interface.

UX
UX means User Experience.

Component
A reusable frontend UI unit with a defined responsibility.

Client State
State owned by the frontend for UI behavior.

Server State
Data originating from backend/application services and synchronized through API mechanisms.
These should not be treated as the same category of state.

A.24 Architecture Design Terminology
HLD
HLD means High-Level Design.
It describes:
Major Components
System Boundaries
Data Flow
Technology Choices
Architectural Relationships


LLD
LLD means Low-Level Design.
It describes:
Classes
Interfaces
Methods
Dependencies
Object Relationships
Detailed Component Behavior


Module
A Module is a cohesive architectural unit with a defined responsibility and boundary.

Component
A Component is an independently meaningful implementation/architectural unit within a module or system.

Service
The term Service should only be used when referring to an actual application/infrastructure service or an explicitly defined service abstraction.
Do not use Service as a generic suffix for every class.

Adapter
An Adapter translates an external implementation/interface into the internal contract expected by StackSense.

Factory
A Factory is responsible for controlled creation/selection of implementations.

Strategy
A Strategy represents interchangeable behavior behind a common contract.

Repository Pattern
A Repository abstraction isolates persistence concerns from higher-level application logic.
Important:

Repository as a software-design pattern must be distinguished from Repository as a source-code project when ambiguity exists.


A.25 Source-of-Truth Terminology
Canonical
Canonical means authoritative within the relevant architectural boundary.

Derived
Derived means generated from another authoritative source and therefore not independently authoritative.

Source of Truth
The Source of Truth is the authoritative source from which correctness is determined for a particular piece of information.

Projection
A Projection is a derived representation optimized for a specific purpose.

Evidence
Information supporting a claim.

Inference
A conclusion derived from available evidence rather than directly observed.
AI-generated reasoning must not be presented as direct evidence.

A.26 Versioning Terminology
Version
A defined version of a system, artifact, schema, API, or analysis rule.

Revision
A specific version/state of a repository or source artifact.

Analysis Version
The version of the analysis engine/rules used to generate an Analysis.

Schema Version
The version of a persisted data schema.

API Version
The version of the public API contract.

A.27 Architecture Change Terminology
ADR
ADR means Architecture Decision Record.
It records a significant architectural decision and its reasoning.

Frozen Decision
A decision that has been approved and must not be changed casually.

Superseded Decision
A previous decision that has been intentionally replaced by a newer approved decision.

Change Control
The formal process used to modify frozen architecture decisions.

A.28 Development Terminology
Feature
A user-visible or system-level capability being implemented.

Vertical Slice
A complete implementation path across the relevant layers.
Example:
Frontend
   ↓
API
   ↓
Application
   ↓
Domain
   ↓
Infrastructure
   ↓
Database


Phase
A major development stage containing a coherent group of capabilities.

Module
A bounded implementation area delivered as part of the project roadmap.

Definition of Done
The criteria that must be satisfied before work can be considered complete.

A.29 Coding Terminology
Low Coupling
Minimizing unnecessary dependencies between components.

High Cohesion
Keeping closely related responsibilities together.

Dependency Injection
Providing dependencies to a component rather than having the component construct them unnecessarily.

SOLID
The five object-oriented design principles:
S — Single Responsibility
O — Open/Closed
L — Liskov Substitution
I — Interface Segregation
D — Dependency Inversion


Design Pattern
A reusable design approach to a recurring software design problem.
A pattern is not mandatory merely because it exists.

A.30 Canonical Naming Distinctions
The following distinctions are particularly important:



Do Not Confuse
Correct Distinction




Repository vs Analysis
Repository is the source project; Analysis is an execution against it


Analysis vs Analysis Job
Analysis is the logical operation; Job executes it


Finding vs Explanation
Finding is deterministic; Explanation may be AI-generated


Architecture Model vs Graph
Model is canonical; Graph is derived


Search vs Retrieval
Search discovers; Retrieval selects relevant evidence


Evidence vs Inference
Evidence is supporting information; inference is a conclusion


AI Provider vs AI Model
Provider abstracts the AI service; Model is the specific model


Diagram vs Architecture Model
Diagram visualizes; Architecture Model represents


Report vs Analysis
Report presents results; Analysis produces them


Scheduler vs Queue
Scheduler determines when; Queue dispatches work


Queue vs Worker
Queue holds work; Worker executes it


Authentication vs Authorization
Authentication identifies; authorization permits


Organization vs Project
Organization is tenant boundary; Project groups resources


HLD vs LLD
HLD defines system architecture; LLD defines implementation design


Canonical vs Derived
Canonical is authoritative; derived is generated


Repository Pattern vs Repository
One is a design pattern; one is the analyzed software project




A.31 Prohibited Ambiguous Terminology
Avoid using these terms as generic architectural names unless their exact meaning is clear:
Manager
Handler
Processor
Helper
Utility
Data
Object
Thing
Common
Misc
Service
Engine
System
Module
Pipeline

These terms are not forbidden universally.
They are discouraged when a more precise term exists.

A.32 Naming Rule for New Concepts
Before introducing a new architectural term:
New Concept
    ↓
Does a canonical term already exist?
       │
   ┌───┴───┐
   │       │
  YES      NO
   │       │
   ▼       ▼
Use it   Define new term
             ↓
       Document it here

Do not introduce synonyms merely for stylistic variation.

A.33 Final Canonical Vocabulary
At the highest level, the StackSense vocabulary can be remembered as:
Repository
    ↓
Revision
    ↓
Ingestion
    ↓
Analysis
    ↓
IR
    ↓
Identity
    ↓
Architecture Model
    ↓
Architecture Entity
    ↓
Architecture Relationship
    ↓
Knowledge Graph
    ↓
Search
    ↓
Retrieval
    ↓
Evidence
    ↓
Context
    ↓
AI Provider
    ↓
Explanation
    ↓
Diagram / Report

And operationally:
Analysis
    ↓
Analysis Job
    ↓
Queue
    ↓
Worker
    ↓
Lifecycle
    ↓
Observability


A.34 Final Terminology Rule

One concept → one canonical name.

If a concept already exists in this appendix, use its defined terminology.
If the implementation reveals a genuinely new concept, do not silently invent terminology. Define the concept, establish its responsibility, and add it to the canonical vocabulary through the appropriate documentation/change-control process.

StackSense terminology is part of the architecture. Consistent language produces consistent design.

END OF APPENDIX A — CANONICAL TERMINOLOGY



APPENDIX B — ENTITY / RELATION VOCABULARY
B.1 Purpose
This appendix defines the canonical entity and relationship vocabulary used by StackSense's architecture model, IR, Knowledge Graph, retrieval system, diagrams, and reports.
The purpose is to ensure that the same architectural concept is represented consistently across:
Source Analysis
      ↓
IR
      ↓
Identity
      ↓
Architecture Model
      ↓
Knowledge Graph
      ↓
Search / Retrieval
      ↓
Diagram / Report / AI

An entity represents something that exists in the analyzed software system.
A relation represents a meaningful connection between two entities.
The vocabulary defined here is the canonical vocabulary. Implementations must not create arbitrary relationship names when an existing canonical relation already represents the same meaning.

B.2 Core Entity Model
At the highest level:
Entity
  │
  ├── Identity
  ├── Type
  ├── Name
  ├── Location
  ├── Metadata
  └── Evidence

Relationships connect entities:
Entity A
    │
    │ Relation
    ▼
Entity B

Conceptually:
┌──────────────┐        imports        ┌──────────────┐
│   Module A   │ ────────────────────► │   Module B   │
└──────────────┘                       └──────────────┘


B.3 Entity Categories
StackSense entities are grouped into the following broad categories:
Repository Entities
Source Entities
Architecture Entities
Execution / Analysis Entities
Knowledge Entities
Product Entities
Artifact Entities

Not every entity category must appear in every analysis.

B.4 Repository Entities
B.4.1 Repository
Represents the complete source repository being analyzed.
Repository

Key conceptual attributes may include:
identity
name
source
metadata
current revision


B.4.2 Repository Revision
Represents a specific version/state of a Repository.
Repository
     │
     ├── Revision A
     ├── Revision B
     └── Revision C

A Repository Revision is important for reproducibility.

B.4.3 Repository File
Represents a file contained within a Repository Revision.
Examples:
main.py
src/api/routes.ts
components/App.tsx
package.json
README.md


B.5 Source Entities
B.5.1 Module
A logical source-code module/package/namespace.
Examples:
backend.analysis
src/auth
app.services


B.5.2 Package
A language/framework-specific packaging unit where the source ecosystem defines such a concept.

B.5.3 Namespace
A logical naming scope used by the language or framework.

B.5.4 Class
A class declaration.

B.5.5 Interface
An explicitly declared interface/contract in languages that support interfaces or equivalent constructs.

B.5.6 Function
A function declaration.

B.5.7 Method
A function associated with a class/object/type.

B.5.8 Variable
A declared variable or binding where relevant to architectural analysis.
Variables should not automatically become architecture-level entities unless they provide meaningful architectural information.

B.5.9 Constant
A declared constant where relevant.

B.5.10 Enum
An enumeration/type containing a defined set of values.

B.5.11 Type
A language-level type declaration or equivalent construct.

B.6 Dependency Entities
B.6.1 Dependency
Represents an externally or internally referenced dependency.
Examples:
Python package
npm package
framework
library
internal module

A Dependency may be represented separately from a Module when the distinction is meaningful.

B.6.2 Framework
Represents a detected framework.
Examples include the approved framework ecosystem:
Express
NestJS
Next.js

and supported Python frameworks.

B.6.3 Library
Represents a reusable software library that is not necessarily classified as a framework.

B.6.4 Runtime
Represents the runtime environment relevant to the analyzed software.
Example:
Node.js

Important:

Node.js is a runtime, not a framework.


B.7 Application Architecture Entities
B.7.1 Application
Represents a logically identifiable application within the analyzed system.

B.7.2 Service
Represents a meaningful application/infrastructure service.
The term should only be used when the architecture supports service-level semantics.

B.7.3 Component
Represents a meaningful architectural component.
A Component should have a clearly defined responsibility.

B.7.4 Layer
Represents a logical architectural layer.
Examples:
API
Application
Domain
Infrastructure


B.7.5 Subsystem
Represents a larger logical grouping of components performing a related capability.

B.7.6 API
Represents an application interface exposed by the system.

B.7.7 Endpoint
Represents a specific API operation.
Conceptually:
API
 │
 ├── Endpoint A
 ├── Endpoint B
 └── Endpoint C

An Endpoint is identified by the relevant API contract information such as method/path where applicable.

B.7.8 Event
Represents a meaningful event emitted/consumed by the system where event-driven behavior is detected.

B.7.9 Queue
Represents an asynchronous work-dispatch mechanism where relevant.

B.7.10 Worker
Represents a runtime component that consumes/executes background work.

B.8 Data Entities
B.8.1 Database
Represents a database used by the analyzed system.

B.8.2 Database Schema
Represents a logical database schema/namespace.

B.8.3 Table
Represents a database table.

B.8.4 Collection
Represents a collection in data stores that use collection-oriented terminology.

B.8.5 Model
Represents a data/domain model detected in the application.
A Model must not automatically be assumed to correspond directly to a database table.

B.8.6 Entity Model
Represents a domain/data entity when the application explicitly models such a concept.

B.9 Infrastructure Entities
B.9.1 Storage
Represents a storage subsystem.

B.9.2 Storage Provider
Represents the implementation providing storage.
Examples:
Local Storage
S3


B.9.3 Cache
Represents a caching subsystem.

B.9.4 Search Index
Represents an indexed/searchable representation of data.

B.9.5 Vector Index
Represents a vector/embedding-based retrieval index where applicable.

B.9.6 Knowledge Graph
Represents the graph-based architectural knowledge representation.

B.9.7 External System
Represents an external dependency/service that the analyzed application communicates with.

B.10 AI Entities
B.10.1 AI Provider
Represents an AI provider implementation.

B.10.2 AI Model
Represents a specific model offered through an AI Provider.

B.10.3 Prompt
Represents a structured instruction/context payload sent to an AI system.

B.10.4 Explanation
Represents an AI-generated natural-language explanation.
An Explanation is not itself an architectural source-of-truth entity.

B.11 Analysis Entities
B.11.1 Analysis
Represents a logical execution of repository analysis.

B.11.2 Analysis Job
Represents the background execution associated with an Analysis.

B.11.3 Finding
Represents an observation produced by analysis.

B.11.4 Evidence
Represents source-derived information supporting a Finding or architectural interpretation.

B.11.5 Analysis Result
Represents the structured output produced by a stage or complete analysis operation.

B.12 Artifact Entities
B.12.1 Artifact
Represents a generated or persisted file/object.
Examples:
Report
Diagram
Repository Archive
Export


B.12.2 Diagram
Represents a visual artifact derived from architecture information.

B.12.3 Report
Represents a generated presentation of analysis/architecture information.

B.13 Product Entities
These entities belong primarily to the StackSense product/domain rather than the analyzed repository.
B.13.1 Organization
The tenant/business boundary.

B.13.2 Project
A logical grouping of resources within an Organization.

B.13.3 Environment
A contextual environment associated with a Project.

B.13.4 User
A StackSense user.

B.13.5 Role
A defined authorization role.

B.13.6 Permission
A capability granted through the authorization model.

B.14 Canonical Relation Categories
Relationships are grouped into:
Containment
Dependency
Invocation
Implementation
Inheritance
Exposure
Data
Runtime
Event
Ownership
Generation
Projection
Analysis
Evidence
Authorization


B.15 Containment Relations
B.15.1 contains
Indicates that one entity contains another.
Module
   │
   └── contains → Class


B.15.2 belongs_to
The inverse semantic of containment where useful.
Class
   │
   └── belongs_to → Module

Implementations should avoid storing both directions as independent truth unless required by the graph/index architecture.

B.16 Dependency Relations
B.16.1 depends_on
Indicates that one entity depends on another.
Service A
   │
   └── depends_on → Service B


B.16.2 imports
Indicates that one source entity imports another.
Module A
   │
   └── imports → Module B


B.16.3 uses
Indicates that an entity uses another entity without necessarily implying a stronger dependency semantic.

B.17 Invocation Relations
B.17.1 calls
Indicates that one callable entity invokes another.
Function A
   │
   └── calls → Function B


B.17.2 invokes
May be used where the architectural language requires a broader invocation relationship.
calls should remain preferred for ordinary source-level callable relationships.

B.18 Type Relations
B.18.1 extends
Represents inheritance.
Child
  │
  └── extends → Parent


B.18.2 implements
Represents implementation of an interface/contract.
Service
   │
   └── implements → Interface


B.18.3 inherits_from
A broader inheritance relation where required by the architecture model.
Use extends for explicit source-language inheritance when possible.

B.19 API Relations
B.19.1 exposes
Indicates that an application/service exposes an API or endpoint.
Service
   │
   └── exposes → Endpoint


B.19.2 handles
Indicates that a controller/handler/component handles an endpoint/request.
Controller
   │
   └── handles → Endpoint


B.19.3 routes_to
Indicates routing from one endpoint/request path to another application component.

B.20 Data Relations
B.20.1 reads_from
Indicates that an entity reads data from another entity.
Service
   │
   └── reads_from → Database


B.20.2 writes_to
Indicates that an entity writes data to another entity.

B.20.3 persists_to
Indicates that an entity is persisted through another entity.

B.20.4 maps_to
Indicates a mapping between representations.
Examples:
Domain Model
   │
   └── maps_to → Database Model


B.21 Event Relations
B.21.1 emits
Indicates that an entity emits an event.
Service
   │
   └── emits → Event


B.21.2 consumes
Indicates that an entity consumes an event.
Worker
   │
   └── consumes → Event


B.21.3 triggers
Indicates that an event or condition triggers another operation.

B.22 Runtime Relations
B.22.1 runs_on
Indicates the runtime on which a component operates.
Application
   │
   └── runs_on → Node.js


B.22.2 deployed_to
Indicates deployment of an application/component to infrastructure.

B.22.3 connects_to
Indicates communication with an external system/infrastructure component.
Application
   │
   └── connects_to → PostgreSQL


B.23 Framework Relations
B.23.1 uses_framework
Indicates that an application/module uses a framework.
Application
   │
   └── uses_framework → Next.js


B.23.2 uses_library
Indicates use of a library.

B.23.3 depends_on_runtime
Indicates runtime dependency.

B.24 Analysis Relations
B.24.1 analyzes
Indicates that an Analysis operates on a Repository/Revision.
Analysis
   │
   └── analyzes → Repository Revision


B.24.2 produces
Indicates that a process produces an output.
Analysis
   │
   └── produces → Finding


B.24.3 derived_from
Indicates that an entity/result is derived from another entity.
Knowledge Graph
      │
      └── derived_from → Architecture Model


B.25 Evidence Relations
B.25.1 supported_by
Indicates that a claim/finding is supported by evidence.
Finding
   │
   └── supported_by → Evidence


B.25.2 located_at
Indicates where evidence originates.
Evidence
   │
   └── located_at → Repository File


B.25.3 observed_in
Indicates that an entity/relationship was observed in a particular source/revision.

B.26 Knowledge Relations
B.26.1 projects_to
Indicates projection into a derived representation.
Architecture Model
      │
      └── projects_to → Knowledge Graph


B.26.2 indexed_as
Indicates that information is represented in a search index.
Architecture Entity
      │
      └── indexed_as → Search Document


B.26.3 retrieved_from
Indicates that evidence/context was retrieved from a knowledge source.

B.27 AI Relations
B.27.1 explains
Indicates that an AI-generated explanation explains a finding/entity/concept.
Explanation
   │
   └── explains → Finding


B.27.2 generated_by
Indicates which provider/model generated an AI artifact.
Explanation
   │
   └── generated_by → AI Model


B.27.3 grounded_in
Indicates that an explanation/context is grounded in retrieved evidence.
Explanation
   │
   └── grounded_in → Evidence


B.28 Diagram Relations
B.28.1 visualizes
Indicates that a Diagram represents an Architecture Model/entity/relationship.
Diagram
   │
   └── visualizes → Architecture Model


B.29 Report Relations
B.29.1 reports_on
Indicates the subject represented by a Report.
Report
   │
   └── reports_on → Analysis


B.29.2 contains_finding
Indicates that a Report includes a Finding.

B.29.3 contains_diagram
Indicates that a Report contains a Diagram.

B.30 Ownership Relations
B.30.1 owns
Indicates ownership of a resource.
Organization
   │
   └── owns → Project


B.30.2 belongs_to
Indicates resource membership.
Project
   │
   └── belongs_to → Organization

Use carefully because belongs_to is contextual and can represent containment/membership.

B.31 Product Resource Relations
Canonical product relationships include:
Organization
    │
    └── owns → Project
                  │
                  └── contains → Environment
                                   │
                                   └── contains → Repository

The exact resource hierarchy follows the product architecture.

B.32 Relation Direction
Relationships should have an intentional direction.
For example:
A depends_on B

means:

A requires/depends upon B.

Do not reverse it and assume the same meaning.

B.33 Relation Inverses
Some relations naturally have inverses:
contains ↔ belongs_to

depends_on ↔ dependency_of

extends ↔ extended_by

However, the system should not automatically persist both directions as independent canonical truth.
Where possible:

Store one canonical direction and derive the inverse during querying/projection.


B.34 Relation Strength
Not all relationships carry the same architectural significance.
Conceptually:
Weak
 │
 ├── uses
 ├── references
 │
 ▼
Medium
 │
 ├── depends_on
 ├── connects_to
 │
 ▼
Strong
 │
 ├── contains
 ├── implements
 ├── extends
 └── persists_to

The exact semantics depend on the relationship and analysis context.

B.35 Relation Evidence
Every meaningful architectural relationship should ideally be traceable to evidence.
Example:
Service A
   │
   └── depends_on → Service B
             │
             ▼
       Evidence
             │
             ▼
      source_file.py:42

This enables:

explainability;
debugging;
graph validation;
AI grounding;
architecture traceability.


B.36 Relation Confidence
Where analysis cannot establish a relationship with absolute certainty, the architecture may represent appropriate confidence/qualification metadata.
Do not convert uncertain inference into deterministic truth.

B.37 Deterministic vs Inferred Relations
Relations may originate from:
DETERMINISTIC
INFERRED
AI-ASSISTED

These categories must remain distinguishable where the system requires it.
A deterministic source-level import is fundamentally different from an AI-generated architectural inference.

B.38 Canonical Relation Naming
Relationship names should generally follow:
verb

or:
verb_phrase

Examples:
contains
imports
depends_on
calls
implements
extends
exposes
reads_from
writes_to
emits
consumes
connects_to

Avoid vague names such as:
related_to
associated_with
linked_to
connected
has
uses_something

unless the relationship genuinely cannot be made more precise.

B.39 Relation Naming Rules
Do not create:
depends
dependency
dependent
is_dependent_on

for the same concept.
Use:
depends_on

as the canonical relationship.
Similarly:
imports

should not randomly become:
imported
imports_from
has_import


B.40 Entity Naming Rules
Entity names should represent nouns.
Preferred:
Repository
Module
Class
Function
Service
Endpoint
Finding
Evidence
Analysis
Diagram
Report

Relations represent verbs.
Preferred:
contains
imports
calls
depends_on
implements
exposes

Therefore:
Entity + Relation + Entity

should read naturally:
Service depends_on Database
Controller handles Endpoint
Module imports Module
Service emits Event
Finding supported_by Evidence
Diagram visualizes Architecture Model


B.41 Canonical Architecture Relationship Examples
Module Dependency
Module A
    │
    └── depends_on → Module B

Source Import
File A
    │
    └── imports → File B

Class Inheritance
ChildClass
    │
    └── extends → ParentClass

Interface Implementation
Service
    │
    └── implements → ServiceInterface

API Exposure
Application
    │
    └── exposes → Endpoint

Database Access
Repository
    │
    ├── reads_from → Database
    └── writes_to → Database

Event Flow
Service
    │
    └── emits → Event
                    │
                    └── consumed_by → Worker

Knowledge Projection
Architecture Model
    │
    └── projects_to → Knowledge Graph

AI Grounding
Explanation
    │
    └── grounded_in → Evidence


B.42 Relationship Rules for the Knowledge Graph
The Knowledge Graph must:

Use canonical entity types.
Use canonical relationship names.
Preserve relationship direction.
Preserve relevant evidence.
Avoid fake relationships.
Avoid duplicate semantic relationships.
Distinguish deterministic information from inference where required.
Remain a derived representation.
Remain reconstructable from authoritative information where the architecture requires.
Never become an independent source of architectural truth.


B.43 Entity Identity Rule
Two entities should not be considered identical merely because they share the same name.
Identity may depend on:
Repository
Revision
Path
Language
Scope
Qualified Name
Entity Type

depending on the entity.

B.44 Qualified Identity
Where names can collide, use qualified identity.
For example:
module_a.Service
module_b.Service

must not automatically become the same entity merely because both are called:
Service


B.45 Entity Lifecycle
Entities derived from source code should be associated with the appropriate Repository Revision/Analysis context.
Historical entities should remain distinguishable when source changes alter their identity or structure.

B.46 Relation Lifecycle
Relationships may change between repository revisions.
Example:
Revision A:

Service A
   └── depends_on → Service B


Revision B:

Service A
   └── depends_on → Service C

StackSense must not silently treat the two revisions as identical architecture.

B.47 Entity/Relation Traceability
Where practical:
Entity
   ↓
Source Location
   ↓
Repository Revision
   ↓
Analysis

and:
Relation
   ↓
Evidence
   ↓
Source Location

should remain traceable.
