B.49 Minimum Required Semantics
Every entity/relation implementation must be able to answer:
What is this?
Who owns it?
Where did it come from?
What does it represent?
What does it connect to?
Why does this relationship exist?
Which repository revision produced it?
Which analysis produced it?

where applicable to the entity type.

B.50 Final Entity/Relation Principle
The Entity/Relation system exists to create a consistent machine-readable architecture vocabulary.
The fundamental model is:
                 ┌──────────────┐
                 │    Entity    │
                 └──────┬───────┘
                        │
                  Relation
                        │
                        ▼
                 ┌──────────────┐
                 │    Entity    │
                 └──────────────┘

Every meaningful relationship should be:
Explicit
Directional
Semantically precise
Evidence-backed where possible
Traceable
Consistent

And the most important rule is:

Do not invent entity types or relationship names when an existing canonical vocabulary already expresses the concept.

END OF APPENDIX B — ENTITY / RELATION VOCABULARY



APPENDIX C — ANALYSIS STATES AND STAGE STATES
C.1 Purpose
This appendix defines the canonical lifecycle states for StackSense Analysis and its internal processing stages.
The purpose is to distinguish clearly between:

the lifecycle of the overall Analysis;
the lifecycle of individual Analysis Stages;
background Job execution;
successful completion;
partial completion;
failure;
cancellation;
retryable and non-retryable failures.

These states are used consistently across:
Backend
API
Workers
Queue
Database
Observability
SSE
Frontend
Reports
Evaluation

The state model must remain explicit and deterministic.

C.2 Analysis vs Stage
The most important distinction is:
Analysis
    │
    ├── Stage 1
    ├── Stage 2
    ├── Stage 3
    ├── Stage 4
    └── ...

An Analysis represents the complete logical analysis operation.
An Analysis Stage represents one bounded processing step within that Analysis.
Therefore:
Analysis ≠ Stage

and:
Analysis State ≠ Stage State


C.3 Overall Analysis Lifecycle
The canonical high-level lifecycle is:
CREATED
   ↓
QUEUED
   ↓
RUNNING
   ↓
COMPLETED

Failure path:
RUNNING
   ↓
FAILED

Cancellation path:
QUEUED / RUNNING
        ↓
   CANCELLING
        ↓
   CANCELLED

The exact implementation may omit CREATED or CANCELLING from externally exposed API states if the API contract requires a smaller state set, but internally the lifecycle must remain logically well-defined.

C.4 Canonical Analysis States
The primary Analysis states are:
CREATED
QUEUED
RUNNING
COMPLETED
FAILED
CANCELLED

These are the canonical states.

C.5 CREATED
CREATED means:

The Analysis record has been successfully created, but processing has not yet begun.

Conceptually:
Request
   ↓
Analysis Created
   ↓
CREATED

At this point:

the Analysis has an identity;
its Repository Revision is known;
its configuration/context is established;
processing may not yet have been dispatched.


C.6 QUEUED
QUEUED means:

The Analysis has been accepted for asynchronous processing and is waiting for execution.

Analysis
   ↓
Queue
   ↓
QUEUED

The Analysis should not be considered actively processing while it remains queued.

C.7 RUNNING
RUNNING means:

The Analysis has begun active processing.

At least one Analysis Stage may be executing.
QUEUED
   ↓
Worker picks job
   ↓
RUNNING


C.8 COMPLETED
COMPLETED means:

The Analysis has successfully finished all required processing stages according to its contract.

A completed Analysis must not contain unresolved required processing stages.
Conceptually:
All Required Stages
        ↓
Successful
        ↓
COMPLETED

COMPLETED is a terminal state.

C.9 FAILED
FAILED means:

The Analysis could not successfully complete according to its contract.

Failure may result from:

unrecoverable analysis errors;
invalid input;
infrastructure failure after retry exhaustion;
unsupported repository conditions;
non-retryable stage failure;
other explicitly defined terminal errors.

FAILED is a terminal state unless the architecture explicitly supports creating a new retry/re-execution operation.
Do not silently transition:
FAILED → RUNNING

without an explicit retry/re-execution mechanism.

C.10 CANCELLED
CANCELLED means:

The Analysis was intentionally stopped before successful completion.

Cancellation may originate from:

user request;
administrative operation;
system shutdown;
policy;
dependency cancellation.

CANCELLED is terminal for that Analysis execution.

C.11 Optional CANCELLING
Where cancellation requires asynchronous cleanup, the internal state may use:
CANCELLING

meaning:

Cancellation has been requested, but active work has not yet fully stopped.

Example:
RUNNING
   ↓
Cancellation Requested
   ↓
CANCELLING
   ↓
Workers Stop
   ↓
CANCELLED

If exposed publicly, this state must be explicitly documented in the API contract.

C.12 Analysis State Machine
The conceptual state machine is:
                    ┌──────────────┐
                    │   CREATED    │
                    └──────┬───────┘
                           │
                           ▼
                    ┌──────────────┐
                    │    QUEUED    │
                    └──────┬───────┘
                           │
                           ▼
                    ┌──────────────┐
                    │    RUNNING   │
                    └───┬────┬─────┘
                        │    │
              success   │    │ failure
                        │    │
                        ▼    ▼
                ┌──────────┐ ┌──────────┐
                │COMPLETED │ │  FAILED  │
                └──────────┘ └──────────┘
                        ▲
                        │
                    terminal
                        
RUNNING / QUEUED
        │
        │ cancel
        ▼
┌──────────────┐
│ CANCELLING   │
└──────┬───────┘
       │
       ▼
┌──────────────┐
│  CANCELLED   │
└──────────────┘


C.13 Valid Analysis Transitions
The primary transitions are:



Current State
Allowed Transition




CREATED
QUEUED


QUEUED
RUNNING


QUEUED
CANCELLED / CANCELLING


RUNNING
COMPLETED


RUNNING
FAILED


RUNNING
CANCELLING


CANCELLING
CANCELLED



The implementation may define additional controlled transitions for retries/re-execution, but those must be explicit.

C.14 Invalid State Transitions
The following must not happen casually:
COMPLETED → RUNNING
COMPLETED → QUEUED
FAILED → RUNNING
CANCELLED → RUNNING
CANCELLED → COMPLETED

If another execution is required, create an explicit new execution/retry mechanism rather than corrupting historical state.

C.15 Terminal States
The canonical terminal states are:
COMPLETED
FAILED
CANCELLED

Once an Analysis reaches a terminal state, its historical execution state must remain stable.
A new attempt should be represented explicitly rather than silently rewriting history.

C.16 Analysis Stage Lifecycle
Each Analysis consists of one or more processing stages.
A canonical stage lifecycle is:
PENDING
   ↓
QUEUED
   ↓
RUNNING
   ↓
COMPLETED

Failure:
RUNNING
   ↓
FAILED

Cancellation:
PENDING / QUEUED / RUNNING
          ↓
      CANCELLED


C.17 Canonical Stage States
The primary stage states are:
PENDING
QUEUED
RUNNING
COMPLETED
FAILED
CANCELLED
SKIPPED

SKIPPED is important because a stage may intentionally not execute without the overall Analysis being invalid.

C.18 PENDING
PENDING means:

The stage is defined as part of the Analysis but is not yet ready for execution.

Possible reasons include:

prerequisite stage has not completed;
dependency is not yet available;
scheduler/worker has not prepared the stage.


C.19 QUEUED
QUEUED means:

The stage is ready for execution and has been dispatched to the processing mechanism.


C.20 RUNNING
RUNNING means:

The stage is actively executing.

A stage should only enter RUNNING when an execution worker/process has actually begun processing it.

C.21 COMPLETED
COMPLETED means:

The stage successfully produced the expected result.


C.22 FAILED
FAILED means:

The stage could not successfully complete.

A stage failure must contain sufficient diagnostic information for the system to determine:
What failed?
Why?
Was it retryable?
Which attempt failed?

where applicable.

C.23 CANCELLED
CANCELLED means:

The stage was intentionally stopped before successful completion.


C.24 SKIPPED
SKIPPED means:

The stage was intentionally not executed because its execution was unnecessary or not applicable.

Example:
Optional Stage
      ↓
Not applicable
      ↓
SKIPPED

SKIPPED must not be treated as equivalent to FAILED.

C.25 Stage State Machine
                 ┌──────────────┐
                 │    PENDING   │
                 └──────┬───────┘
                        │
                        ▼
                 ┌──────────────┐
                 │    QUEUED    │
                 └──────┬───────┘
                        │
                        ▼
                 ┌──────────────┐
                 │    RUNNING   │
                 └───┬─────┬────┘
                     │     │
                success   failure
                     │     │
                     ▼     ▼
              ┌──────────┐ ┌──────────┐
              │COMPLETED │ │  FAILED  │
              └──────────┘ └──────────┘

PENDING / QUEUED / RUNNING
          │
          ▼
      CANCELLED

PENDING / QUEUED
          │
          ▼
       SKIPPED


C.26 Analysis Stage Ordering
Stages should have explicit ordering/dependency semantics.
Conceptually:
Repository Validation
        ↓
File Discovery
        ↓
Language Detection
        ↓
Parsing
        ↓
IR Construction
        ↓
Identity Resolution
        ↓
Architecture Construction
        ↓
Knowledge Projection
        ↓
Indexing
        ↓
Report / Diagram Generation

The exact stage list is defined by the analysis engine architecture.

C.27 Stage Dependencies
A stage may depend on another stage.
Example:
Parsing
   ↓
IR Construction
   ↓
Identity Resolution

Identity Resolution must not run as though the required IR does not exist.

C.28 Stage Dependency Failure
If:
Stage A → FAILED

and:
Stage B depends on Stage A

then Stage B should generally become:
SKIPPED

or:
FAILED

according to the defined dependency semantics.
It must not falsely report COMPLETED.

C.29 Optional Stage Failure
If an optional stage fails but the core Analysis can still produce a valid result:
Core Stages → COMPLETED
Optional Stage → FAILED

the overall Analysis may still complete only if the contract explicitly defines that stage as non-critical.
The system must never silently hide this condition.

C.30 Analysis Completion Rule
An Analysis may become:
COMPLETED

only when all required stages have successfully completed.
Optional stages may be:
COMPLETED
SKIPPED

or potentially FAILED if the architecture explicitly permits degraded completion.

C.31 Partial Completion
If the system supports partial results, the distinction must remain explicit.
Example:
Analysis
    │
    ├── Parsing       → COMPLETED
    ├── IR            → COMPLETED
    ├── Graph         → FAILED
    └── Report        → SKIPPED

This must not simply be represented as:
COMPLETED

without qualification.

C.32 Partial Analysis
A Partial Analysis means:

The system successfully produced some valid analysis information, but one or more expected capabilities could not be completed.

If partial analysis is exposed as a product concept, it must have explicit semantics rather than being inferred from arbitrary stage states.

C.33 Retry States
Retries should not corrupt the lifecycle.
Prefer:
Stage Attempt 1
      ↓
FAILED
      ↓
Retry
      ↓
Stage Attempt 2
      ↓
RUNNING
      ↓
COMPLETED

rather than:
RUNNING
 ↓
FAILED
 ↓
RUNNING
 ↓
FAILED
 ↓
RUNNING

without attempt tracking.

C.34 Attempt
An Attempt represents one execution attempt of a stage/job.
An Attempt may contain:
attempt number
started_at
completed_at
worker
error
retryable

where applicable.

C.35 Retryable Failure
A failure is retryable when another execution attempt may reasonably succeed without changing the underlying input.
Examples may include:
temporary network failure
temporary provider unavailability
transient infrastructure failure


C.36 Non-Retryable Failure
A failure is non-retryable when another identical attempt is expected to fail for the same reason.
Examples:
invalid input
unsupported syntax
invalid configuration
authorization failure
permanent validation failure


C.37 Retry Policy
Every retryable stage/job must have a bounded retry policy.
Conceptually:
Attempt
   ↓
Failure
   ↓
Retryable?
 ┌───────┴───────┐
 NO              YES
 │                │
 ▼                ▼
FAILED       Retry Limit?
                │
          ┌─────┴─────┐
         YES          NO
          │            │
          ▼            ▼
       FAILED       RETRY


C.38 No Infinite Retries
The system must never create:
FAILED
 ↓
RETRY
 ↓
FAILED
 ↓
RETRY
 ↓
...

without a bounded stopping condition.

C.39 Cancellation Semantics
Cancellation is an intentional state transition.
Cancellation must not be represented merely by:
deleted = true

when the execution history needs to remain traceable.

C.40 Cancellation During Queue
If an Analysis is:
QUEUED

and cancellation is requested before execution:
QUEUED
   ↓
CANCELLED

No worker should subsequently begin normal execution.

C.41 Cancellation During Execution
If an Analysis is:
RUNNING

and cancellation is requested:
RUNNING
   ↓
CANCELLING
   ↓
Worker stops safely
   ↓
CANCELLED

The exact cancellation mechanism depends on the worker infrastructure.

C.42 Cancellation Must Be Cooperative Where Necessary
Workers should safely respond to cancellation rather than leaving:
orphaned processes
half-written artifacts
corrupt state


C.43 Progress
Progress should be based on actual stage/job state.
For example:
Stage 1 → COMPLETED
Stage 2 → RUNNING
Stage 3 → PENDING

can provide meaningful progress information.

C.44 Do Not Fake Progress
Do not generate arbitrary progress values such as:
10%
20%
30%
40%
...

unless they correspond to actual measurable progress.

C.45 Stage Progress vs Analysis Progress
These are different concepts.
Stage Progress
    = progress inside one stage

Analysis Progress
    = progress across the complete Analysis

Do not expose one as the other.

C.46 SSE State Updates
Where SSE is used, the frontend may receive events such as:
analysis.created
analysis.queued
analysis.started
stage.started
stage.completed
stage.failed
analysis.completed
analysis.failed
analysis.cancelled

The exact event names belong to the API/event contract.
The important requirement is that event semantics remain consistent with the canonical state model.

C.47 State Events Must Reflect Actual State
Do not emit:
analysis.completed

before the Analysis is actually in COMPLETED.
State events must represent real state transitions.

C.48 API State Representation
The API should expose canonical states consistently.
For example:
{
  "status": "RUNNING"
}

The frontend must not invent a separate vocabulary such as:
"in-progress"
"working"
"processing-now"

for the same backend state unless the UI translation is intentional and documented.

C.49 Frontend State Mapping
The frontend may translate backend state into presentation language.
Example:
Backend:
RUNNING

Frontend:
"Analysis in progress"

But the underlying canonical state remains:
RUNNING


C.50 Terminal State Rules
Terminal states must not silently mutate.
COMPLETED
FAILED
CANCELLED

represent historical outcomes.
If another analysis is required, create a new execution/retry representation according to the architecture.

C.51 State Persistence
Important state transitions must be persisted reliably enough to survive:
worker restart
application restart
process crash
temporary infrastructure failure

where required by the reliability contract.

C.52 State and Observability
State transitions should be observable.
For example:
Analysis ID
Stage
Previous State
New State
Timestamp
Worker/Execution Context
Failure Information

where appropriate.

C.53 State and Auditability
Important user-triggered lifecycle changes such as cancellation should remain auditable where required by the security/audit architecture.

C.54 State Consistency
There must not be contradictions such as:
Analysis = COMPLETED

Stage A = RUNNING

for a required stage.
Similarly:
Analysis = FAILED

All required stages = COMPLETED

would require an explicit explanation, such as a post-processing failure.

C.55 State Ownership
The backend is authoritative for Analysis and Stage state.
The frontend must not directly mutate canonical lifecycle state.

C.56 Worker Ownership
Workers may request/perform state transitions through the approved application boundary.
They must not arbitrarily rewrite lifecycle state outside the defined transition rules.

C.57 Database Representation
The persistence model should represent state explicitly.
Conceptually:
Analysis
 ├── id
 ├── status
 ├── repository_revision
 ├── created_at
 ├── started_at
 ├── completed_at
 └── failure information

AnalysisStage
 ├── id
 ├── analysis_id
 ├── stage_type
 ├── status
 ├── started_at
 ├── completed_at
 └── failure information

The exact schema is defined by the implementation.

C.58 Stage Type vs Stage State
Do not confuse:
Stage Type

with:
Stage State

Example:
Stage Type:
PARSING

Stage State:
RUNNING


C.59 Example Stage Types
The following represent conceptual stage types:
REPOSITORY_VALIDATION
FILE_DISCOVERY
LANGUAGE_DETECTION
PARSING
IR_CONSTRUCTION
IDENTITY_RESOLUTION
ARCHITECTURE_CONSTRUCTION
GRAPH_PROJECTION
INDEXING
REPORT_GENERATION
DIAGRAM_GENERATION

The final implementation may split/merge stages according to the approved analysis architecture.

C.60 Stage Type Stability
Stage types should have stable semantics.
Do not reuse:
PARSING

for one purpose in one version and a completely different purpose later.
A material semantic change requires appropriate versioning/change control.

C.61 Stage Output
Each stage should have a clearly defined output contract.
Conceptually:
Input
 ↓
Stage
 ↓
Output

A stage should not silently mutate unrelated system state without a defined responsibility.

C.62 Stage Failure Metadata
A failed stage should retain enough information to diagnose the problem.
Conceptually:
Stage
 ├── status = FAILED
 ├── error_code
 ├── message
 ├── retryable
 ├── attempt
 └── timestamp

Sensitive internal details must not automatically be exposed through public APIs.

C.63 Error Classification
Failures should be classified where useful.
Example:
VALIDATION_ERROR
PARSING_ERROR
UNSUPPORTED_INPUT
INFRASTRUCTURE_ERROR
TIMEOUT
PROVIDER_ERROR
AUTHORIZATION_ERROR
INTERNAL_ERROR

The exact taxonomy should be defined by the implementation/API contract.

C.64 Stage Independence
Stages should be independently observable where practical.
This allows the system to determine:
Which stage failed?
Which stage completed?
Which stage was skipped?
Which stage is currently running?


C.65 Stage Idempotency
Stages that may be retried should be designed so that repeated execution does not corrupt canonical state.
Where a stage is not naturally idempotent, the implementation must use:
deduplication
transaction boundaries
attempt identifiers
idempotency keys

or another appropriate mechanism.

C.66 Stage Ordering vs Parallelism
Not every stage must necessarily execute sequentially.
If dependencies permit:
Stage A ───────► Stage C
      \
       └───────► Stage D

A and another independent stage may execute in parallel.
However:

Parallelism must never violate stage dependencies or determinism requirements.


C.67 Deterministic Stage Ordering
Where ordering affects deterministic output, the execution order must be controlled.
Do not introduce uncontrolled concurrency that changes architecture results.

C.68 Analysis Completion With Parallel Stages
An Analysis can complete only when:
All Required Stages
       ↓
Terminal Successful State

regardless of whether they ran sequentially or concurrently.

C.69 Stage Skip Semantics
A stage may be skipped when:

it is not applicable;
its feature is disabled;
its prerequisite makes it unnecessary;
the architecture explicitly defines it as optional.

Skipped must be distinguishable from failed.

C.70 Analysis-Level Skip Semantics
An entire Analysis should generally not be considered SKIPPED.
If an analysis was intentionally not executed, the system should use an explicit lifecycle state such as:
CANCELLED

or another approved product-level state.
SKIPPED is primarily a stage-level concept.

C.71 Analysis State and Job State
An Analysis Job may have its own execution state.
Do not automatically equate:
Job State

with:
Analysis State

For example:
Analysis = RUNNING

Job Attempt = RETRYING

can be valid.

C.72 Worker Failure
If a worker crashes while processing:
Analysis Stage

the system must recover according to the job/retry architecture.
It must not leave the Analysis permanently stuck in:
RUNNING

without detection/recovery.

C.73 Stuck Analysis
The system should be able to identify potentially stuck work using mechanisms such as:
heartbeat
timeout
lease
worker state
job visibility

as defined by the infrastructure architecture.

C.74 Recovery From Worker Failure
Conceptually:
RUNNING
   ↓
Worker Failure
   ↓
Failure Detection
   ↓
Retryable?
 ┌──────┴──────┐
 YES           NO
 │              │
 ▼              ▼
Retry         FAILED


C.75 No Orphaned Processing
The system should avoid situations where:
Database says RUNNING
        +
No worker exists
        +
No recovery mechanism

for an indefinite period.

C.76 State History
For important lifecycle operations, retaining state-transition history may be useful for:

debugging;
auditability;
observability;
evaluation;
user experience.

The exact retention strategy is defined by the persistence/audit architecture.

C.77 State History vs Current State
Do not confuse:
Current State

with:
State History

Current state answers:

"Where is the Analysis now?"

History answers:

"How did it get here?"


C.78 State Transition Event
A state transition can conceptually be represented as:
Previous State
      ↓
Transition
      ↓
New State

Example:
QUEUED
  ↓
worker_started
  ↓
RUNNING


C.79 Invalid Transition Handling
If an invalid state transition is requested:
Do not silently accept it.

The system should reject it or handle it through an explicitly defined recovery mechanism.

C.80 State Concurrency
Multiple workers must not be able to corrupt lifecycle state through race conditions.
State transitions should use appropriate concurrency controls such as:
atomic updates
optimistic locking
leases
transaction boundaries

where required.

C.81 State and Frontend UX
The frontend should map lifecycle states into clear user-facing experiences.
Example:
QUEUED
→ "Waiting to start"

RUNNING
→ "Analysis in progress"

COMPLETED
→ "Analysis completed"

FAILED
→ "Analysis failed"

CANCELLED
→ "Analysis cancelled"

These labels are UX representations, not replacement canonical states.

C.82 State and Notifications
Notifications should be triggered from meaningful lifecycle events rather than arbitrary polling.
Examples:
analysis.completed
analysis.failed
analysis.cancelled

where notifications are required.

C.83 State and Reports
Reports should only be generated when their required source stages have successfully completed.
For example:
Architecture Construction
        ↓
COMPLETED
        ↓
Report Generation


C.84 State and Diagrams
Similarly:
Architecture Model
        ↓
Ready
        ↓
Diagram Generation

A diagram must not claim to represent architecture that has not been successfully constructed.

C.85 State and Knowledge Projection
Graph projection should operate on valid architecture information.
Architecture Construction
        ↓
COMPLETED
        ↓
Graph Projection

If graph projection fails:
Architecture Model
    = valid

Graph
    = unavailable/degraded

The canonical architecture must remain valid.

C.86 State and Search Indexing
Indexing is a derived stage.
If indexing fails:
Canonical Architecture
      = valid

Search Index
      = stale/unavailable

The system must not mark the architecture itself as failed merely because a derived index failed, unless the product contract defines indexing as required for successful completion.

C.87 State and AI
AI generation should be downstream from valid evidence/context.
An AI failure should generally not invalidate the deterministic Analysis.
Example:
Analysis
  → COMPLETED

AI Explanation
  → FAILED

if explanation generation is an optional downstream capability.

C.88 State Semantics Must Be Consistent
The same state must mean the same thing everywhere.
For example:
RUNNING

must not mean:
"queued on another worker"

in one subsystem and:
"actively executing"

in another.

C.89 State Naming
Use uppercase canonical state identifiers internally/API-side where the contract specifies enum semantics:
CREATED
QUEUED
RUNNING
COMPLETED
FAILED
CANCELLED

Frontend display text may use human-readable language.

C.90 State Extensibility
New states must not be introduced casually.
Before adding a state:
Identify why existing states are insufficient
        ↓
Define exact semantics
        ↓
Define valid transitions
        ↓
Update contracts
        ↓
Update frontend
        ↓
Update tests
        ↓
Document


C.91 No Semantic Overloading
Do not use one state to represent multiple unrelated meanings.
For example:
FAILED

must not simultaneously mean:
temporary retry
permanent failure
cancelled
unsupported
skipped

Those are distinct conditions.

C.92 Final Analysis State Vocabulary
CREATED
    Analysis exists.

QUEUED
    Analysis is waiting for execution.

RUNNING
    Analysis is actively executing.

COMPLETED
    Required processing successfully completed.

FAILED
    Analysis could not successfully complete.

CANCELLED
    Analysis was intentionally stopped.


C.93 Final Stage State Vocabulary
PENDING
    Stage exists but is not ready to execute.

QUEUED
    Stage is ready and waiting for execution.

RUNNING
    Stage is actively executing.

COMPLETED
    Stage successfully completed.

FAILED
    Stage could not successfully complete.

CANCELLED
    Stage was intentionally stopped.

SKIPPED
    Stage was intentionally not executed.


C.94 Final State Model
The complete conceptual model is:
                         ANALYSIS
                            │
                            ▼
                    ┌──────────────┐
                    │    CREATED   │
                    └──────┬───────┘
                           │
                           ▼
                    ┌──────────────┐
                    │    QUEUED    │
                    └──────┬───────┘
                           │
                           ▼
                    ┌──────────────┐
                    │    RUNNING   │
                    └──────┬───────┘
                           │
               ┌───────────┼───────────┐
               │           │           │
               ▼           ▼           ▼
          COMPLETED      FAILED     CANCELLED
               │
               │
               ▼
        Analysis Complete


       INSIDE RUNNING ANALYSIS

             Analysis
                 │
       ┌─────────┼─────────┐
       ▼         ▼         ▼
     Stage A   Stage B   Stage C
       │         │         │
       ▼         ▼         ▼
   PENDING → QUEUED → RUNNING
                         │
                  ┌──────┼──────┐
                  ▼      ▼      ▼
             COMPLETED FAILED CANCELLED

Additional:
PENDING / QUEUED → SKIPPED


C.95 Final State Rules
The following rules are mandatory:
1. Analysis state and Stage state are separate concepts.

2. States must have explicit semantics.

3. State transitions must be controlled.

4. Terminal states must remain historically stable.

5. Retries must not corrupt execution history.

6. Retryable and non-retryable failures must be distinguishable where required.

7. Infinite retries are prohibited.

8. Cancellation must be explicit.

9. SKIPPED is not equivalent to FAILED.

10. COMPLETED requires all required stages to succeed.

11. Optional-stage failures may only permit degraded completion if explicitly defined.

12. Frontend state is derived from backend state.

13. Frontend must not become the source of lifecycle truth.

14. SSE events must reflect real state transitions.

15. Progress must reflect actual processing.

16. Fake progress is prohibited.

17. Worker failure must not leave permanent orphaned RUNNING jobs.

18. State transitions must be concurrency-safe.

19. State history should remain available where required for auditability/debugging.

20. New states require explicit architectural/contract consideration.

21. The same state must have the same meaning throughout the system.

22. State names must not be overloaded with multiple meanings.

23. Analysis execution must remain traceable to its Repository Revision.

24. Stage results must remain traceable to their Analysis.

25. Derived-stage failures must not unnecessarily invalidate canonical analysis data.

26. AI failures must not unnecessarily invalidate deterministic analysis.

27. Graph/search/index failures must respect the distinction between canonical and derived state.

28. If required information about an existing state implementation is unavailable, inspect the relevant file or ask for it rather than guessing.


C.96 Final Principle

A state is a contract, not a label.

Every state must define:
What does it mean?
When can it be entered?
When can it be exited?
What work is allowed?
What work is prohibited?
Is it terminal?
Can it be retried?
What happens if the process crashes?
How is it exposed to the API?
How is it represented in the frontend?

If these questions cannot be answered, the state is not sufficiently defined.

StackSense must always represent the actual lifecycle of its work, not an approximation invented for the UI.

END OF APPENDIX C — ANALYSIS STATES AND STAGE STATES



APPENDIX D — EVENT VOCABULARY
D.1 Purpose
This appendix defines the canonical event vocabulary used throughout StackSense.
Events represent meaningful occurrences or state transitions within the system. They provide a consistent communication language between:
API
Backend Modules
Analysis Engine
Queue
Workers
Knowledge Platform
AI Platform
Notification System
Frontend
Observability

The event vocabulary exists to ensure that components communicate through explicit, well-defined events rather than undocumented assumptions or direct coupling.
Events must have clear semantics, ownership, producers, consumers, and lifecycle behavior.

D.2 Event Philosophy
An event represents:

Something that happened.

For example:
analysis.started

means:

An Analysis has actually started execution.

It does not mean:
Analysis was requested
Analysis was queued
Analysis might start

Those are different events/states.
Therefore:
Command ≠ Event ≠ State


D.3 Command vs Event vs State
Command
A command represents:

Something that should happen.

Example:
start_analysis

Event
An event represents:

Something that happened.

Example:
analysis.started

State
A state represents:

The current condition of something.

Example:
RUNNING

Conceptually:
Command
   ↓
Action
   ↓
State Change
   ↓
Event


D.4 Event Naming Convention
Canonical event names use:
<aggregate>.<past-tense-event>

Examples:
analysis.created
analysis.queued
analysis.started
analysis.completed
analysis.failed
analysis.cancelled

For stage events:
analysis.stage.started
analysis.stage.completed
analysis.stage.failed

The naming convention should remain consistent across the system.

D.5 Event Names Describe Facts
Events should describe facts rather than intentions.
Preferred:
analysis.completed

Not:
complete.analysis
complete_analysis
analysis.should_complete
analysis.complete_request

Similarly:
repository.ingested

means the ingestion actually occurred.

D.6 Canonical Event Categories
StackSense events are grouped into:
Repository Events
Analysis Events
Stage Events
Job Events
Architecture Events
Knowledge Events
Retrieval Events
AI Events
Diagram Events
Report Events
Product Events
Security Events
System Events

Not every event must be implemented immediately.
The vocabulary defines the canonical terminology available to the architecture.

D.7 Repository Events
D.7.1 repository.created
Indicates that a Repository resource has been created in StackSense.
repository.created


D.7.2 repository.updated
Indicates that Repository metadata/configuration has been updated.

D.7.3 repository.deleted
Indicates that a Repository has been deleted.
Deletion semantics must follow the storage/security architecture.

D.7.4 repository.ingestion.started
Indicates that repository ingestion has actually started.

D.7.5 repository.ingested
Indicates that repository ingestion successfully completed.
repository.ingested


D.7.6 repository.ingestion.failed
Indicates that repository ingestion failed.

D.7.7 repository.revision.detected
Indicates that a new or selected Repository Revision has been identified.

D.8 Analysis Events
The core Analysis events are:
analysis.created
analysis.queued
analysis.started
analysis.completed
analysis.failed
analysis.cancelled

These correspond closely to the Analysis lifecycle defined in Appendix C.

D.9 analysis.created
Indicates:

An Analysis record has been created.

This does not mean execution has started.
analysis.created


D.10 analysis.queued
Indicates:

The Analysis has been accepted for asynchronous execution and placed into the processing pipeline.


D.11 analysis.started
Indicates:

The Analysis has actually begun execution.

This should correspond to the Analysis transitioning into:
RUNNING


D.12 analysis.completed
Indicates:

The Analysis has successfully completed according to its contract.

This should correspond to:
COMPLETED


D.13 analysis.failed
Indicates:

The Analysis has reached a terminal failed state.

This should correspond to:
FAILED


D.14 analysis.cancelled
Indicates:

The Analysis has been intentionally cancelled.

This should correspond to:
CANCELLED


D.15 Analysis Cancellation Event
Where cancellation requires an intermediate asynchronous state, the architecture may also use:
analysis.cancellation.requested

This means:

Cancellation has been requested.

It does not mean the Analysis has already stopped.
The terminal event remains:
analysis.cancelled


D.16 Analysis Retry Events
Where retry behavior is exposed through events:
analysis.retry.requested
analysis.retry.started
analysis.retry.exhausted

These should only be used when retry is an explicit part of the lifecycle.
A retry must not silently rewrite an existing execution history.

D.17 Stage Events
Analysis stages use:
analysis.stage.created
analysis.stage.queued
analysis.stage.started
analysis.stage.completed
analysis.stage.failed
analysis.stage.cancelled
analysis.stage.skipped

These events describe individual stages rather than the entire Analysis.

D.18 analysis.stage.created
Indicates that a Stage record has been established for an Analysis.

D.19 analysis.stage.queued
Indicates that a Stage is ready and waiting for execution.

D.20 analysis.stage.started
Indicates that a Stage has actually started execution.

D.21 analysis.stage.completed
Indicates that a Stage successfully completed.

D.22 analysis.stage.failed
Indicates that a Stage failed.
The event should carry enough information to identify:
Analysis
Stage
Attempt
Failure classification
Retryability

where appropriate.

D.23 analysis.stage.cancelled
Indicates that a Stage was intentionally stopped.

D.24 analysis.stage.skipped
Indicates that a Stage was intentionally not executed.
This is distinct from:
analysis.stage.failed


D.25 Job Events
Background processing may produce:
job.created
job.queued
job.started
job.completed
job.failed
job.retrying
job.cancelled

These events describe execution infrastructure, not necessarily the business-level Analysis lifecycle.

D.26 Job vs Analysis Events
Do not automatically substitute:
job.started

for:
analysis.started

A Job is an execution mechanism.
An Analysis is a product/domain operation.
For example:
analysis.queued
      ↓
job.created
      ↓
job.queued
      ↓
job.started
      ↓
analysis.started

The exact sequence depends on the implementation, but the semantic distinction remains.

D.27 Job Retry Event
job.retrying means:

The current Job execution failed or became unavailable and another execution attempt is being initiated.

It does not necessarily mean the overall Analysis has failed.

D.28 Job Completion
job.completed

means:

The execution unit completed.

It does not automatically mean:
analysis.completed

The Analysis lifecycle remains authoritative for Analysis status.

D.29 Architecture Events
Architecture-related events may include:
architecture.model.created
architecture.model.updated
architecture.entity.detected
architecture.relationship.detected
architecture.model.completed

These events should only be emitted when the relevant architecture operation actually occurs.

D.30 architecture.entity.detected
Indicates that the deterministic analysis process identified an architecture/source entity.
Examples:
Class
Module
Function
Endpoint
Service


D.31 architecture.relationship.detected
Indicates that a relationship between architecture entities has been identified.
Example:
Service A
   │
   └── depends_on → Service B


D.32 architecture.model.created
Indicates that an Architecture Model has been successfully established.

D.33 architecture.model.updated
Indicates that the Architecture Model has been changed/rebuilt according to the appropriate revision/version semantics.

D.34 architecture.model.completed
Indicates that the Architecture Model construction stage has successfully completed.

D.35 Knowledge Events
Knowledge-related events include:
knowledge.graph.projection.started
knowledge.graph.projection.completed
knowledge.graph.projection.failed
knowledge.indexing.started
knowledge.indexing.completed
knowledge.indexing.failed


D.36 Graph Projection Events
knowledge.graph.projection.started
Graph projection has started.
knowledge.graph.projection.completed
The Knowledge Graph projection has completed successfully.
knowledge.graph.projection.failed
Graph projection failed.
A graph-projection failure must not automatically invalidate the canonical Architecture Model.

D.37 Indexing Events
knowledge.indexing.started
Indexing has started.
knowledge.indexing.completed
Required indexing has successfully completed.
knowledge.indexing.failed
Indexing failed.
The system must preserve the distinction between:
Canonical Architecture

and:
Derived Search Index


D.38 Retrieval Events
Retrieval is primarily request-oriented and does not necessarily require persistent domain events for every operation.
Where observability/events are required, canonical events may include:
retrieval.started
retrieval.completed
retrieval.failed


D.39 retrieval.started
Indicates that retrieval processing has begun.

D.40 retrieval.completed
Indicates that relevant evidence/context has been successfully selected.

D.41 retrieval.failed
Indicates that retrieval could not complete according to its contract.

D.42 AI Events
AI-related events may include:
ai.request.started
ai.request.completed
ai.request.failed
ai.request.retrying
ai.explanation.generated

These should be used primarily for observability and lifecycle tracking where appropriate.

D.43 ai.request.started
Indicates that an AI provider request has actually been initiated.

D.44 ai.request.completed
Indicates that an AI provider request successfully returned a usable result.

D.45 ai.request.failed
Indicates that an AI request failed.
Failure may be caused by:
provider unavailable
timeout
rate limit
invalid request
authentication failure
model failure

where applicable.

D.46 ai.request.retrying
Indicates that another AI request attempt is being initiated after a retryable failure.

D.47 ai.explanation.generated
Indicates that an AI-generated Explanation has successfully been produced.
This does not make the Explanation canonical architecture truth.

D.48 AI Failure Rule
AI events must not be interpreted as Analysis events.
For example:
ai.request.failed

must not automatically become:
analysis.failed

unless AI generation is explicitly defined as a required stage for that Analysis.

D.49 Diagram Events
Diagram-related events include:
diagram.generation.started
diagram.generated
diagram.generation.failed


D.50 diagram.generation.started
Indicates that diagram generation has begun.

D.51 diagram.generated
Indicates that a Diagram artifact has successfully been generated.

D.52 diagram.generation.failed
Indicates that Diagram generation failed.
A diagram failure must not modify the underlying Architecture Model.

D.53 Report Events
Report-related events include:
report.generation.started
report.generated
report.generation.failed


D.54 report.generation.started
Indicates that Report generation has begun.

D.55 report.generated
Indicates that a Report has successfully been generated.

D.56 report.generation.failed
Indicates that Report generation failed.
The failure should not invalidate the underlying Analysis unless the Report is explicitly a required Analysis stage.

D.57 Product Events
Product-level resource events follow the general pattern:
<resource>.created
<resource>.updated
<resource>.deleted

Examples:
organization.created
project.created
environment.created
repository.created

These events represent actual completed mutations.

D.58 Security Events
Security-sensitive events may include:
auth.login.succeeded
auth.login.failed
auth.logout
authorization.denied
secret.accessed
api_key.created
api_key.revoked

The exact security event set should be kept intentionally controlled.
Sensitive information must never be included in event payloads unnecessarily.

D.59 Audit Events
Security/audit events must capture meaningful administrative or security-sensitive actions.
Examples:
project.created
project.deleted
user.role.changed
api_key.created
api_key.revoked
repository.deleted
analysis.cancelled

The exact audit requirements are defined by the security architecture.

D.60 System Events
System-level events may include:
system.started
system.shutdown
worker.started
worker.stopped
worker.heartbeat.missed
dependency.unavailable

These are primarily operational events.

D.61 Event Payload
Every event should have a predictable envelope.
Conceptually:
{
  "event_id": "unique-event-id",
  "event_type": "analysis.completed",
  "occurred_at": "timestamp",
  "aggregate_type": "analysis",
  "aggregate_id": "analysis-id",
  "tenant_id": "tenant-id",
  "project_id": "project-id",
  "payload": {}
}

The exact schema is determined by the event/API contract.

D.62 Event ID
Every externally meaningful event should have a unique identifier where the event architecture requires it.
This supports:
deduplication
tracing
debugging
auditability


D.63 Event Timestamp
Events should record when the event actually occurred.
Do not use:
received_at

as a replacement for:
occurred_at

when the distinction matters.

D.64 Aggregate
The Aggregate identifies the domain object to which the event belongs.
Example:
event_type:
analysis.completed

aggregate_type:
analysis

aggregate_id:
abc123


D.65 Tenant Context
Tenant-scoped events should carry sufficient tenant context to enforce isolation and support observability.
Never use tenant metadata as a substitute for authorization checks.

D.66 Correlation ID
Events involved in the same logical operation should be correlatable.
Example:
correlation_id

may connect:
API Request
   ↓
Analysis
   ↓
Job
   ↓
Stages
   ↓
Report


D.67 Causation ID
Where the architecture supports it, events may identify the event/command that caused them.
Example:
causation_id

This is particularly useful for asynchronous workflows.

D.68 Event Version
Event schemas should be versionable where events are persisted, externally consumed, or otherwise contractually stable.
Conceptually:
event_type:
analysis.completed

event_version:
1


D.69 Event Immutability
Once an event has been published as a fact:

Its meaning must not be silently changed.

If the event schema or semantics materially change, version it or follow the project's change-control/versioning process.

D.70 Event Ordering
Do not assume global ordering across the entire system.
Ordering should only be relied upon where the architecture explicitly guarantees it.
For example:
analysis.started

should logically precede:
analysis.completed

for the same Analysis.
But events from unrelated Analyses may arrive in any order.

D.71 Event Delivery
Event delivery may be:
at-most-once
at-least-once
exactly-once

depending on the infrastructure.
The implementation must not assume stronger delivery guarantees than the underlying system actually provides.

D.72 Duplicate Events
Consumers should be designed to tolerate duplicate events where at-least-once delivery is used.
Use:
event_id
idempotency
deduplication

where appropriate.

D.73 Event Consumer Rule
Consumers must not assume that every event arrives exactly once or in perfect order unless explicitly guaranteed.
A consumer should validate current state where necessary.

D.74 Event Producer Rule
A producer must emit an event only after the corresponding fact actually occurs.
For example:
analysis.completed

must not be emitted merely because:
worker.completed

occurred.
The Analysis must actually satisfy its completion contract.

D.75 Event vs Database State
Events and current database state serve different purposes.
Database State
    ↓
What is true now?

Event
    ↓
What happened?

Neither should be casually substituted for the other.

D.76 Event vs SSE
SSE is a delivery mechanism.
An Event is a semantic fact.
Therefore:
Event
  ↓
SSE
  ↓
Frontend

is valid.
But:
SSE = Event

is conceptually incorrect.

D.77 Event vs Queue Message
A Queue Message is a transport/execution mechanism.
An Event represents a fact.
For example:
Command:
analyze_repository

Queue Message:
execute_analysis_job

Event:
analysis.started

These have different semantics.

D.78 Commands
Commands may use imperative naming:
create_analysis
start_analysis
cancel_analysis
retry_analysis
generate_report

Events use factual/past-tense naming:
analysis.created
analysis.started
analysis.cancelled
analysis.retry.started
report.generated


D.79 Event-Driven Architecture Rule
Use events where they provide meaningful decoupling.
Do not turn every method call into an event.
For example, this is unnecessary:
ServiceA
   ↓ event
ServiceB

if ServiceB is simply a required synchronous dependency and no meaningful asynchronous/event semantics exist.

D.80 Event Granularity
Events should represent meaningful domain/system facts.
Too coarse:
system.changed

Too fine:
variable.read
object.created
line.processed

unless there is a genuine requirement for those events.

D.81 Analysis Event Flow
A typical Analysis event flow is:
analysis.created
       ↓
analysis.queued
       ↓
analysis.started
       ↓
analysis.stage.started
       ↓
analysis.stage.completed
       ↓
...
       ↓
analysis.completed

Failure:
analysis.stage.failed
       ↓
analysis.failed

Cancellation:
analysis.cancellation.requested
       ↓
analysis.cancelled


D.82 Complete Example
repository.ingested
        ↓
analysis.created
        ↓
analysis.queued
        ↓
analysis.started
        ↓
analysis.stage.started
        ↓
analysis.stage.completed
        ↓
analysis.stage.started
        ↓
analysis.stage.completed
        ↓
architecture.model.completed
        ↓
knowledge.graph.projection.completed
        ↓
knowledge.indexing.completed
        ↓
analysis.completed

Optional downstream operations:
analysis.completed
       │
       ├──► diagram.generation.started
       │          ↓
       │     diagram.generated
       │
       └──► report.generation.started
                  ↓
             report.generated


D.83 Failed Example
analysis.started
      ↓
analysis.stage.started
      ↓
analysis.stage.failed
      ↓
Retryable?
   ┌────┴────┐
  YES       NO
   │          │
   ▼          ▼
retrying   analysis.failed
   │
   ▼
analysis.stage.started
   │
   ▼
analysis.stage.completed

The exact retry event sequence depends on the queue/job contract.

D.84 AI Event Flow
A typical AI explanation flow:
retrieval.started
      ↓
retrieval.completed
      ↓
ai.request.started
      ↓
ai.request.completed
      ↓
ai.explanation.generated

Failure:
ai.request.started
      ↓
ai.request.failed
      ↓
ai.request.retrying

or, after retry exhaustion:
ai.request.failed

The deterministic Analysis remains unaffected unless AI is explicitly required.

D.85 Event Security
Event payloads must follow the same security principles as APIs and logs.
Never publish unnecessary:
Passwords
API Keys
Tokens
Private Keys
Database Credentials
Full Secrets
Sensitive Repository Contents


D.86 Event Tenant Isolation
Consumers must enforce tenant boundaries.
Receiving:
tenant_id = A

does not automatically authorize a consumer to access all resources associated with Tenant A.
Authorization remains authoritative.

D.87 Event Observability
Events should be integrated with tracing/observability where useful.
A lifecycle can therefore be reconstructed:
Request
 ↓
Analysis
 ↓
Job
 ↓
Stage
 ↓
Graph
 ↓
AI
 ↓
Report

using correlation/trace information.

D.88 Event Failure Handling
A consumer failure must not automatically cause the producer's domain operation to fail unless that dependency is explicitly required.
Example:
analysis.completed
        ↓
Notification consumer fails

should not normally turn:
Analysis = FAILED

The Analysis already completed.

D.89 Event Consumer Independence
Consumers should be independently deployable/recoverable where the architecture requires it.
A failed notification consumer should not necessarily prevent:
graph projection
report generation
frontend updates

unless explicitly coupled.

D.90 Event Replay
If event persistence supports replay, consumers must be designed to process historical events safely.
Replay must not:
duplicate reports
duplicate entities
corrupt current state
re-trigger dangerous side effects

without appropriate idempotency controls.

D.91 Event Retention
Not every event must be retained forever.
Retention depends on:
audit requirements
debugging requirements
operational value
storage cost
compliance requirements

The retention policy belongs to the infrastructure/security architecture.

D.92 Event Schema Evolution
When an event changes:
Check consumers
Check frontend
Check workers
Check integrations
Check persisted events

before changing the contract.
Breaking event changes require versioning/change control.

D.93 Event Naming Anti-Patterns
Do not create event names such as:
something_happened
data_changed
process_done
analysis_event
job_event
update
notification

when a precise event name exists.
Prefer:
analysis.completed
job.completed
repository.updated
report.generated


D.94 Canonical Event Index
Repository
repository.created
repository.updated
repository.deleted
repository.ingestion.started
repository.ingested
repository.ingestion.failed
repository.revision.detected

Analysis
analysis.created
analysis.queued
analysis.started
analysis.completed
analysis.failed
analysis.cancellation.requested
analysis.cancelled
analysis.retry.requested
analysis.retry.started
analysis.retry.exhausted

Analysis Stage
analysis.stage.created
analysis.stage.queued
analysis.stage.started
analysis.stage.completed
analysis.stage.failed
analysis.stage.cancelled
analysis.stage.skipped

Job
job.created
job.queued
job.started
job.completed
job.failed
job.retrying
job.cancelled

Architecture
architecture.entity.detected
architecture.relationship.detected
architecture.model.created
architecture.model.updated
architecture.model.completed

Knowledge
knowledge.graph.projection.started

D.95 Event Naming Matrix



Category

Example
