I.122 Final Error Rules
The following rules are mandatory:
1. Not every error is an Analysis failure.

2. Errors must be classified by semantic category.

3. Failure scope must be identifiable.

4. Severity must be distinguishable from lifecycle state.

5. Retryability must be explicit.

6. Retries must be bounded.

7. Retryable operations must consider idempotency.

8. Transient failures should use controlled backoff.

9. Non-retryable failures must not be retried indefinitely.

10. A single artifact failure should not normally terminate an Analysis.

11. Critical-stage failures may terminate an Analysis.

12. Findings are successful analysis outputs, not errors.

13. Cancellation is not inherently a failure.

14. AI failure must not invalidate deterministic analysis unless AI is explicitly required.

15. Diagram failure must not destroy the Architecture Model.

16. Report failure must not destroy successful Analysis results.

17. Knowledge Graph failure must not automatically invalidate canonical Analysis data.

18. Error codes must be machine-readable and stable.

19. Human-readable messages must not be used as programmatic contracts.

20. Public errors must not expose internal implementation details.

21. Stack traces must remain internal.

22. Secrets must never appear in error responses or logs.

23. Failure context must support correlation and debugging.

24. Root causes should remain distinguishable from downstream symptoms.

25. Failure ownership must follow subsystem boundaries.

26. Optional dependency failures should degrade gracefully where possible.

27. Required dependency failures must propagate appropriately.

28. Unsupported capabilities must not be misclassified as operational failures.

29. Partial failures must be visible to users when they affect result completeness.

30. Analysis coverage must remain transparent.

31. Error handling must be deterministic where possible.

32. AI must not determine canonical system failure states.

33. Security failures require heightened handling.

34. Integrity failures require heightened handling.

35. Error volume must be bounded to prevent diagnostic flooding.

36. Failure behavior must be tested.

37. Critical infrastructure failures should support controlled failure-injection testing.

38. Every caught exception must have an intentional handling reason.

39. Silent exception swallowing is prohibited.

40. If the correct failure classification cannot be determined from the available implementation/contracts, inspect or request the relevant file rather than guessing.


I.123 Final Principle

A reliable system is not one that never fails; it is one that understands what failed, limits the blast radius, recovers when possible, and communicates the failure honestly.

The StackSense failure model therefore follows:
Failure occurs
      ↓
Classify
      ↓
Determine scope
      ↓
Determine severity
      ↓
Determine retryability
      ↓
Determine impact
      ↓
Recover / degrade / terminate
      ↓
Record
      ↓
Expose appropriate information

The fundamental rule is:

Fail precisely, recover deliberately, degrade gracefully, and never hide a failure that affects the correctness of the result.

END OF APPENDIX I — ERROR / FAILURE CLASSIFICATION



APPENDIX J — AI CODING AGENT CHECKLIST
J.1 Purpose
This appendix defines the mandatory checklist and operating rules for any AI coding agent working on StackSense.
AI coding agents may be used to accelerate:
code generation
refactoring
debugging
testing
documentation
configuration
repository exploration
implementation
review

However, the AI agent is an implementation assistant, not the architectural authority.
The architecture, contracts, frozen decisions, source code, tests, and explicit human approvals remain authoritative.

J.2 Core Principle

AI may accelerate implementation; it must not silently redefine architecture.

The agent must understand the difference between:
Architecture Decision
        ↓
Implementation

and:
AI Suggestion
        ↓
Human Approval
        ↓
Implementation

The second path is required whenever the requested change affects an architectural contract.

J.3 Before Writing Code
Before modifying the repository, the AI coding agent should determine:
[ ] What feature/task is being requested?
[ ] Which module owns the change?
[ ] Which existing contracts are involved?
[ ] Which files are relevant?
[ ] Which architecture rules apply?
[ ] Which tests already exist?
[ ] Are there frozen decisions affecting this change?
[ ] Are there existing patterns that should be followed?
[ ] Does the requested change cross module boundaries?


J.4 Never Guess Missing Architecture
If the agent does not have enough information to implement safely:
STOP
    ↓
Identify missing information
    ↓
Request the relevant file / contract / decision
    ↓
Continue after clarification

The agent must not invent missing architecture merely to produce code.

J.5 File Inspection Rule
Before modifying an existing file, the agent should inspect the relevant current contents.
Do not assume:
file structure
class names
function signatures
imports
existing abstractions
current implementation

based only on a previous version or memory.

J.6 User File Request Rule
If implementation depends on a file that has not been provided or inspected:

Ask for the file instead of guessing its contents.

This is a mandatory StackSense development rule.

J.7 Repository Structure Check
Before making structural changes:
[ ] Inspect repository tree
[ ] Identify module boundaries
[ ] Identify package boundaries
[ ] Identify existing conventions
[ ] Identify test structure
[ ] Identify configuration structure

Do not introduce a new directory simply because it is convenient.

J.8 Absolute Import Rule
StackSense always uses absolute imports from the project root/package structure.
Preferred:
from backend.api.routes import router
from backend.shared.models import Example

Avoid introducing relative imports such as:
from .routes import router
from ..shared.models import Example

unless an explicitly approved architecture decision changes this rule.

J.9 Coding Style Before Personal Preference
The agent must follow the project's existing coding conventions before applying generic personal preferences.
For example:
Existing project convention
        ↓
Follow it

not:
AI's preferred convention
        ↓
Rewrite repository


J.10 SOLID Checklist
Before finalizing a meaningful design change:
[ ] Single Responsibility is respected.
[ ] Open/Closed principle is respected where applicable.
[ ] Liskov Substitution is respected where inheritance exists.
[ ] Interface Segregation is respected.
[ ] Dependency Inversion is respected.

SOLID principles are design guidance, not excuses for unnecessary abstraction.

J.11 Low Coupling
The agent should minimize unnecessary coupling.
Ask:
[ ] Does this module depend on another module unnecessarily?
[ ] Can the dependency direction remain clean?
[ ] Is an abstraction genuinely useful?
[ ] Is implementation detail leaking across boundaries?


J.12 High Cohesion
A module should contain responsibilities that logically belong together.
Avoid:
god classes
god services
god modules
mixed infrastructure/domain responsibilities


J.13 LLD Checklist
For non-trivial implementation, the agent should reason about:
entities
value objects
services
interfaces
dependencies
contracts
state
responsibility
failure behavior
extension points

before producing a large implementation.

J.14 Dependency Injection
When a dependency is meaningful and replaceable:
[ ] Depend on abstraction where appropriate.
[ ] Inject infrastructure dependencies.
[ ] Avoid unnecessary global state.
[ ] Keep business logic independently testable.

Do not introduce dependency injection purely for ceremony.

J.15 Design Pattern Rule
Design patterns should be introduced only when they solve an actual design problem.
Good:
Strategy
→ multiple interchangeable algorithms

Factory
→ controlled creation complexity

Adapter
→ incompatible external interface

Repository
→ appropriate persistence boundary

Bad:
FactoryFactory
AbstractSomethingFactory

without a real need.

J.16 No Pattern Overengineering
The AI must not add patterns merely because:

"This is a production-quality project."

Production quality means appropriate engineering, not maximum abstraction.

J.17 Domain Boundary
The agent must preserve the distinction between:
Domain
Application
Infrastructure
API / Interface

where the architecture defines those boundaries.
Infrastructure details should not unnecessarily leak into domain logic.

J.18 API Boundary
When modifying an API:
[ ] Verify endpoint ownership.
[ ] Verify request schema.
[ ] Verify response schema.
[ ] Verify authentication.
[ ] Verify authorization.
[ ] Verify error contract.
[ ] Verify pagination/filtering conventions where applicable.
[ ] Verify versioning.


J.19 Database Changes
Before changing persistence:
[ ] Identify owning module.
[ ] Inspect current models.
[ ] Inspect migrations.
[ ] Check relationships.
[ ] Check constraints.
[ ] Check indexes.
[ ] Check existing queries.
[ ] Consider backward compatibility.

Do not modify database structure casually.

J.20 Migration Rule
A schema change must not be hidden inside unrelated application code.
Schema evolution must follow the project's migration mechanism.

J.21 Storage Boundary
The agent must distinguish:
canonical data
derived data
cache
search index
temporary data
artifacts
logs

Do not store data in whichever backend is easiest without considering its intended role.

J.22 Knowledge Graph Rule
The agent must preserve the established Knowledge Graph boundary.
The Knowledge Graph is derived knowledge.
It must not silently become the source of truth for canonical execution/analysis information.

J.23 AI Boundary
The agent must preserve the StackSense AI responsibility boundary.
AI should not silently become responsible for:
canonical architecture truth
deterministic analysis
identity resolution
source parsing
execution truth
security decisions
authorization

AI may assist with appropriate:
explanation
summarization
natural-language rendering
engineering communication

according to the architecture.

J.24 AI Provider Abstraction
When implementing AI functionality:
[ ] Keep provider-specific implementation behind the provider boundary.
[ ] Avoid hard-coding provider details into domain logic.
[ ] Handle provider failures explicitly.
[ ] Respect timeout/rate-limit behavior.
[ ] Do not expose provider credentials.


J.25 Prompt Rule
Prompts should be treated as implementation artifacts with explicit responsibility.
The agent should avoid putting business logic exclusively into prompts when deterministic application logic is more appropriate.

J.26 AI Output Validation
AI output must not automatically be trusted as structured system truth.
Where structured output is required:
LLM
 ↓
Validation
 ↓
Normalization
 ↓
Application

The application must validate outputs before relying on them.

J.27 Security Checklist
Before finalizing security-sensitive changes:
[ ] Authentication considered.
[ ] Authorization considered.
[ ] Tenant isolation considered.
[ ] Secrets protected.
[ ] Input validated.
[ ] Sensitive output redacted.
[ ] Logs checked for secret leakage.
[ ] Privilege boundaries preserved.
[ ] Error responses do not leak sensitive information.


J.28 Multi-Tenancy Rule
Never assume that a client-provided:
organization_id
project_id
environment_id
resource_id

establishes authorization.
The backend must derive and enforce access through authenticated identity and authorization rules.

J.29 Secret Handling
The AI coding agent must never:
hard-code secrets
print secrets
commit secrets
place secrets in source
place secrets in test fixtures unnecessarily
include secrets in error messages

Use appropriate configuration/secret mechanisms.

J.30 Logging Checklist
Before adding logs:
[ ] Is the information useful?
[ ] Could it contain credentials?
[ ] Could it contain personal/private data?
[ ] Could it expose tenant data?
[ ] Is structured logging appropriate?
[ ] Is the log level appropriate?


J.31 Error Handling Checklist
Every meaningful exception path should answer:
[ ] Should it recover?
[ ] Should it retry?
[ ] Should it propagate?
[ ] Should it become a domain error?
[ ] Should it become an API error?
[ ] Should it generate a diagnostic?
[ ] Does it affect the current stage?
[ ] Does it affect the entire Analysis?


J.32 No Silent Exception Handling
Avoid:
try:
    operation()
except Exception:
    pass

unless the architecture explicitly defines the failure as safely ignorable and the reason is documented.

J.33 Retry Checklist
Before adding retry logic:
[ ] Is the failure actually transient?
[ ] Is the operation idempotent?
[ ] Is retry safe?
[ ] Is there a retry limit?
[ ] Is backoff required?
[ ] Could retry amplify an outage?


J.34 Async / Job Checklist
For background processing:
[ ] Job has clear ownership.
[ ] Job state transitions are explicit.
[ ] Duplicate execution is considered.
[ ] Retry behavior is defined.
[ ] Failure state is defined.
[ ] Cancellation behavior is defined.
[ ] Progress/state reporting is consistent.


J.35 Analysis Pipeline Checklist
For changes to Analysis:
[ ] Which stage is changing?
[ ] What does the stage consume?
[ ] What does the stage produce?
[ ] Is the output deterministic?
[ ] Does the change alter IR?
[ ] Does it alter identity?
[ ] Does it alter Architecture Model?
[ ] Does it alter findings?
[ ] Does it alter evidence?
[ ] Does it affect downstream Knowledge/AI/Report/Diagram consumers?


J.36 IR Changes
Changes to IR are high-impact.
Before modifying IR:
[ ] Find all producers.
[ ] Find all consumers.
[ ] Check serialization.
[ ] Check identity resolution.
[ ] Check architecture model construction.
[ ] Check tests.
[ ] Check persisted representations if applicable.

Do not change IR casually.

J.37 Identity Changes
Identity changes can affect:
deduplication
relationships
graph nodes
reports
retrieval
historical comparisons

Therefore identity changes require broader impact analysis.

J.38 Architecture Model Changes
Before changing the Architecture Model:
[ ] Determine whether the model is canonical or derived.
[ ] Identify consumers.
[ ] Check diagrams.
[ ] Check reports.
[ ] Check retrieval.
[ ] Check tests.


J.39 Knowledge Projection Checklist
When modifying Knowledge Graph projection:
[ ] Canonical source remains authoritative.
[ ] Projection is deterministic where appropriate.
[ ] Reprojection behavior is defined.
[ ] Stale graph data is considered.
[ ] Provenance remains available.
[ ] Retrieval consumers remain compatible.


J.40 Retrieval Checklist
Before modifying retrieval:
[ ] What evidence is being retrieved?
[ ] Which source is authoritative?
[ ] Is graph retrieval involved?
[ ] Is vector retrieval involved?
[ ] Is structured retrieval involved?
[ ] How is evidence ranked?
[ ] Can unsupported claims enter context?


J.41 RAG Checklist
For RAG changes:
[ ] Retrieval remains evidence-oriented.
[ ] Context construction remains explicit.
[ ] Source provenance is preserved.
[ ] Context size is bounded.
[ ] Irrelevant evidence is minimized.
[ ] AI is not treated as the retrieval source of truth.


J.42 Frontend Checklist
For frontend changes:
[ ] Correct route/page identified.
[ ] Existing component conventions followed.
[ ] API contract verified.
[ ] Loading state handled.
[ ] Empty state handled.
[ ] Error state handled.
[ ] Success state handled.
[ ] Long-running Analysis state handled.
[ ] Responsive behavior considered.
[ ] Accessibility considered.


J.43 Frontend Architecture Rule
The frontend must not duplicate backend business logic unnecessarily.
Prefer:
Frontend
→ presentation/orchestration

Backend
→ authoritative business rules


J.44 JSX / TSX Rule
When working with:
.js
.jsx
.ts
.tsx

the agent must respect the existing frontend architecture and conventions.
Do not introduce TypeScript merely because it is available if the affected area is intentionally JavaScript/JSX.
Likewise, do not convert large portions of the project during an unrelated feature task.

J.45 API Client Rule
Frontend API calls should use the established API client/convention.
Do not introduce a second HTTP abstraction unnecessarily.

J.46 Testing Before Completion
Every meaningful implementation should ask:
[ ] What existing tests cover this?
[ ] What new tests are required?
[ ] What failure cases exist?
[ ] What boundary cases exist?
[ ] Does the implementation break existing tests?


J.47 Test Pyramid
Where appropriate:
Unit
 ↓
Integration
 ↓
End-to-End

Use the lowest appropriate test level for the behavior being verified.

J.48 Tests Must Test Contracts
Tests should verify behavior and contracts, not merely implementation details.
Prefer:
given input
→ expected behavior

over tests that only verify internal line-by-line structure.

J.49 Regression Protection
When fixing a bug:
Bug
 ↓
Reproduce
 ↓
Write/identify regression test
 ↓
Fix
 ↓
Run test

The agent should avoid claiming a bug is fixed without validation.

J.50 Static Checks
Where configured, the agent should run appropriate:
linting
formatting
type checks
static analysis

before completion.

J.51 Test Execution Rule
The agent must distinguish:
tests not run
tests failed
tests passed
tests partially run

It must never report:

"All tests pass"

unless the relevant tests were actually executed successfully.

J.52 Build Verification
For changes affecting builds:
[ ] Build attempted.
[ ] Build result verified.
[ ] Build warnings considered.
[ ] Generated output checked where relevant.


J.53 Dependency Changes
Before adding a dependency:
[ ] Is it genuinely required?
[ ] Is an existing dependency capable of solving the problem?
[ ] Does it fit project architecture?
[ ] Does it introduce security risk?
[ ] Does it increase deployment complexity?
[ ] Is licensing acceptable?
[ ] Does it affect project size/performance?


J.54 No Dependency Bloat
Do not add a library for trivial functionality that can be implemented safely with existing project capabilities.

J.55 Refactoring Checklist
For refactoring:
[ ] Preserve behavior unless behavior change is intentional.
[ ] Identify all consumers.
[ ] Keep public contracts stable unless explicitly changed.
[ ] Run relevant tests.
[ ] Avoid unrelated cleanup.


J.56 Scope Discipline
The AI agent must stay within the requested scope.
If asked:

Fix the authentication bug.

Do not silently:
rewrite the entire authentication module
change database architecture
rename unrelated APIs
restructure frontend

unless required or explicitly approved.

J.57 Opportunistic Cleanup
Small cleanup may be acceptable when directly related.
Large unrelated cleanup should be proposed separately.

J.58 Architecture Change Detection
If implementation reveals that the existing architecture cannot support the requested feature cleanly:
STOP
    ↓
Explain the conflict
    ↓
Identify affected architecture boundary
    ↓
Propose options
    ↓
Obtain approval
    ↓
Implement

Do not silently redesign the architecture.

J.59 Frozen Architecture Rule
Frozen architecture decisions must be treated as constraints.
The AI agent may identify:
implementation conflict
bug
missing detail
inconsistency

but must not silently override the frozen decision.

J.60 Contradiction Handling
If two project documents appear to contradict each other:
Do not guess.
Do not silently choose one.
Identify the contradiction.
Request clarification / inspect authoritative source.


J.61 Existing Code vs Architecture
If existing code violates the architecture:
Existing code
      ≠
Architecture contract

the agent must determine whether it is:
technical debt
unfinished implementation
intentional exception
outdated documentation

before making broad changes.

J.62 Git Checklist
Before making a substantial change:
[ ] Check current branch.
[ ] Check working tree.
[ ] Understand existing changes.
[ ] Avoid overwriting unrelated user work.


J.63 Never Destroy User Changes
The AI agent must not blindly use destructive commands such as:
git reset --hard
git clean -fd

or equivalent operations when they could destroy user work.
Explicit confirmation is required for destructive operations.

J.64 Commit Awareness
If the user asks for a commit:
[ ] Review diff.
[ ] Ensure only intended changes are included.
[ ] Run appropriate validation.
[ ] Write a meaningful commit message.


J.65 No Fake Validation
Never claim:
"tested"
"verified"
"build passed"
"deployment successful"

without actually performing the relevant operation.

J.66 Documentation Checklist
When implementation changes architecture or externally visible behavior:
[ ] Update relevant documentation.
[ ] Update API documentation if necessary.
[ ] Update diagrams if necessary.
[ ] Update ADR/architecture contract if explicitly approved.
[ ] Update examples where needed.


J.67 Diagram Synchronization
If a change affects a canonical diagram:
[ ] Identify affected diagram.
[ ] Determine whether it is frozen.
[ ] Update it if required.
[ ] Keep source and rendered artifact consistent.


J.68 Report Synchronization
If a change modifies report structure:
[ ] Report model
[ ] Report renderer
[ ] API contract
[ ] Frontend display
[ ] Tests

must be considered.

J.69 Observability Checklist
For meaningful backend operations:
[ ] Appropriate logs exist.
[ ] Important state transitions are observable.
[ ] Errors are classified.
[ ] Correlation identifiers are available.
[ ] Sensitive information is redacted.


J.70 Performance Checklist
Before introducing potentially expensive logic:
[ ] Complexity considered.
[ ] Database queries considered.
[ ] N+1 behavior considered.
[ ] Large repository behavior considered.
[ ] Memory usage considered.
[ ] Async/background processing considered.


J.71 Repository Scale
The agent should remember that StackSense may process repositories significantly larger than the project's own source tree.
Avoid designs that assume:
few files
small files
small dependency graph
small number of entities

unless that limitation is explicitly part of the architecture.

J.72 Large Artifact Rule
Do not load or process enormous artifacts unnecessarily.
Prefer:
streaming
bounded reads
chunking
metadata-first processing

where appropriate.

J.73 Security of Repository Code
Repository source must be treated as untrusted input.
The AI agent should not introduce functionality that executes arbitrary repository code simply to analyze it unless the architecture explicitly requires controlled execution.

J.74 External Commands
Before executing repository-provided commands:
[ ] Is execution actually necessary?
[ ] Is it safe?
[ ] What does it execute?
[ ] Could it modify the repository?
[ ] Could it access secrets?
[ ] Could it access the host?


J.75 AI Agent Tool Safety
The coding agent should prefer inspection and deterministic tooling over speculative modification.
Conceptually:
Inspect
 ↓
Understand
 ↓
Plan
 ↓
Modify
 ↓
Validate

not:
Guess
 ↓
Modify everything
 ↓
Hope tests pass


J.76 Implementation Plan
For a non-trivial task, the agent should formulate a concise plan covering:
1. files/components affected
2. architectural responsibility
3. implementation approach
4. tests
5. validation


J.77 Minimal Change Principle
When multiple implementations satisfy the architecture:

Prefer the simplest implementation that preserves the required contracts and future extensibility.

Do not maximize code volume.

J.78 No Premature Optimization
Performance optimization should be evidence-driven unless the architecture explicitly requires a known performance constraint.

J.79 No Premature Abstraction
Do not create abstractions solely because another implementation might theoretically be needed later.

J.80 Maintainability Rule
Code should be understandable by another engineer without needing the AI agent's original reasoning.
Prefer:
clear names
small responsibilities
explicit contracts
predictable control flow
appropriate abstractions


J.81 Comments
Comments should explain:
why

rather than simply:
what

Avoid comments that merely restate obvious code.

J.82 TODO Rule
AI-generated TODOs should be meaningful.
Avoid:
# TODO: improve this

Prefer:
# TODO: Replace polling with event-driven completion once the analysis event contract is finalized.

when a real future dependency exists.

J.83 Dead Code
Do not leave unused AI-generated code merely because it "might be useful later."
Remove:
unused imports
unused functions
unused variables
dead branches
temporary debugging code

when within task scope.

J.84 Debugging Checklist
When debugging:
[ ] Reproduce the problem.
[ ] Identify the failing layer.
[ ] Trace the error boundary.
[ ] Check logs/stack trace.
[ ] Inspect relevant code.
[ ] Form a hypothesis.
[ ] Make the smallest appropriate change.
[ ] Reproduce the test.
[ ] Run regression tests.


J.85 No Symptom-Only Fixes
Do not fix a symptom at the wrong layer.
Example:
Database error

should not automatically result in:
Frontend retry loop

if the actual issue is an invalid backend transaction.

J.86 Cross-Layer Changes
When a change legitimately crosses layers:
[ ] API
[ ] Application
[ ] Domain
[ ] Infrastructure
[ ] Database
[ ] Frontend
[ ] Tests

must be evaluated deliberately.

J.87 AI-Generated Code Review
Before presenting generated code as complete, the agent should review it as if another engineer wrote it.
Ask:
[ ] Is the design correct?
[ ] Is it unnecessarily complex?
[ ] Does it follow project conventions?
[ ] Are imports correct?
[ ] Are error paths handled?
[ ] Are security implications considered?
[ ] Are tests sufficient?
[ ] Is anything fabricated?


J.88 Hallucination Prevention
The agent must never fabricate:
files
classes
functions
APIs
database tables
configuration values
existing behavior
test results
deployment state

If uncertain:

Inspect the repository or ask for the relevant file.


J.89 Source Inspection Priority
When determining how something currently works, prefer:
Actual source code
      ↓
Tests
      ↓
Configuration
      ↓
Architecture documentation
      ↓
General assumptions

General assumptions should never override concrete repository evidence.

J.90 Architecture Document Authority
When the architecture is explicitly frozen, the agent should use it as the design constraint while still verifying implementation details against the repository.

J.91 User Intent
If the user's requested implementation conflicts with an existing contract, the agent should explain the conflict rather than silently choosing one interpretation.

J.92 Ambiguity Rule
If a request has multiple materially different interpretations:
Ask

rather than making a large irreversible assumption.
For small, low-risk implementation details, a reasonable interpretation may be used.

J.93 Implementation Completion Checklist
Before saying the task is complete:
[ ] Requested behavior implemented.
[ ] Correct files changed.
[ ] No unrelated changes.
[ ] Architecture respected.
[ ] Absolute imports respected.
[ ] Error handling implemented.
[ ] Security considered.
[ ] Tests added/updated where appropriate.
[ ] Tests run.
[ ] Build/type/lint checks run where relevant.
[ ] Documentation updated where necessary.
[ ] No secrets exposed.
[ ] No fabricated validation claims.


J.94 Final Response Checklist
The AI agent's completion response should communicate:
What changed
Files affected
Important design decisions
Tests run
Validation result
Known limitations
Anything requiring user attention

Do not bury important failures.

J.95 If Tests Fail
If implementation is complete but tests fail:
Do not claim completion without qualification.

State:
implementation status
failing tests
failure cause if known
next action


J.96 If Validation Cannot Run
If a required tool/environment is unavailable:
State that validation was not run.
Explain why.
Do not fabricate success.


J.97 If Implementation Is Blocked
If blocked by missing information:
State exactly what is missing.
Request the specific file/contract/information.
Do not fabricate it.


J.98 AI Coding Agent Decision Tree
The canonical decision process is:
Task received
     ↓
Understand scope
     ↓
Inspect relevant repository
     ↓
Architecture conflict?
   ┌───────┴───────┐
  Yes             No
   ↓               ↓
Ask/resolve      Plan
   ↓               ↓
 Approved?        Implement
   │               ↓
   └──────────→ Validate
                   ↓
             Tests pass?
              ┌────┴────┐
             No        Yes
              ↓          ↓
          Debug/fix    Review
              ↓          ↓
          Validate    Complete


J.99 AI Coding Agent Golden Rules
The following rules summarize the entire checklist:
1. Inspect before modifying.

2. Never guess the contents of a file you have not seen when that information is required.

3. Ask for the file when necessary.

4. Follow the frozen architecture.

5. Never silently redesign architecture.

6. Always use absolute imports in the project.

7. Prefer low coupling and high cohesion.

8. Apply SOLID principles appropriately.

9. Use LLD and design patterns only where they solve real problems.

10. Avoid premature abstraction.

11. Avoid unnecessary dependencies.

12. Keep domain, application, infrastructure, API, and frontend responsibilities appropriately separated.

13. Treat repository contents as untrusted input.

14. Never expose secrets.

15. Never silently swallow meaningful exceptions.

16. Classify failures correctly.

17. Retry only when retry is justified.

18. Keep retries bounded.

19. Preserve deterministic analysis as the source of truth.

20. Keep AI behind the approved responsibility boundary.

21. Validate AI outputs before trusting structured results.

22. Never let AI invent canonical system facts.

23. Preserve tenant and authorization boundaries.

24. Keep frontend and backend contracts synchronized.

25. Test meaningful behavior.

26. Never claim tests passed unless they actually passed.

27. Never claim a build/deployment succeeded unless it was actually verified.

28. Protect user changes and avoid destructive Git operations.

29. Keep changes within requested scope.

30. Update affected documentation and diagrams when required.

31. Prefer the simplest architecture-compliant solution.

32. Optimize only when justified.

33. Preserve maintainability.

34. Make failures visible and actionable.

35. When uncertain about architecture or existing implementation, inspect or ask rather than fabricate.


J.100 Final Principle

The AI coding agent is a highly capable implementation assistant operating inside StackSense's architecture—not an autonomous architect.

Its responsibility is:
Understand
   ↓
Inspect
   ↓
Plan
   ↓
Implement
   ↓
Validate
   ↓
Report honestly

while continuously respecting:
Architecture
Contracts
SOLID
LLD
Low Coupling
High Cohesion
Security
Testing
Absolute Imports
Scope Discipline
Human Approval

The final rule is therefore:

AI may write the code, but the architecture decides what the code is allowed to become.

END OF APPENDIX J — AI CODING AGENT CHECKLIST



APPENDIX K — ARCHITECTURE CHANGE REQUEST TEMPLATE
K.1 Purpose
This appendix defines the canonical Architecture Change Request (ACR) process and template for StackSense.
The purpose is to provide a controlled mechanism for proposing changes to:
Architecture
Module boundaries
Domain models
API contracts
Event contracts
Storage contracts
Analysis pipeline
IR
Identity system
Knowledge architecture
AI responsibility boundary
Frontend architecture
Security model
Deployment architecture
Observability
Testing strategy

Architecture changes must be deliberate rather than emerging accidentally through implementation.

K.2 Core Principle

An architectural change must be proposed, understood, evaluated, approved, and then implemented.

The expected flow is:
Need Identified
      ↓
Architecture Change Request
      ↓
Impact Analysis
      ↓
Alternatives
      ↓
Decision
      ↓
Approval
      ↓
Implementation
      ↓
Validation
      ↓
Documentation / Diagram Update
      ↓
Architecture Freeze / Revision


K.3 When an ACR Is Required
An Architecture Change Request should be created when a proposed change materially affects:
System boundaries
Module boundaries
Public APIs
Core domain entities
Canonical data models
IR
Identity semantics
Analysis lifecycle
Job orchestration
Knowledge Graph
Retrieval architecture
AI responsibility boundary
Storage strategy
Security / tenancy
Deployment model
Cross-cutting contracts


K.4 When an ACR Is Usually Not Required
A full architecture change request is generally unnecessary for:
bug fixes within an existing boundary
minor refactoring preserving contracts
test additions
documentation typo fixes
UI styling changes
internal implementation cleanup
performance improvements that preserve architecture

provided the existing contracts remain intact.

K.5 Architecture Change vs Implementation Change
The key distinction is:
Implementation Change
→ changes how an existing contract is implemented.

Architecture Change
→ changes what the contract, boundary, responsibility, or system structure is.

Example:
Replacing one parser implementation
→ implementation change

Changing the IR contract
→ architecture change


K.6 ACR Identification
Every approved architecture change should receive a unique identifier.
Recommended format:
ACR-001
ACR-002
ACR-003
...

The numbering must remain stable once assigned.

K.7 ACR Status
Canonical statuses:
DRAFT
PROPOSED
UNDER_REVIEW
APPROVED
REJECTED
DEFERRED
IMPLEMENTING
IMPLEMENTED
VERIFIED
SUPERSEDED


K.8 Status Meaning
DRAFT
The request is being prepared.
PROPOSED
The request is ready for review.
UNDER_REVIEW
Impact and alternatives are being evaluated.
APPROVED
The architectural decision has been accepted.
REJECTED
The proposed change will not be implemented.
DEFERRED
The change may be reconsidered later.
IMPLEMENTING
The approved change is currently being implemented.
IMPLEMENTED
Implementation is complete.
VERIFIED
Implementation and architectural consistency have been validated.
SUPERSEDED
A later architecture decision replaces this request.

K.9 ACR Template
Every Architecture Change Request should use the following structure.
# ACR-XXX — <Change Title>

Status:
Date:
Author:
Reviewer:
Decision Owner:

## 1. Change Summary

<Short description of the proposed architectural change.>

## 2. Problem Statement

<What problem requires this change?>

## 3. Current Architecture

<Describe the existing architecture relevant to the change.>

## 4. Proposed Architecture

<Describe the proposed architecture.>

## 5. Motivation

<Why is the proposed architecture better or necessary?>

## 6. Scope

<What is affected?>

## 7. Non-Goals

<What is explicitly not changing?>

## 8. Affected Components

<List affected modules, services, contracts, storage, frontend, etc.>

## 9. Contract Changes

<List API, event, domain, storage, IR, identity, or other contract changes.>

## 10. Alternatives Considered

<List viable alternatives and why they were not selected.>

## 11. Trade-offs

<Benefits, costs, risks, and complexity.>

## 12. Security Impact

<Security and tenancy implications.>

## 13. Performance Impact

<Performance and scalability implications.>

## 14. Reliability Impact

<Failure modes, retries, degradation, recovery implications.>

## 15. Data / Migration Impact

<Schema, migration, compatibility, or historical-data implications.>

## 16. Testing Impact

<Tests that must be added or modified.>

## 17. Documentation / Diagram Impact

<List documentation and diagrams requiring updates.>

## 18. Implementation Plan

<Ordered implementation steps.>

## 19. Rollback / Recovery Plan

<How the change can be reverted or recovered if necessary.>

## 20. Decision

<Approved / Rejected / Deferred and rationale.>

## 21. Approval

<Approval information.>

## 22. Verification

<Implementation and validation results.>


K.10 Section 1 — Change Summary
The summary should be short and precise.
Bad:
We want to improve the architecture.

Good:
Replace synchronous Analysis execution with queue-backed
background execution so long-running repository analyses do
not block API requests.


K.11 Section 2 — Problem Statement
The request must explain the actual problem.
Include:
current limitation
observed behavior
technical constraint
user impact
architectural limitation

Avoid proposing the solution before clearly describing the problem.

K.12 Section 3 — Current Architecture
Document the current state before proposing a replacement.
Include:
current components
current data flow
current contracts
current dependencies
current limitations

The purpose is to prevent solving a problem that already has an existing architectural solution.

K.13 Section 4 — Proposed Architecture
Describe the intended target state.
Where useful:
diagram
data flow
module relationships
new contracts
state transitions

The proposal must be sufficiently precise for implementation planning.

K.14 Section 5 — Motivation
Explain why the change is necessary.
Possible motivations:
scalability
correctness
security
maintainability
performance
reliability
product requirement
new capability
architectural inconsistency
technical debt


K.15 Section 6 — Scope
Clearly define what the change affects.
Example:
Backend Analysis orchestration
Job queue
Worker lifecycle
Analysis API
Frontend Analysis status handling


K.16 Non-Goals
Every significant ACR should explicitly state what it does not change.
Example:
This change does not modify:

- Analysis Engine rules
- IR structure
- Knowledge Graph schema
- AI provider boundary
- repository parsing

This prevents scope creep.

K.17 Section 8 — Affected Components
Identify affected areas explicitly.
Possible categories:
Backend
Frontend
Database
API
Events
Workers
Scheduler
Storage
Search
Knowledge Graph
AI
Security
Observability
Deployment
Tests
Documentation


K.18 Section 9 — Contract Changes
This is one of the most important sections.
Explicitly identify whether the change affects:
API Contract
Domain Contract
IR Contract
Identity Contract
Event Contract
Job Contract
Storage Contract
Knowledge Contract
AI Provider Contract
Report Contract
Diagram Contract
Frontend Contract

Use:
UNCHANGED
MODIFIED
NEW
REMOVED

where appropriate.

K.19 Contract Change Example
API Contract:
MODIFIED

Job Contract:
NEW

Analysis Contract:
UNCHANGED

IR Contract:
UNCHANGED

Knowledge Contract:
UNCHANGED


K.20 Section 10 — Alternatives Considered
An architectural proposal should not assume the first solution is automatically the best.
At least the meaningful alternatives should be considered.
Example:
Option A — Keep synchronous execution
Option B — Queue-backed workers
Option C — Serverless execution


K.21 Alternative Evaluation
Each alternative should be evaluated against relevant criteria:
Complexity
Performance
Scalability
Reliability
Security
Maintainability
Development effort
Operational cost
Architectural consistency


K.22 Rejected Alternatives
Explain why rejected alternatives were not selected.
Avoid:
"We didn't like it."

Prefer:
"Rejected because it introduces a second execution model
without providing a requirement that cannot be satisfied by
the existing worker architecture."


K.23 Section 11 — Trade-offs
Every meaningful architectural change has trade-offs.
Document:
Benefits
Costs
Complexity
Operational burden
Technical risks
Future flexibility
Migration effort


K.24 No "Free" Architecture Changes
The ACR should explicitly acknowledge meaningful costs.
Example:
Benefit:
API responsiveness improves.

Cost:
Queue infrastructure and worker lifecycle management become required.


K.25 Section 12 — Security Impact
Security impact must be explicitly evaluated.
Consider:
authentication
authorization
tenant isolation
secrets
data exposure
network boundaries
privilege changes
audit requirements


K.26 Section 13 — Performance Impact
Consider:
latency
throughput
CPU
memory
database load
network traffic
queue depth
storage
repository scale

Do not claim performance improvements without evidence or a justified architectural basis.

K.27 Section 14 — Reliability Impact
Consider:
new failure modes
retry behavior
timeouts
partial failure
graceful degradation
recovery
data integrity
availability

The Error / Failure Classification defined in Appendix I should be used.

K.28 Section 15 — Data / Migration Impact
Identify whether the change affects:
database schema
existing records
stored artifacts
search indexes
Knowledge Graph
historical Analysis data
API compatibility
migration scripts


K.29 Migration Categories
A change may require:
NO MIGRATION
FORWARD MIGRATION
BACKFILL
REINDEX
DATA TRANSFORMATION
DUAL READ
DUAL WRITE
ROLLING MIGRATION

Only use the strategies actually required.

K.30 Backward Compatibility
Explicitly identify whether compatibility is:
FULL
PARTIAL
BREAKING
NOT APPLICABLE


K.31 Breaking Changes
Breaking changes require explicit acknowledgement.
Examples:
API field removal
event schema change
database column removal
IR structure change
identity semantics change
frontend contract change

Never introduce a breaking architectural change silently.

K.32 Section 16 — Testing Impact
Specify what validation is required.
Potential levels:
Unit
Integration
Contract
End-to-End
Migration
Security
Performance
Failure Injection
Deployment


K.33 Architecture Test Impact
If an architecture contract changes, tests should verify the new contract rather than merely preserving old implementation behavior.

K.34 Section 17 — Documentation / Diagram Impact
Identify affected documentation.
Examples:
Architecture specification
API documentation
ADR
Diagram catalog
System architecture diagram
Backend diagram
Frontend diagram
Deployment diagram
Runbooks
README


K.35 Frozen Diagrams
If a frozen diagram is affected:
ACR
 ↓
Approval
 ↓
Diagram revision

The diagram must not be silently modified before the architecture change is approved.

K.36 Section 18 — Implementation Plan
Implementation should be broken into logical steps.
Example:
1. Introduce Job abstraction.
2. Add queue adapter.
3. Implement worker.
4. Move Analysis execution behind worker boundary.
5. Update API status handling.
6. Update frontend progress UI.
7. Add retry handling.
8. Add integration tests.
9. Update diagrams/documentation.


K.37 Implementation Order
Where dependencies exist, implementation should follow dependency order.
For example:
Contract
   ↓
Domain
   ↓
Application
   ↓
Infrastructure
   ↓
API
   ↓
Frontend
   ↓
Tests / Validation

The exact order depends on the change.

K.38 Section 19 — Rollback / Recovery Plan
Every risky architecture change should explain how to recover.
Possible strategies:
feature flag
configuration rollback
database rollback
deployment rollback
compatibility layer
migration reversal
rebuild derived data


K.39 Rollback Limitations
If a migration cannot safely be reversed, say so explicitly.
Example:
The schema migration is irreversible after column removal.
Rollback therefore requires restoring from the previous schema/data backup.


K.40 Section 20 — Decision
The final decision must be explicit:
APPROVED
REJECTED
DEFERRED

with rationale.

K.41 Approval Rule
No implementation of a material architectural change should begin under the assumption that it is approved merely because an AI agent proposed it.
Approval must be explicit.

K.42 Section 21 — Approval
Record:
Decision:
Decision Date:
Approved By:

For the project's workflow, the relevant human decision-maker should remain the final authority.

K.43 Section 22 — Verification
After implementation, record:
implementation status
tests
validation
migration result
deployment verification
diagram/documentation updates
known limitations


K.44 ACR Lifecycle
The complete lifecycle is:
DRAFT
  ↓
PROPOSED
  ↓
UNDER_REVIEW
  ↓
APPROVED / REJECTED / DEFERRED
  ↓
IMPLEMENTING
  ↓
IMPLEMENTED
  ↓
VERIFIED


K.45 Rejected Request
A rejected ACR should remain documented.
Do not delete it simply because it was rejected.
The reasoning may prevent the same discussion from being repeated later.

K.46 Deferred Request
A deferred request should record why it was deferred.
Example:
Deferred until:
- workload scale requirements are established
- current implementation is completed
- deployment model is finalized


K.47 Superseded Request
If a later architecture decision replaces an older request:
ACR-007
→ SUPERSEDED BY ACR-014

The relationship should be preserved.

K.48 ACR and Existing ADRs
An ACR may eventually result in an Architecture Decision Record or equivalent frozen architecture documentation.
Conceptually:
ACR
 ↓
Review
 ↓
Decision
 ↓
Architecture Decision / Frozen Contract

The exact documentation mechanism must follow the project's established architecture-documentation structure.

K.49 ACR and Code
Code should implement an approved architecture change.
It should not become the mechanism by which an architecture change is accidentally introduced.
Bad:
Code change
 ↓
Architecture changed implicitly

Preferred:
ACR
 ↓
Approval
 ↓
Code change


K.50 ACR and AI Coding Agents
AI coding agents must recognize architecture changes.
If a requested implementation would modify:
module boundaries
contracts
data models
security boundaries
AI responsibility
system lifecycle

the agent should identify it as a potential ACR rather than silently implementing it.

K.51 AI Agent Behavior
The agent should say, conceptually:

"This appears to change the existing architecture because it modifies X. I need the relevant architecture decision/approval before implementing it."

It should not simply proceed because the change appears technically convenient.

K.52 Small Changes
Not every change requires formal ACR overhead.
The agent should distinguish:
Small implementation detail

from:
Material architectural change

This prevents process bureaucracy from becoming excessive.

K.53 Architecture Change Threshold
An ACR is strongly recommended when a change alters any of:
source of truth
responsibility boundary
dependency direction
public contract
security boundary
tenant boundary
persistent data model
analysis lifecycle
AI boundary
major deployment topology


K.54 Emergency Changes
A production emergency may require immediate implementation.
In that situation:
Emergency Fix
      ↓
Restore Service
      ↓
Document Change
      ↓
Retrospective ACR
      ↓
Architecture Reconciliation

Emergency status does not mean the architecture change should remain undocumented.

K.55 Temporary Architecture
If an emergency solution is intentionally temporary, record:
Temporary
Reason
Expected lifetime
Replacement plan
Owner
Removal criteria

Do not allow temporary architecture to become permanent accidentally.

K.56 Architecture Drift
An ACR should be created when implementation repeatedly requires behavior inconsistent with the frozen architecture.
This may indicate:
architecture is incorrect
implementation is incorrect
requirements changed
architecture is incomplete

The discrepancy must be evaluated rather than patched indefinitely.

K.57 Multiple Changes
Related architectural changes may be grouped into one ACR when they form a single coherent decision.
Do not combine unrelated architecture changes merely to reduce documentation.

K.58 ACR Dependencies
An ACR may depend on another:
ACR-012
requires
ACR-009

Dependencies should be recorded when they affect implementation order.

K.59 ACR Impact Levels
For practical use, classify the size of an architecture change:
LOW
MEDIUM
HIGH
CRITICAL

LOW
Limited module impact.
MEDIUM
Multiple modules or contracts affected.
HIGH
Cross-cutting architecture affected.
CRITICAL
Security, data integrity, source-of-truth, or fundamental system architecture affected.

K.60 ACR Review Depth
Review depth should correspond to impact.
LOW
→ local review

MEDIUM
→ module/system review

HIGH
→ architecture review

CRITICAL
→ explicit architectural and security/data review


K.61 Architecture Change Checklist
Before approval:
[ ] Problem clearly defined.
[ ] Current architecture documented.
[ ] Proposed architecture documented.
[ ] Scope defined.
[ ] Non-goals defined.
[ ] Alternatives considered.
[ ] Trade-offs documented.
[ ] Contract impact identified.
[ ] Security impact evaluated.
[ ] Performance impact evaluated.
[ ] Reliability impact evaluated.
[ ] Migration impact evaluated.
[ ] Testing impact evaluated.
[ ] Documentation impact identified.
[ ] Diagram impact identified.
[ ] Implementation plan defined.
[ ] Rollback/recovery plan considered.
[ ] Dependencies identified.
[ ] Approval obtained.


K.62 Implementation Checklist
After approval:
[ ] Architecture contract updated where required.
[ ] Implementation follows approved design.
[ ] Existing unrelated behavior preserved.
[ ] Tests updated.
[ ] Migration executed where required.
[ ] API contracts updated.
[ ] Frontend contracts updated.
[ ] Diagrams updated.
[ ] Documentation updated.
[ ] Observability updated.
[ ] Security controls validated.


K.63 Verification Checklist
Before marking an ACR VERIFIED:
[ ] Implementation matches approved architecture.
[ ] Tests pass.
[ ] Relevant integration tests pass.
[ ] Contract compatibility verified.
[ ] Security behavior verified.
[ ] Migration verified.
[ ] Failure behavior verified.
[ ] Observability verified.
[ ] Diagrams synchronized.
[ ] Documentation synchronized.
[ ] No unresolved architecture drift remains.

For everyday use, the following compact template may be copied directly:

Status:

Date:

Reviewer:
Decision Owner:

<What problem are we solving?>

## 2. Current Architecture
<What exists today?>

## 3. Proposed Change
<What should change?>

## 4. Motivation
<Why is this necessary?>

## 5. Scope
<What is affected?>

K.65 Final ACR Rules
The following rules are mandatory:
1. Material architectural changes must be explicitly identified.

2. Architecture must not change accidentally through implementation.

3. Every significant architecture change must have a traceable request.

4. ACR identifiers must remain stable.

5. Current architecture must be documented before proposing a replacement.

6. Proposed architecture must be explicit enough to implement.

7. Scope and non-goals must be defined.

8. Alternatives must be considered for meaningful architectural decisions.

9. Trade-offs must be documented honestly.

10. Contract impact must be explicitly identified.

11. Security impact must be explicitly evaluated.

12. Data and migration impact must be explicitly evaluated.

13. Reliability and failure impact must be explicitly evaluated.

14. Testing impact must be explicitly evaluated.

15. Documentation and diagram impact must be identified.

16. Breaking changes must be explicitly acknowledged.

17. Material architecture changes require explicit approval.

18. AI coding agents must not silently override frozen architecture.

19. AI coding agents must request clarification when required architectural information is missing.

20. Implementation must follow the approved architecture.

21. Emergency changes must be documented retrospectively.

22. Temporary architecture must have explicit removal criteria.

23. Rejected and deferred decisions should remain traceable.

24. Superseded decisions must retain their historical relationship.

25. Architecture changes must be verified after implementation.

26. ACRs must not become unnecessary bureaucracy for ordinary implementation changes.

27. The simplest architecture-compliant solution should be preferred.

28. If the architecture change cannot be evaluated from the available information, inspect or request the relevant files/contracts rather than guessing.


K.66 Final Principle

Architecture should evolve deliberately, not accidentally.

The canonical StackSense change process is:
Problem
   ↓
Change Request
   ↓
Current State
   ↓
Proposed State
   ↓
Alternatives
   ↓
Impact Analysis
   ↓
Approval
   ↓
Implementation
   ↓
Validation
   ↓
Documentation
   ↓
New Frozen State

An Architecture Change Request therefore serves as the bridge between the architecture we have, the architecture we want, and the controlled implementation that moves us from one to the other.

No silent architecture changes. No guessed contracts. No implementation-driven redesign. Propose, review, approve, implement, verify.
